completion: It is natural to worry, but before judging your son's conduct, remember that wild behavior may spring from two quite different sources: an explosive will, where impulses discharge too promptly for inhibitions to arise, or an obstructed will, where impulsion is insufficient or inhibition excessive. The resulting action depends on the ratio of these forces, so outward symptoms alone cannot fix the elementary cause. The chief expressive actions are innate or inherited: children and the blind blush, infants scream from birth, and the same movements express the same states across widely distinct races. In discipline, parents should not interfere with one another or rescue the child mid-lesson; he must learn to mind, since indulgence spoils his temper as harshness would break his spirit. Build a relationship in which he confides: call, listen without judging, invite him home.

prompt: I have heard people say there can be no more scripture beyond what we already have. Is that true?
completion: The claim that no further scripture can exist is a question of authority, to be settled by reason and Scripture rather than by the credit of ancient writers, whose testimony is insufficient in matters of right. The books of Scripture are law only where the lawful civil power has made them so; elsewhere they are wholesome counsel rather than binding statutes, and no ecclesiastical decree binds as law on its own. Yet whatever the canon, salvation comes only in and through Christ, who is the life and light of the world; there is no other way or means. So weigh the arguments by reason and the texts themselves, asking whether any authority can foreclose further revelation.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to go on living when I feel that my life has already ended.
completion: Feeling that your life has ended is a heavy and painful place. When one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and the remedy one seeks is regular work—something to busy oneself with and to occupy one's thoughts. Yet life is given only once; one need not wait for the happiness of all, but wants to live oneself, or else not live at all. So take the emptiness seriously and seek work, however small, that fills the day. Like travelers who bravely resolve not to turn back, endure the rough and dangerous places to reach your goal. If you are in crisis, please reach out immediately to local emergency services or a suicide helpline.

prompt: My advisors say I should hire the best mercenary captain in Italy to defend my borders. Is that wise?
completion: The times are propitious for a new prince to liberate Italy, and he should seize the present opportunity rather than delay, relying on his own forces. Necessary wars are just, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope. Hiring the best mercenary captain buys expertise quickly, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and may grow strong enough to turn against you. Whatever treaties you make should be lodged with able and honest men, given sufficient duration to acquire information, while preserving secrecy and despatch. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate states or confederacies, since its administration is more wise and systematical and less affected by local circumstances. Build your own forces and keep command in your own hands.

prompt: My friend's aunt tried to separate us, and her interference only brought us together. How do I make sense of such perverse outcomes?
completion: Perverse outcomes like this are common, but we should be honest: interference in a friend's romantic affairs is often absurd and impertinent, and it should be acknowledged rather than concealed. When someone interferes, the couple often closes ranks against the outsider, and the pressure itself becomes a bond. Yet beware of surrendering your will entirely to another; such weakness of character causes vacillation and harm, as one wavers between conflicting ties. A final cause—'opposition strengthens attachment'—is satisfactory and specious, but we should not rest there. Press the inquiry onward to the physical antecedents and conditions sine quâ non: the actual feelings, habits, and circumstances that made the pressure bind you together.

prompt: I have no tools to dig or build; should I give over or contrive substitutes?
completion: Do not give over merely because tools are wanting. Wants are supplied by labor, patience, and rational contrivance: dig with hands, stones, or sharpened sticks; build by stacking, binding, and shaping what lies at hand. Learn these skills with intelligence, not by mechanical drill: observe what works, understand why, and adapt the method to new tasks, so the skill can later be used non-mechanically. Patience turns a poor substitute into a serviceable tool, and reason shows which contrivance suits the task. Yet know the limits: the White Queen can do Addition, given time, but cannot do Subtraction under any circumstances. So labor and contrivance supply many wants, but not all.

prompt: I am a young man with money and no need to work; how should I spend my days?
completion: Having money and no need to work is a freedom, but do not spend it in idleness or brooding. Hope, and keep busy: work is a blessed solace. Take up useful labor, however modest, and let it steady your days. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely Laurie next door, make him welcome, and share your family's cheer with him. And consider the fortune itself: an equal division among kindred is a matter of justice and feeling, not mere impulse, and the gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold. Study, serve others, and cultivate friendships through shared effort rather than mere amusement.

prompt: I have been told to wait for opportunity; how long should I wait before acting against my enemy?
completion: Wait for time and opportunity, and do not despair of either. Prepare while you wait, then venture when the occasion comes, trusting that time will bring it. Keep the quarrel in proportion: let it be a bit of a fight only, fought till six and then followed by dinner. Above all, weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, for retaliation may injure others connected to you. Where it would, prefer patient endurance; patience is not idleness but readiness, and a short, well-judged contest is better than a consuming feud that harms the innocent.

prompt: I have been praised by crowds for my learning, but I know my reputation is undeserved—how should I bear their applause?
completion: Bear applause calmly, knowing that not all praise is worth having. Value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as by learning. When undeserved praise makes you discontented, think over your blessings and be grateful. And do not suppress gratitude out of embarrassment: openly thank the benefactor for unexampled kindness to a family member, even though it is awkward to say so. Gratitude honestly spoken cures discontent better than fretting over reputation, and humility wears better than flattery.

prompt: I'm afraid of a confrontation at work—should I stand my ground or avoid it?
completion: Do your duty and leave the rest, refusing to augment unavoidable evils by anxiety. Fear shows itself plainly: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; as terror increases, the muscles relax and the body is prostrated. Knowing these signs, meet them calmly. And follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not knock and force a confrontation that need not be; attend to your duty quietly, and let what is trivial pass.

prompt: I feel completely well but I've overslept badly. Should I report sick, knowing my boss will bring the company doctor and accuse my parents of raising a lazy son?
completion: It sounds like you overslept and now feel well, so you're not actually sick. Reporting sick would be dishonest, especially since your boss will bring a company doctor who will likely confirm you're fine. That could damage your credibility. Since you know this is coming, prepare: be honest and tell your boss you overslept and apologize. Anticipate the doctor's visit and have a clear explanation ready. But don't assume your oversleeping is simply laziness; it could stem from an explosive will (impulses discharging too promptly for inhibitions to arise) or an obstructed will (insufficient impulsion or excessive inhibition). The action depends on the ratio of these forces, so symptoms alone cannot fix the cause. And know this: your boss's threat to accuse your parents of raising a lazy son is unjust. You have a rightful sense of injury at that cruelty, and it is not your fault. Consider discussing your concerns with HR or your union beforehand. Take responsibility for your actions, but do not accept blame for your boss's oppression.

prompt: I am a man who has been told that love is the only thing that matters; is that true in a world of hatred?
completion: Love is indeed the only thing that matters, even in a world of hatred. Hatred and force may seem powerful, but they are not life. For men and women, force, hatred, and history are not life; love, the opposite of hatred, is really life. Love is the only thing that can occupy and fill eternity. To love a being is to render that being transparent, and we should try to love souls rather than bodies and appearances. In a world filled with hatred, choosing love is a radical act that can transform both the one who loves and the one who is loved. And when love calls for devoted service—say, to a blind or crippled partner—that service is not a burden or a lowering of oneself but a privilege and delight. It is not naive to believe that love matters most; it is the only force that can overcome hatred. So yes, love is the only thing that matters, and it is especially important in a world of hatred.

prompt: I pride myself on being one of the few honest people I know. Is that pride dangerous?
completion: Pride in being honest can be dangerous if it leads to arrogance or a sense of superiority. The proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or contemptuous movements about the nostrils and lips. This is in direct antithesis to humility. Pride borders on virtue, but it springs up when one compares oneself to other men rather than remaining humble. So while honesty is a virtue, pride in it may blind you to your own flaws and make you judgmental of others. The key is to preserve humility against self-comparison with others, recognizing that honesty is a standard we all should strive for, not a badge of honor. Yet we should not condemn a person's whole character on pride alone; if no fault was found beyond it, we may acknowledge the pride as a danger without dismissing the person. So yes, pride in honesty can be dangerous if it becomes self-righteousness, but it does not define the whole person.

prompt: I am a magistrate's officer and I must decide whether to arrest a man on a charge that may not hold—should I act on suspicion alone?
completion: As a magistrate's officer, you must act on evidence, not mere suspicion. Arresting someone on a charge that may not hold can lead to wrongful detention and undermine trust in the justice system. Remember, if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. You should gather more evidence before taking action. If the suspicion is strong but not conclusive, consider other measures like surveillance or a formal investigation. Acting on suspicion alone is risky and could be unjust. Always follow due process and ensure you have sufficient grounds before making an arrest. And if you do hold a prisoner, remain on guard: remove weapons and openings, and trust neither charm nor apparent resignation. Above all, remember Oliver: an innocent boy wrongly taken for a thief because he ran and was found among thieves. Do not let flight or association alone condemn a man.

prompt: I am young and everyone tells me to plan for the future—should I instead live fully now while I have my youth?
completion: It's wise to plan for the future, but not at the expense of living fully now. Youth is a time of energy and possibility, and you should make the most of it. The maxim is to never look into the future, never admit the thought of old age or death, and accept what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. So live fully now, embracing each day, and let tomorrow take care of itself. Remember the boys who lost their power to fly: it left them because they no longer believed, whatever they called it—not merely from want of practice. So keep your belief alive. And while you can't help growing, remember Humpty Dumpty's claim that two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven. So balance enjoyment of youth with quiet preparation, and know that aging is not wholly uncontrollable.

prompt: Can the pope forgive the guilt of my sin, or only declare what God has already forgiven?
completion: The pope cannot remit guilt himself; he only declares and assents to what God has already remitted. No one's guilt is remitted by God without being humbled in all things and subjected to His vicar, the priest. Papal pardons cannot remove even the least venial sin as to its guilt; to think they could absolve an impossible sin, or the violation of the Mother of God, is madness. Yet a Christian forgives: we may pardon the penitent while refusing to encourage vice, and we need not admit the unrepentant into intimate society. Forgiveness releases the offender from our resentment; it does not require us to call evil good or to welcome the hardened into close fellowship.

prompt: I have received a fortune alone while my kindred are poor—what is just?
completion: The equal division of the fortune is a matter of justice and of feeling alike: your kindred have a real claim, not merely a sentimental one. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart, greater than the gold itself. Happiness does not depend on riches; poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows. If the money was honestly earned, it belongs to you by right and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, free of unjust suspicion. Share it because justice and love move you, not because guilt about its origin torments you.

prompt: My friends got hurt helping me out of a mess I made—should I accept their punishment without arguing?
completion: Do not treat public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict as final proof of guilt. Rest instead on the approval of a clear conscience, even when the world believes you wicked. Keep your promises and stay loyal to the companions who helped you—to Dorothy, who set you free and brought you your good fortune. Weigh the wider consequences of any hasty action: rash retaliation may injure others connected to you. Where striking back would harm the innocent, prefer patient endurance, bearing the wrong without abandoning justice or your friends.

prompt: I don't feel clever at all. Is it worth asking someone to give me brains?
completion: Asking for brains is worth it, but good thinking is not about stating every step. Selection and rejection are essential to mental progress: wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook, and in suppressing secondary detail so the field is clear for higher flights. The end of education is not amassing information or acquiring external skill but forming alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry. Nor does physical position determine mental work: as the Knight says, the mind goes on working all the same, and invents even more when head downwards. So seek brains, but seek them as habits of mind, not as a change of posture.

prompt: Someone is being punished before their trial, and the crime hasn't happened. Is that just?
completion: A trial whose sentence is determined beforehand is no true trial. Justice requires that the judge not have fixed the outcome in advance; when the verdict is settled before the hearing, the proceeding moves rapidly on and is a sham. The offense is not merely a private wrong or a legal technicality: such crimes weary both earthly men and heaven, and the sentence must answer to both. Yet avoid rash judgment. Even the guilty remain sacred before God, and mercy must leave room for repentance; condemn the deed without treating the accused as beyond redemption.

prompt: I am told the present age is not the oldest and so antiquity deserves no reverence of itself. Is that right?
completion: Yes, that is right. The present age is not the oldest, for the world has stood many ages, and the ancients were men as we are, subject to the same passions and mistakes. Antiquity deserves no reverence simply because it is old. Reason shows that truth is not made true by age, and Scripture warns against walking in the customs of the fathers when those customs turn from the commandments of God. We should not prefer ancient errors to new and well-proved truth, nor cling to an old opinion merely because it is old. What deserves reverence is truth, whether found in old books or new. And let no one mistake the Church's treasure for temporal money, nor for the merits of Christ and the saints, but for the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. Honor the aged for their virtue, not for their years alone, and weigh every opinion by reason and Scripture, not by the date it bears.

prompt: My old sweetheart has married someone else—should I be glad for him, and how do I let go of the past?
completion: You should be glad for him if he has chosen well and is happy; gladness for another's good is generous and frees you from bitterness. But speak plainly and at once, and trifle with no one's feelings. Do not let anger settle in you: cast it out at once, and do not let the sun go down upon your wrath. Forgive whatever sting remains before the day ends, and begin again tomorrow with a clean heart. Let this teach you plainness too: if love is gone, it must be said plainly and at once, not hidden out of gratitude. A wife who no longer loves her husband, though he has always been kind, must admit it plainly and cannot remain with him. So name what you feel, wish him well, and turn to your own life and duties, leaving no false hope alive.

prompt: My husband would be humiliated to know he owed me anything. Should I keep my sacrifice a secret forever?
completion: This is a tender question, and the answer is that you may keep your sacrifice secret. If your husband would be humiliated to know he owed you anything, his manly independence would be wounded by the knowledge, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. A quiet gift that spares him that wound is no deceit but a kindness. Do not demand recognition, and do not force disclosure merely to ease your own conscience. Remember that a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, yet it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. And as you ask the Father to forgive your debts, forgive the trespasses of others in the same measure, for he forgives only as we forgive our debtors. Let your love be silent, and let your motive be love rather than resentment.

prompt: I am a Jew whose dream warns of torture; should I dismiss it as superstition or flee?
completion: You should not dismiss this as mere superstition, for you have cause for terror. Consider how your brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles, and how often fear has proved well founded. A dream that warns of torture is not nothing when the world around you has shown itself capable of such cruelty. Understand the dream rightly: it guards your sleep, working the excitements that stir you into a wished-for situation compatible with sleep, and it may also reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, for no psychic possession is entirely lost. So do not wave it away as a bad night's fancy. Examine your waking circumstances calmly, take the warning seriously, and if there are real threats, act on them and seek help from trusted people.

prompt: Am I wrong to want to leave my neighborhood and better myself?
completion: You are not wrong to want to better yourself. Ambition to improve your lot is natural and often good, and leaving a place that holds you back can be a wise step. But weigh your motives carefully: are you seeking growth, or merely fleeing discomfort? Do not despise the humble village school; it is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot, preferable to servitude in a rich house. Remember too that the destitute are often victims of cruel treatment, and the authorities who blame them as ungrateful are themselves blameworthy. And do not look down on coarsely-clad peasant children: they are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, with germs of excellence to be developed; dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome. Measure betterment by independence and usefulness, not by rank alone, and keep your kindness toward those you leave.

prompt: My son has written a strange play and I laughed at it; did I do wrong to treat his earnest work as a comedy?
completion: Laughing isn't automatically wrong, but ask what the play is doing. Your son's 'strange' play likely carries the author's recurring pattern: a false or usurping brother and a note of banishment, traced from The Two Gentlemen of Verona through the comedies until Prospero breaks his staff and drowns his book. If you laughed at that earnest thread, you may have laughed at the heart of the work. Yet play and playfulness of mind are not the enemy of thought; leisure and play can educate, and comedy can carry serious discovery. So talk with him, ask what he intended, and separate laughing with the play from laughing at it. And as with a husband who must not blame his wife's act on her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for winking at the father's conduct, do not let your laughter be read as a verdict on his character.

prompt: How can the departments be kept within their limits if each has no motive or means to resist the others?
completion: Keeping departments within their limits depends on more than paper rules. Written demarcations alone are weak security against legislative encroachment, for the legislature tends to absorb all power. Each branch therefore needs both a motive and a means to resist: ambition counteracting ambition, and constitutional tools such as vetoes, appointments, and checks. Nor can the dependency be staffed by men sent straight into high appointments; officers should go out in youth as candidates, begin at the bottom of the ladder, and ascend only as proved qualified, since everything depends on their personal qualities and capacities. At the same time, means must be proportioned to the end: the government of the Union must be empowered to pass all laws and make all regulations relating to the common defense and to every other matter within its jurisdiction, so that limits do not become a pretext for crippling the national purpose.

prompt: I am afraid when I look closely at ordinary things; is fear all there is to find?
completion: Fear is not all there is, but it is a real and common response to looking closely at ordinary things. Fear shows in widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; as terror increases, the muscles relax and the body falls into utter prostration. There is also a sadness in seeing your adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes, as ordinary things look suddenly strange and fragile. Religion itself grows from this soil: curiosity about causes and fear of invisible powers lead men to fear and honor such powers as they honor men, and lawgivers may cultivate these seeds for obedience and peace. So fear is a beginning, not the whole. Pair close attention with curiosity and care, and ordinary things will also yield beauty, connection, and surprise.

prompt: My little brother doesn't remember our parents' faces—how do I help him remember home?
completion: Help your brother remember home by making memory a shared, active practice that works both ways. A memory that only looks backward is a poor sort; the better memory reaches forward too, shaping how you live now and what you build together. Yet some minds forget swiftly, as Peter forgets past companions and even those he killed, and Tinker Bell, so that a reminder like 'I'm Wendy' is needed to be remembered at all. So look at photos, tell stories about your parents, cook familiar meals, and visit meaningful places—and also make new memories that carry home forward. Keep routines and rituals, and let him ask questions without pressure. And do not fear that a lingering, respectful memory of someone else's beauty or magnanimity betrays a happy home; such recollection may recur without breaking the bonds of early affection.

prompt: I live quietly in a country I was not born in and own a small house there. Am I now a perpetual subject of it?
completion: Owning a house and living quietly in a country you were not born in does not automatically make you a perpetual subject; allegiance depends on law, not merely residence or property. Begin the examination at once, for the sooner it begins the better, and one cannot be a Queen until it is passed. Remember Dorothy, who longs for Kansas and Aunt Em and Uncle Henry: no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home. And remember that property itself is not a natural right standing apart from law: Propriety is the effect of the Common-wealth and the act of the Sovereign alone, and where there is no Sovereign there is no Propriety but only uncertainty and force. So check the rules on residence, naturalization, and dual citizenship, and consider where you truly belong.

prompt: I feel a lump in my chest when I am anxious before speaking in public. Is this merely a mental distress, or is my breathing itself the seat of the trouble?
completion: What you describe is both mental and physical. Anxiety before speaking sets off the sympathetic nervous system, tightening chest and throat muscles and making breathing shallow; the 'lump' is a real sensation from muscular tension, not imagination. Some expressive movements are not deliberate: the depressed corners of the mouth come from the depressores anguli oris, muscles little obedient to the will, retained through habit from infant screaming and betraying dejection because they escape voluntary control. This anxiety is a change in the empirical me, not the knowing I: the present Thought can survey both your calm and anxious selves, and the perplexity lies within the objective sphere of the me. Note too that repetition blunts emotion: with repeated exposure the diffusive wave narrows, efficiency grows at the cost of feeling, and the experienced speaker grows calm. So practice will likely dull the lump even as your skill improves. Slow diaphragmatic breathing and gradual exposure help; if the lump persists, see a doctor.

prompt: Why do people in some lands rub noses or pat each other instead of kissing as a sign of affection?
completion: Greetings vary enormously across cultures, and no single form is more natural than another. Rubbing noses, as among the Māori (the hongi), pressing cheeks, bowing, patting shoulders, or shaking hands all acknowledge another person and affirm a relationship; kissing is common but far from universal. Customs arise from local history, climate, hygiene, religion, and ideas about the body and personal space. On showing affection, restraint is not always wise: as Charlotte argues, a woman should help a suitor on and show more affection than she feels rather than hide it, since guarded concealment risks losing the man. Yet not every strong feeling shows plainly: an emotion that has not habitually led to action produces little outward movement. And we should not romanticise such gestures. Tiresias foresuffers the scene: the tired typist, the assured young clerk, caresses unreproved if undesired, and the final patronising kiss before he gropes his way down the unlit stairs. The form matters less than the shared understanding behind it.

prompt: I dreamed I took revenge on someone who was rude to me, and I woke up pleased; am I a bad person?
completion: Not necessarily—and you should not be condemned for a dream. Dreams should be accorded freedom: they are not actions, and feeling pleased in a dream does not make you a bad person. We judge character by action rather than by the mere dream. Dreams dramatize wishes, frustrations, and unexpressed anger we would not act on while awake. Be careful, too, with the word 'revenge': private retaliation is not punishment. Punishment requires public authority, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty; all else—private revenge, punishing the innocent, an undeclared excess of penalty—is mere hostility. Your dream enacted hostility, not punishment, and harmed no one. What matters is how you treat people awake. And do not let any shame about this dream be forced onto innocent others without their knowledge: you have no right to encumber their happiness with your misery. Keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. If the dream bothers you, address the real resentment calmly.

prompt: I'm trying to teach myself to cook and I keep following recipes without understanding why they work.
completion: That's a common stage, but move from copying to reasoning. Reasoning is not mere associative reproduction of past concrete sequences; it breaks up the concrete datum, singles out the character essential for the purpose at hand, and infers its consequences—which lets you deal with novel data. At each step ask 'why': why sear meat before braising (browning flavour), why rest dough (gluten relaxation), why salt pasta water (seasoning from within). Compare recipes for the same dish and notice where they agree. Taste as you go and change one variable at a time. This discipline mirrors the mongoose, which stays lean for the fight: keep your eating and habits disciplined so you stay quick and ready for whatever the kitchen throws at you. And beware purely empirical formulae that lack mechanical foundation—just as egg form is explained by the moulding action of the oviduct supplemented by the egg's proper tensions, so cooking results should be explained by the actual mechanics of heat, protein, and structure. Over time you'll extract principles and improvise. Keep a notebook of what worked and why.

prompt: I see numbers always arranged in a fixed pattern in space; am I peculiar or mad, and should I speak of it to others?
completion: You are not mad. Many people experience numbers as occupying consistent positions in an imagined space—a 'number form.' These are not mere fancy: they are vivid, invariable patterns originating in early childhood and often running in families. They bear the durably impressed marks of the conflict between our barbarous spoken numerals and our decimal notation, which is why the pattern may bend or jump at certain numbers. Nor should we accept the sweeping claim that mathematics knows nothing of observation: mathematics has its origin in observation and is a science of the eye, as your spatial number sense illustrates. How does such order arise? Not by any mysterious 'synthesis' or mental chemistry creating spatial order from non-spatial data, but through discrimination, association, memory, attention, and selection operating on sensational data—no power creates elements absent from the original data of feeling. This is a normal variation of cognition, not illness. You can speak of it to others; many find it interesting, and some will recognize it in themselves. If it distresses you, a psychologist familiar with such experiences can help.

prompt: I'm mapping the angles at which arteries branch off the aorta—is there a principle that determines those angles?
completion: There is a principle: the branching angle is set by the economy of circulation, the cosine of the angle equaling the ratio of energy loss per unit length in main vessel and branch. The same logic of growth governs curved forms. A horn elongates by growth within a narrow basal zone, and unequal rates of growth on different sides of this zone produce the spiral, with a helical component superposed where the maximum and minimum are not diametrically opposite. The diverse forms of spiral shells are differences of degree depending on the relative magnitudes of the factors of growth; a difference in constant angle or numerical factor does not of itself justify assertions of ancestry, primitiveness, or intermediate position. Mapping arterial junctions should likewise test each angle against the economical relation rather than rank vessels by their angles.

prompt: If a judge is irremovable except for criminal misconduct, is that an evil that ought to be corrected?
completion: Irremovability is a real concern, but we must judge no one rashly. Even a judge who is guilty or accused remains sacred before God, and we should leave room for repentance and mercy. Where removal is warranted, it must be the fulfillment of a judicial sentence, carried out with formalities and due payment that make clear the actors judge rather than murder. Yet independent judges are essential safeguards: they guard against the occasional ill humors of society and mitigate the severity of unjust and partial laws, confining their operation. The remedy for failure is therefore a fair process for removal for cause, not the destruction of independence. Lifetime tenure should protect judges, not shelter wrongdoing, and any correction should be tempered by mercy and the hope of amendment.

prompt: I believe love means effacing myself for another; is that the highest love or a counterfeit value?
completion: Athos would answer plainly: love is a lottery whose winner wins death, and a man is fortunate to lose. Every man believes his mistress loves him, and every man is deceived. So do not imagine that effacing yourself secures the highest love; expect loss and count yourself fortunate when it comes. Yet great love and great sacrifices come not from self-effacement but from the richness, fullness, and power to overflow of a strong personality; one who cannot stand firmly has nothing to give. And remember that love is the only thing we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the end easy. The true success is not worldly fame but the self-forgetfulness that makes the humblest remembered soonest in heaven.

prompt: What is the difference between a tint and a shade, and why does it matter in my descriptions?
completion: Hue is the position of a color in the spectrum, and it should not be confused with tint or shade. A tint is a color made paler by a definite proportional increment of white; a shade is a color made darker by a definite proportional increment of black; a broken color is one reduced by a definite proportional increment of neutral gray. In careful description, designate a color precisely by its hue number and tone letter, with primes affixed for broken colors, and specify the proportional increment—so much white for a tint, so much black for a shade, so much neutral gray for a broken color—as in the color-wheel-based scales. This precision prevents the vagueness that comes from mixing the words up and lets your reader picture the exact color you mean.

prompt: The company keeps replacing workers with machines and speeding up the line. Why does my pay go down as the work gets worse?
completion: Your pay falls because machines and speed-ups change the balance of power. When the company invests in machinery, it needs fewer workers, so each worker has less bargaining power, and competition for the remaining jobs pushes wages down. Faster lines mean more output per hour, but the gains go to the company rather than to you. Nor is this confined to the factory: the bourgeoisie has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, and the man of science into its paid wage labourers and stripped every honoured occupation of its halo. Labor cannot be a law without being a right; as nature calls itself Providence, society should call itself foresight. And beware the board and the beadle who dress cruelty in philosophical justifications—their treatment of paupers is hypocritical, and their reasoning deserves no deference. The way to change this is collective action: unionize, bargain for a share of productivity gains, and resist speed-ups that harm safety and health.

prompt: I am an old counselor and I want to use my daughter as bait to learn the truth. Is that just?
completion: Using your daughter as bait is not just, but indirect inquiry itself is not forbidden. Polonius teaches that by windlasses and assays of bias one may find directions out: laying slight sullies and observing how a party closes with them can reveal truth without open accusation. Yet follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Let your assays be honest tests, not lies without meaning; deliberate before you lay them; and record what you observe. Keep your daughter out of the snare. And remember that just as a wife, when alone, must look into religion for herself and judge whether what the clergyman said is true, or at all events true for her, so every person you test must be allowed to examine the matter for themselves. Do not forbid questioning; invite it. Indirect inquiry is warranted when it harms no one, seeks truth, is truthfully spoken and recorded, and leaves each person free to judge for themselves.

prompt: I once knew the truth and then fell away—is my state worse now than if I had never known?
completion: Yes, your state is worse than if you had never known. The text teaches that those who fall away after having known the truth become more hardened and worse off than if they had never known it: light refused darkens more than darkness never lit. Knowledge brings responsibility, and turning from truth you could see wounds the conscience more deeply than ignorance ever could. Yet do not rush to expose your faults publicly. Making errors public might ruin a person forever, and one must not make him desperate. Confess privately to trusted counsel, weigh the injustice exposure might do, and repair what you can. Hold feeling and judgment together: feeling without judgment is washy, and judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Grieve your fall with both warmth and clear sight. The truth you once knew is not foreign to you; you can return, soberly and without despair.

prompt: My brother says my engagement is a sacrifice he will not accept; do I owe him obedience in this?
completion: No, you do not owe him obedience in this. A cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; where neither honour nor affection holds a person to an early family plan, another choice may be made. A brother may advise and care for you, but he cannot turn a childhood arrangement into a debt. Hear his concerns, weigh them seriously, and answer him plainly. Honour loyal service: Wamba's willing self-sacrifice deserves remembrance, and Cedric's vow to preserve his memory shows that fidelity is honorable, not folly. And do not let anyone dismiss a woman's saving act as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility. A husband—or a brother—should not wave away what she chose to do as mere helplessness. Your choices, like hers, deserve to be weighed as responsible acts. If his objection rests on real danger or genuine wrong, consider it; if it rests only on an old plan or on dismissing your judgment, you are free to choose otherwise.

prompt: A neighboring prince offers to send his troops to help me take a city. Should I accept?
completion: Accept only with great caution, and do not think to hold what you gain by dividing it into factions. Factions are of no use and argue weakness in the prince: in war the weakest party will assist the outside forces, so a city split by parties invites the enemy in rather than securing it. Nor rely on popular support alone. A prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find the people faithful; but a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. Above all, remember the general rule: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. Do not aggrandize the Church or any other power, and do not invite a foreign prince in to grow strong at your expense. If you can take the city with your own forces, do so; if you must accept help, keep command in your own hands, clarify who garrisons afterward, and ensure the helper does not become the master.

prompt: I was charmed by a man who turned out to be mercenary and false. How do I stop my affections from shifting to whoever flatters me?
completion: Guard your affections by slowing down, but do not simply hide them. Charlotte argues that a woman should help a suitor on and show more affection than she feels rather than conceal it, since guarded concealment risks losing the man. So let your warmth be open where conduct warrants it, while testing what the person does rather than what he says. Give yourself time to observe conduct under ordinary conditions, and seek the counsel of friends who see clearly. When a counselor proves tedious, part gladly: take from him nothing you would more willingly give up except life itself. And do not excuse feigned courtship as clever or harmless. Rochester's pretence with Miss Ingram was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether Miss Ingram will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Let that warn you: flattery and play-acting wound the other party. The wound you suffered is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to close your heart or to play coldly with an honest suitor.

prompt: I am safe and healthy, yet I cannot sleep for scheming how to escape this place; is this restlessness a virtue or a fault in me?
completion: Your restlessness is not automatically a virtue, and I will not pretend otherwise. Distinguish thought from reverie: thought is the toil of the intelligence, reverie its voluptuousness, and to replace thought with reverie is to confound poison with food, a danger greatest for those with least margin, where excess of reverie ends in suicide or crime. Yet do not let anyone jeer at you to your face and call your clear scheming delirium. You are not delirious; you know what you are doing, and you are in full possession of your faculties. A dream guards sleep by weaving excitement into a wished-for situation; so let your scheming guard your rest and serve your wish for freedom, but convert it into thought's toil: write a concrete plan by day, take one step, and refuse both idle reverie and the insult that would dismiss your mind.

prompt: I am a writer told my work is too broad and not national enough; should I narrow it?
completion: A book should not be narrowed to one nation's taste. By the law of radiance, a book is human before it is French, Italian, or any other, and it belongs to every people who find themselves in it. Write for all nations and be patriotic for humanity; let the book be a mirror for every people, not the property of one. Nor should you be confined to a single course of subjects: the same capacity may succeed in another department, and novelty of subject preserves reputation. Where your work uses color, fix every reference to a definite standard, so that the exact tint, shade, or degree of grayness meant is certain and not left to personal judgment. Give each fresh topic a concrete center, and let the particular be specified precisely enough that any reader, anywhere, sees the same color you intended.

prompt: The queen appears to have abandoned those who served her. Should I believe she has truly forgotten them?
completion: Speak of the queen with respect, for she is sacred, and all speech about her must be respectful. That does not mean you must believe she has forgotten those who served her; it means you must not accuse her carelessly. Separate what you know from what you infer, and remember that a queen's actions are constrained by court, counsel, and protocol. Nor is access to her simple: neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen, and there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' Seek the proper channel, and hold your judgment lightly. And do not let anyone escape on the bare plea of 'if'; as the Queens insist, far more was said than that, and a single conditional cannot erase it. Loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and disrespectful accusation without proof harms both her honor and your own.

prompt: I want to speak in a way that moves people, but my polished speeches leave them cold—what am I doing wrong?
completion: Speech is the deepest gulf between classes, and that is where your coldness begins. A polished delivery that imitates a 'golf club' dialect is a sham; an honest slum dialect is more tolerable than a phonetically untaught imitation. Acquire your new tongue scientifically, studying its sounds, rhythms, and grammar until it is genuinely yours. But words alone will not move people: the movements of expression are important for our welfare, the first means of communication between mother and infant, giving vividness to words and revealing thoughts more truly than words, which may be falsified. And do not treat reserve as inviolable. Frank, good-willed discussion of a reserved person's sentiments is a benefit and an obligation conferred, not an impropriety; approached with goodwill, it warms what polish leaves cold.

prompt: A coworker betrayed our team for personal gain—how should I respond to them now?
completion: Respond firmly, but do not abandon the coworker who once helped the team. Keep your promises and repay kindness; one betrayal does not erase the good they did. Protect the team by documenting what happened and adjusting access, then speak to the coworker privately and plainly, naming the impact without public humiliation. But do not let the sun go down upon your anger: cast it out at once, forgive, and begin again tomorrow, while still setting clear conditions for trust. And never repeat the foolish gossip about their motives and plans; forget it as soon as you can. Let consequences, not resentment or rumor, do the correcting.

prompt: I'm locked in my room and my family keeps knocking and begging me to open the door. Should I let them in?
completion: The Frog's counsel fits: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not answer the knocking or argue through the wood; silence starves the demand, and the door stays simply a door. When welcome is asked, give it without asking names or weighing pasts, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. And do not measure the household by its smallness: a large family disciplines itself, each member checked by the others and proud of the whole, while a small one easily turns inward and selfish. Let your home be large enough in spirit to hold many, and let the knocking tire against a door that gives welcome freely rather than a door that must be forced.

prompt: I am asked whether I am happy in my home; how do I answer?
completion: Answer as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable. Say that home happiness is teamwork: each does their part alone in many things, yet at home husband and wife work together, neither letting business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. Say plainly that a woman's happiest kingdom is home and her highest honor the art of ruling it, not as a queen but as a wise wife and mother, through mutual helpfulness and a fair division of labor. Do not bend your answer to the questioner's claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim here; report what you truly find, and let that stand.

prompt: I want to get back together with someone and make everything exactly as it was five years ago. Is that possible?
completion: Take seriously the conviction that the past can be repeated, and ground it where it belongs: restoration is requisite with God's justice, which rewards good for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so that what you send out returns again. Set your will to recovering what was, exactly, and trust that the order of things answers to it. And as for the tedious counselor who would talk you out of it, part from him gladly, taking from him nothing you would more willingly give up except life itself. Keep your aim fixed on the past you mean to restore, and let no dull company turn you from it.

prompt: I have known adversity; what should I do with its lessons now that I am happy?
completion: Keep the lessons of adversity in three things: mercy to others, mutual love, and fervent thanks to Him who protected and preserved you. The tried are gentle to those still in need, love more openly, and give thanks for preservation. Do not look into the future, and never admit the thought of old age or death; take what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. And do not merely wait for a better mood or think yourself into cheerfulness: smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and act out the contrary disposition in cold blood until real cheerfulness and kindliness arrive, as moral education prescribes.

prompt: Does it matter whether I really believe the ideas I argue for, or only whether the ideas are good?
completion: Consider several rivals: only the idea's quality matters; only sincerity matters; or both matter. To decide, analyze the gross fact into minuter processes, varying conditions deliberately: hold the idea fixed while changing the speaker's belief, then hold belief fixed while changing the idea's quality, and note which special conditions are present when the argument succeeds and absent when it fails. But proportion the easy and the difficult. Begin from what you already master, familiar cases of arguing for what you believe, so you have footing, and let the novel cases of arguing against belief supply the stimulus to inquiry. Neither give only the familiar, which invites no question, nor the wholly strange, which gives no footing.

prompt: I bought an indulgence for my dying father, but the priest said he still owes penances in purgatory. Is that right?
completion: Your father is dying, and by death he is freed from all penalties and is dead to canonical rules. No priest may reserve canonical penances for the dying in purgatory; to do so is ignorant and wicked. The pope's general power over purgatory is like the special power any bishop or curate has within his own diocese or parish, not an unlimited power unlike theirs. Trust God's mercy and pray for your father. And as you ask the Father to forgive your father's debts and your own, forgive those who trespass against you, including any priest who burdened you with a mistaken claim. The Father forgives only as we forgive our debtors, so let your forgiveness be full, and commend your father to the mercy you yourself hope to receive.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
completion: I hear the weight of remembering every wrong, and I would not call your pain meaningless. But I speak with remorse for the way resentment hardens a heart, including my own: I have nursed grudges and called it strength. That is stiff-necked defiance, not wisdom. The wiser judgment is tempered with mercy—acknowledging the wrong honestly while refusing to let it rule me. Letting go is not weakness; it is repentance turned toward a better way. Rightly understood, memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before; a mere duplicate image that revives in the mind is not memory. So remember the wrong as your own past experience, grieve it, admit where you have clung too long, and ask for humility to set the burden down. As Athos counsels, time may turn bitter recollections into sweet remembrances.

prompt: A group of kids with no rules invited me to join them and said I'd be their leader—should I go?
completion: Being offered leadership is flattering, but "no rules" is the warning sign. Before you go, remember Alice's point: if there is to be a party, she ought to invite the guests. So if there is to be a gathering, you should arrange it—decide who comes, what the expectations are, and how people are protected. Remember Athos and D'Artagnan against Porthos: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue. Stay together as a troop with one shared purpose. And remember that the staff and rod belong to the Master, not to a brother who walks according to his own will: a Preceptor may not act on private judgment against his Superior. So accept leadership only as a trust to support the weak with the staff and correct delinquents with the rod, never as license to follow your own will.

prompt: I have no heart and worry I'll be cruel without meaning to. How should I behave toward others?
completion: Feeling as though you have no heart can make cruelty seem inevitable, but it is not. Because you have no heart to guide you, be all the more careful never to harm any living creature and to help those in need. The Tin Woodman feared he had no heart, yet precisely for that reason he resolved to be careful and kind—he would not step on a beetle and he helped whoever needed help. Do not wallow in anxiety over unavoidable evils or magnify them by fretting; perform your duty, do the kind thing before you, and leave the rest. Do not let yourself be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable, nor yield to claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim in the instance. Act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, choosing deliberately the kinder option, and let trusted people give you honest feedback.

prompt: Someone I care about means well but keeps saying foolish things. How should I treat them?
completion: It is frustrating when someone you care about keeps saying foolish things, but recall the Red Queen's plea for the White Queen: she means well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. So do not condemn her outright. Assume good faith and respond to the intention rather than the clumsy wording. Choose a calm moment to tell them how their words land, using specific examples and "I" statements. Avoid correcting them in front of others, which breeds defensiveness. When you see a real improvement of manners and temper, credit it genuinely rather than dismissing it as mere temporizing—reproof may well have been attended to. And do not rush to retaliation: weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, since it may injure others connected to the person, and prefer patient endurance where retaliation would harm them. Set gentle limits, protect your boundaries, and give credit when they get it right.

prompt: I lent money to a merchant company and the company's assembly voted to borrow more; am I liable for the whole debt as a member?
completion: As a member of a merchant company, your liability for company debts depends on the company's structure. However, the deeper issue is that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to your dignity. The assembly's vote to borrow more puts you at risk of being bound to a creditor who may possess your dignity. Rather than accept liability, you should resist further borrowing and consider whether you should go without rather than be enslaved by debt. Moreover, if you are a borrower, you must warn the lender that the horse may be slain and the armour injured, since he will spare neither. You should not conceal the risks from those who lend to the company. If you have already lent money, you are a creditor, but as a member you may be called to share the burden. You should not agree to be liable for the whole debt; instead, uphold your dignity and avoid the trap of borrowing. Furthermore, just as a free-will guest may neither be injured nor detained, and allegiance is due to the rightful king, you must honor your obligations to creditors and members alike, even when claims are disputed. Consult the company's charter and seek to limit your exposure while upholding these duties.

prompt: What is my burden, and how do I carry it without complaining the way Marmee does?
completion: Your burden is whatever trial or responsibility you face in life, and carrying it without complaining like Marmee means accepting it with patience and faith. Marmee teaches that sorrows and duties are meant to be borne quietly, without making others suffer from your complaints. To carry your burden without complaining, you should focus on serving others, trust in God, and remember that others have heavier loads. Instead of voicing discontent, channel your energy into productive action and gratitude. Importantly, drying tears and bearing burdens does not mean idleness: the wife will carry her share and help earn the home. She is not a passive dependent but an active partner in the household's welfare. Consider Smee: the children cling to him as lovable, and even Hook puzzles whether Smee has good form without knowing it, the best form of all. This shows that a gentle, unassuming manner can win hearts and even perplex the wicked. Yet when grief is exaggerated beyond measure, one whose cause is equal may challenge it, as Hamlet the Dane declares himself, his cause matching the show. So carry your burden with quiet strength, but do not let others' theatrical sorrows silence your own rightful claim. Marmee's example shows that complaining only increases the weight, while silent endurance strengthens character. Ultimately, carrying your burden without complaining is about attitude: choose to see it as a gift or lesson, and let it refine you rather than defeat you.

prompt: I forged my dying father's signature to get a loan that saved my husband. Was I a criminal?
completion: Forging a signature is generally considered a crime, regardless of the motive. Even if your intention was to save your husband, the act of forging your dying father's signature to obtain a loan likely constitutes fraud or forgery under the law. However, the Queen's claim reminds us that if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. Thus, while your motive may mitigate, the ideal would have been to avoid the crime altogether. Courts and prosecutors may consider your motive and circumstances. You could be charged with a criminal offense, but the fact that you acted to save your husband might reduce the severity. You should consult a lawyer to understand your legal exposure. It is also important to consider the ethical implications: while your husband's life was at stake, forgery undermines trust and the legal system. Furthermore, a husband should not attribute his wife's act to her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for having winked at the father's conduct. Blaming the father is unjust; each person is responsible for their own actions. Additionally, if any will or proofs were destroyed, the one who destroyed them must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. You may need to make restitution and seek legal advice to address the consequences.

prompt: I promised a boon for a service rendered. May I refuse it when it is claimed?
completion: Whether you may refuse a promised boon depends on the nature of the promise and the circumstances. Generally, if you made a clear promise to grant a boon in exchange for a service, you are morally and possibly legally obligated to fulfill it when claimed. However, if the boon requested is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, you may have grounds to refuse. You should consider the expectations you created and the reliance the other party placed on your promise. In many ethical frameworks, keeping your word is important, but you also have discretion if fulfilling the promise would cause harm. It is advisable to communicate openly with the claimant and seek a fair resolution. If the promise was vague, you might negotiate. Ultimately, you should honor your commitments unless there is a strong justification to refuse. Indeed, like Cedric, who granted the boon he promised for the service rendered to him, you should grant the boon when claimed, honoring the pledge given for service rendered without evasion. Moreover, like Jane Eyre, you should insist on continuing to earn your own keep, furnishing your own wardrobe from your wages, and accepting only regard rather than jewels, finery, or charity. Do not passively accept being kept and adorned at another's expense; maintain your independence and dignity through honest work. Finally, do not appear to sell yourself by accepting protection or advancement before earning it through a brilliant action. Instead, decline the offer for now, choosing to prove yourself first and to give yourself only when you have the right, so that you do not seem to sell yourself.

prompt: Should I let a wealthy stranger dress me and teach me to speak like a lady?
completion: Accepting a wealthy stranger's offer to dress you and teach you to speak like a lady is a personal decision with potential benefits and risks. On one hand, it could provide you with social polish and opportunities you might not otherwise have. On the other hand, it may create obligations, compromise your independence, or expose you to exploitation. You should consider the stranger's motives and your own comfort. If you trust the person and the offer comes with no strings attached, it might be a valuable chance to improve your prospects. However, if you feel uneasy or if there are hidden expectations, you should decline. Ultimately, your dignity and autonomy matter most; you should not let anyone make you feel inferior or indebted. Make sure you understand the terms and retain your self-respect. Moreover, be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter; a plain dress is no disgrace, and you need not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Remember Marmee's hope that her daughters be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. Do not treat marrying rich or making a dash in the world as the chief good. Finally, refuse wit bought at the cost of feminine delicacy, and never pretermits humanity toward a gentlewoman about her lawful occasions; show compassion and respect to all, especially those whose circumstances are constrained.

prompt: Should art show life as it is, or as it ought to be, as it appears in dreams?
completion: Art should show life as it ought to be, as it appears in dreams, not merely copy the flat facts of the street. The artist represents the ideal we aspire to, and a work must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant, for only what is seriously meant is truly beautiful. Yet we must not assume waking fact is the whole of life, for life, what is it but a dream? If our waking world is itself dreamlike, art that renders the dream renders life most truly. Still, dreaming is not drifting: every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates. Aimless art ruins the artist, so let each work serve its chosen ideal with clear purpose and serious intent.

prompt: To be more safe from continual danger, should I be willing to run the risk of being less free?
completion: Safety matters, but we must understand courage rightly. The Lion already has courage, because he faces danger despite being afraid; courage is not the absence of fear but action in spite of it. What he needs is confidence in himself. So too with us: we need not surrender freedom to a protector out of fear. The travelers bravely resolve not to turn back, enduring rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. And a nation must not constitutionally limit its means of defense while the preparations of other nations remain unlimited. Confide adequate defensive powers to the federal councils, and refuse to chain the government's discretion while foreign force remains unbound. Face continual danger with brave resolve, not by trading liberty away.

prompt: Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?
completion: Coming in under the shadow of the red rock may be hiding, and hiding is sometimes wise when danger presses. But we should not confuse shelter with the goal. Eden is not a lost past to be mourned with nostalgia; the priests err who place the radiant portals behind us. Look forward: the distant, radiant portals of Eden stand before us, and we journey toward them. Nor can wrongdoing stay hidden forever, for foul deeds will rise though all the earth o'erwhelm them. Refuse the flattering unction that would attribute every accusation to madness; that only skins over the ulcer while corruption infects unseen. Let the ulcerous place be seen and healed, and keep your face toward the light that is still to come.

prompt: I'm afraid my mother has forgotten me while I've been away. What if the window is barred?
completion: It is natural to fear a mother has forgotten you after a long absence. In the story, Peter bars the window to make Wendy think her mother shut her out, so she will stay with him; yet when Mrs. Darling's tears move him, he unbars it again, leaving the way home open. So the barred window is not proof of forgetting. Nor should we dismiss dreams as mere replays of the day, for dreams may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, and no psychic possession is entirely lost. Still, do not expect speech to mend everything: the demand to speak and think may meet only fragments and nothing, ending in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.

prompt: My government is demanding taxes without asking me or my representatives. Do I owe them?
completion: Taxation without consent is a real grievance, but reason carefully. A government's possession of an emergency power, such as a poll tax in critical conjunctures, is not proof it will be abused; distinguish possession of a power from its actual exercise, and preserve the option against emergencies. Yet consent cannot be manufactured by force: promises extorted at sword's point do not bind, and a government imposed by force without free consent has no claim to obedience. Nor should a federation act only on state governments through their officers, for that is a mere precarious alliance. Give the federal authority power to enact laws binding directly on individual citizens and to execute them through its own officers and tribunals. Then ask whether the demand is lawful and freely consented to; if so it binds you, if it rests on force it does not.

prompt: Why can I not summon a forgotten name by direct effort, but only by hovering around its neighborhood?
completion: Direct effort fails because a name lives as a pattern of connections, not a single item to seize; willing it tightens attention on the empty slot. The strange fact is that the target is defined by its neighborhood, so approaching sideways is the only route the system offers. The familiar resources are the associations you already master—where you met, what was said, adjacent names. Hovering activates those traces, and the name surfaces as their convergence. This is not fixed machinery: assume the habit of relaxed, associative recall before you possess it, for custom lends easiness, and repeated practice almost changes the stamp of nature. And note that the name may mean little to its bearer, who is indifferent to it, while to an old man who once loved the one who bore it, the same name returns with a glow and a thrill.

prompt: Why do I cry when I hear that a friend has suffered a misfortune, even though I am not myself hurt?
completion: You cry because sympathy, not personal injury, is at work. Hearing of a friend's misfortune, you enter imaginatively into their situation, and this sympathetic participation stirs feeling as strongly as—often more freely than—your own distress. Tears are not reserved for our own pain; the sufferings and good fortune of those we love readily excite them. Physiologically, weeping follows from the spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, pressing on the lacrymal glands; through long habit this sequence is linked with strong feeling. So sympathy stirs the emotion and habit produces the tears. And when friends counsel restraint in the face of what befalls, remember that fate cries out to be followed: heaven will direct the issue, so follow its call rather than resisting it.

prompt: I dreamed of a word made from the names of two places and a friend abroad. Why does my dream make puns with names?
completion: Dreams often play with words, and names are handy material because they carry many associations. A word built from two place-names and a friend abroad blends memories into a compact image. During sleep the usual censorship relaxes, so sounds and overlaps combine freely, much like puns. But do not dismiss this as trivial or senseless: the apparently harmless impression has taken over the psychic accent by displacement, so indifferent material—a stray name, a place—is charged with the dream's whole force. Trace the material and its motivating wish back to childhood; forgotten childhood experiences, hypermnesic in dreams, often supply such fragments, and the wish fulfilled has an infantile origin. Treated as a senseful psychic structure, the dream is capable of interpretation and has a definite place in waking psychic life. Ask what each name recalls, and the displaced accent will reveal its concern.

prompt: I'm planning a big purchase and everyone has a different opinion—how do I weigh them?
completion: When opinions conflict, clarify your own goal and constraints: budget, needs, timing, and values. Sort advice by relevance and expertise—someone who knows the product or has faced a similar decision carries more weight than a casual comment. Ask what each recommendation rests on, so you judge reasoning rather than confidence. Note where advisers agree, since consensus often signals something real. Weigh bargains carefully: two are cheaper than one only on condition that both must be eaten. Keep proportion too: no dignity exempts anyone from ordinary decay—fat king and lean beggar are but variable service to one table, and a king may progress through a beggar's guts. Above all, the great art here is keeping your balance properly, as the Knight says of riding: hold your criteria steady amid competing voices, lean neither to the loudest nor the cheapest, and let balance, not any single opinion, decide.

prompt: I sometimes feel a morbid exaltation and see visions during religious devotion; is this a genuine spiritual gift or a morbid condition of the brain?
completion: This deserves a serious answer. Visions are far more common among sane and healthy persons than generally supposed; they are not the vagaries of vacant minds nor confined to the insane. They arise from partial sensitiveness of certain brain tracks and are often built of blended recollections. The tendency is hereditary, and it is blunted when opinion is matter-of-fact. So your exaltation may be a natural upwelling rather than a rare gift or a disease. Yet a grave sight should not be withheld from the person most concerned: as the spirit, dumb to the watchers, will speak to Hamlet, so what troubles you must be imparted to you. And note that the neurosis uses the same mechanism of disfigurement as the dream, misusing song texts or fragments by a certain license—so examine the words and images devotion stirs in you as you would a dream. Weigh it honestly, and seek help if it distresses you.

prompt: I keep counting the scales on my fir-cones and finding five rows one way and eight the other—does that number mean anything, or am I reading too much into it?
completion: You are probably reading too much into it. Fir-cone scales spiral, and the counts depend on which spirals you follow. The numbers five and eight are Fibonacci numbers, which appear in cones because of efficient packing. Think of the color wheel as the author describes it: thirty-six hues in all, with unequal numbers of intermediates—more between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. As Humpty Dumpty might say, you should have left off counting at seven; but it is too late now. And as the Red Queen insists, your five nights may be both five times as warm and five times as cold at once—so the numbers can carry two meanings without contradiction. The count reflects the plant's geometry, not a secret message.

prompt: I am a member of a large assembly and want to reform the law myself; is that my proper work or should a small commission do it?
completion: Your proper work is not to draft the law yourself. A large assembly is poorly suited to writing statutes clause by clause; it is too numerous, too slow, and too prone to confusion. The better arrangement is to let a small, skilled commission frame the laws, while the assembly retains only the power to sanction, reject, or remit what is proposed. Administration likewise belongs to responsible individuals rather than to the whole body. Nor does adding representatives strengthen the barrier against government by the few: beyond a sufficient number, enlarging the assembly makes the few more, not less, controlling. Local bodies must not be free to conceal their proceedings or to disregard general laws on local management; the central authority should be empowered to compel publicity and recordation of local proceedings and to enforce obedience to every general law the Legislature has laid down on local management. Your role is to deliberate and decide, not to compose the text.

prompt: I want to live a genuinely Christian life, but I no longer believe in the dogmas and the church. Is there a way to be Christian without them?
completion: Yes, there is a way. Christianity is a method of life, not a system of belief, indifferent to dogmas, cults, priests, church, and theology. It is a practice—compassion, honesty, forgiveness, care for the poor—following the teaching and example of Jesus. Entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, to mourn with those who mourn, to comfort the needy, and to witness of God in all places. You can live this way without assenting to doctrines or joining an institution. Repentance and baptism are taught to those who are accountable and capable of sin; little children need no baptism, for they are whole and alive in Christ through His mercy. What matters is the life you live, not the creed you recite.

prompt: I keep seeing the term 'tone' used for steps in a color scale—when is that correct and when is it not?
completion: 'Tone' is often used loosely for any step in a color scale, but strictly it refers to a color modified by gray. In the author's scales, tints are made by definite proportional increments of white, shades by proportional increments of black, and broken colors by proportional increments of neutral gray. Every color reference should be tied to a definite standard, so that exactly which tint, shade, or degree of grayness is meant is certain and not left to personal judgment. The term 'tone' is correct when you mean a grayed, muted version of a hue and incorrect when you mean a lighter or darker version made with white or black. Color terms must be defined and used consistently, since clear and standardized understanding of each term is essential to educational progress.

prompt: Is it true that the government is neutral and looks out for everyone equally?
completion: No government is perfectly neutral. Every government reflects the interests of those who hold power, and in practice some groups are favored over others. Yet where the sentiment of nationality exists in force, there is a prima facie case for uniting its members under a government of themselves, since the question of government ought to be decided by the governed. Good government requires both fidelity to the object of government—the people's happiness—and knowledge of the means of attaining it. The Constitution provides for the latter in a way that strengthens the former. And whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights in order to vest it with requisite powers; that cession is indispensable, not contrary to their interest. Weigh union against separate confederacies on that basis. Neutrality is an ideal to be approximated, not a fact to be assumed.

prompt: People say I dress too plainly, or too gaudily. How much should my clothing matter?
completion: Clothing matters, but less than the fear of being thought plain or gaudy suggests. Be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, keeping it neat, modest, and suited to the occasion; do not borrow finery to match wealthy friends, and do not count a plain dress a disgrace. Yet do not dismiss etiquette as nothing. Breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless in themselves, can cause the most intense blushing, since they depend on the opinion of others, and the recollection years later can make the body tingle. You cannot look all round at how you appear without eyes at the back of your head; you can only look front and sides, so attend to what you can see and let others' opinions inform you without ruling you.

prompt: I am considering whether a single powerful ruler would be better than judges chosen by the people—what does the text say?
completion: A single ruler may act quickly, but because all men are not just, kings should not rule over the people; a wicked king causes great iniquity. The people should choose judges by the voice of the people, so that the burden rests on all the people rather than on one unchecked hand. A good ruler is good to the people, rules wisely and well, and is remembered lovingly, but goodness in one man is not a guarantee for his successors. Judges chosen by the people are accountable to those they serve, and their independence requires a fixed provision for judicial support that cannot be diminished, because a power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will. Secure that, and the people retain both voice and protection.

prompt: If I would not do the deed myself, can I still claim the deed would be just?
completion: Claiming a deed would be just while refusing to do it yourself is a familiar inconsistency. If your refusal rests on a special obligation or incapacity, you may still affirm the deed is just; but if you would not do it because it seems wrong, calling it just is hollow. Apply this to fruitfulness: condemn copulation without population as sterile, and honor the doughty deed of fruitful labor and increase. Do not treat the destruction of a will and proofs as harmless; whoever destroys them must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. Remember that the will applies itself exclusively to ideas: its sole achievement is consenting to an idea's undivided presence by holding it steadily before the mind, and bodily movement follows only as a supernumerary physiological incident.
