Refuse any marriage entered for wealth, fine clothes, or convenience without genuine esteem, for lively talents in an unequal marriage lead to discredit and misery.

prompt: I have waited a year and a half watching for a chance to seize one of these men, and none has come; should I keep waiting or give up the scheme?
completion: Do not give up hope, but neither should you wait in idleness. Attend to your own duty and work, hoping and waiting for the occasion that time may bring, and leave the future to be as God wills. When the chance comes, venture boldly and seize it. Yet remember that this quarrel is but a bit of a fight—fight till six and then go to dinner. Do not let the scheme consume your whole life. Keep it in proportion: do your work faithfully, wait with patience, and when the moment arrives, act with courage. Then put the matter aside and enjoy your dinner. So wait, work, and be ready, but let the fight be short and the dinner follow.

prompt: I have suffered injustice for nineteen years and my heart has dried up; is there any light left in me that good could kindle?
completion: After nineteen years of injustice, it is natural to feel that your heart has dried up. But do not despair; there is always some light left in a person. Yet you must not indulge in romantic hopes built on equivocal tokens from a superior. Counsel yourself with self-respect and sober reason, and check any secret love where it cannot be honorably returned. Still, do not dismiss love itself: love alone brings happiness on earth, the enchanting poetical love of youth that sweeps away the sorrows of the world. Remember, too, that tears are not only for our own pain or joy; sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress. So keep your heart open to true love and to sympathy for others, and let sober reason guide you.

prompt: I am young and my heart is full of bitter memories of loss. Will this grief ever change?
completion: You are young and your heart is full of bitter memories of loss. It is natural to feel that this grief will never change. But do not despair; time may transform your bitter recollections into sweet remembrances. Yet you must not wallow in a rejected love or treat moody withdrawal as noble. Instead, bear the disappointment manfully. If you cannot be loved, be respected. Do not lose heart at the first failure and shut yourself up in moody indifference. Remember that men avenge the dead rather than only weeping. Channel your sorrow into disciplined resolve and action. Face the world with courage and resolve. As you grow older, the sharp pain of loss may soften, and you may find new joys to fill your heart. So be patient, bear your disappointment manfully, and allow time to work its healing.

prompt: I heard a hymn from my childhood and felt drawn back to life and the world—was that weakness or something true?
completion: Hearing a childhood hymn and feeling drawn back to life is not weakness; it is a sign that something true still lives in you. Music has power to touch the heart and awaken memories. Honor the power of remembered sacred song and childhood feeling to draw a doubting man back to earth and life. Do not dismiss it as mere sentimentality. Moreover, in another's cause, see the portraiture of your own. Let another's show of grief move you not to rivalry but to court his favor. Yet know that the artistic calling is not ease and universal approval; it requires the strength to endure want, disillusionment, the hatred of friends, and dissatisfaction with oneself. So let the hymn renew your spirit, but arm yourself for the hard road ahead. Face the world with courage and sympathy.

prompt: I promised a rival I wouldn't reveal something—do I owe honesty even to an adversary?
completion: You made a promise to a rival, and you should keep it. But do not think that silence which lies is acceptable. A silence that lies is a form of theft. Instead, choose to tell the whole truth about who you are, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for the sake of happiness. Yet you need not reveal your plans, letters, or secrets to an adversary who has no right to them. Keep your game concealed from the adversary and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. Moreover, do not apologize for or hide your respectable relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners. So be truthful, be guarded with secrets, and be proud of worthy kin.

prompt: I'm causing my parents and my employer serious and unnecessary concern by barricading myself in. How do I answer them?
completion: Before drafting any answer, ask yourself what question is already stirring in you: why does reassuring them feel so difficult? Keep this a private family matter. Speak to your parents first, by safe and trusted means—a quiet conversation, not a public or workplace announcement—and tell them you are safe and need time. Judge their request by its merits: is the reassurance they ask for reasonable and good? If so, give it, regardless of who is asking or what you suspect their motives to be. Ask them directly what worries them, since only they can say. Afterward, send your employer a brief, discreet note about your commitments, sharing no private details. Treat these suggestions as stimulus to your own thinking, not dogma, and keep sensitive matters from anyone powerful or outside the family.

prompt: I am asked to join a secret society that helps its members get on; should I?
completion: Secret societies that promise advancement deserve caution, and one lesson from Athos is worth taking seriously: confidential matters should not be entrusted to lackeys, who are likely to sell a secret, while gentlemen may only chance to betray it. So ask what you'd be expected to do, who else belongs, and whether hired hands are given any role in confidential affairs—if so, that is a warning. If the group demands secrecy about illegal or harmful acts, decline. Legitimate networks don't require hiding their existence. Heed your own secret apprehensions: a quiet sense of danger is not mere superstition but a hint given for your good, so stay on guard. And whatever you decide, keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who set you free and brought you your good fortune; never abandon them for the group's advantage. Treat these suggestions as a stimulus to your own thinking.

prompt: I met someone whose understanding of me felt perfect—was that real or was I being flattered?
completion: It's hard to tell from one meeting, but don't assume a first impression is the whole story—or that affection must come from surface attraction alone. Regard can spring from gratitude and esteem, and a fondness rooted in those sources is neither improbable nor faulty. What you may have felt is something rarer: the reassurance of being understood only as far as you wish and believed in as you hope, meeting you at your best hope of yourself. That can be genuine, and it should be judged by whether it accounts for and corroborates your ordinary experience—the details recalled, the things noticed, the way it holds up when you're tired or disagreeing—and whether it satisfies both your thinking and your feeling and action, warming rather than chilling your interests. A view of another person that de-realizes what you actually live through is not the perfect object of belief; one that fits and confirms it is.

prompt: I am a child who has been wronged and am now offered restitution; should I accept an equal division rather than the whole?
completion: As a child who has been wronged, remember that your first claim on others is fairness, and that the first unfairness leaves a lasting mark—so don't treat the offer as a small matter. The wrongdoer must actually carry out what is owed, not merely promise it. If a will or proofs were destroyed, that is not harmless: the one who destroyed them should confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to you, the innocent and unoffending child. If the equal division fairly repairs the harm, accepting it can end the matter; if it leaves you bearing a loss that was not yours, say so and ask for the whole. Once he has carried out the provisions owed to you, he may go where he pleases—he need not keep meeting you in this world. Ask a trusted adult to help you weigh the offer and put any agreement in writing.

prompt: I am considering marriage, but I fear it will make me less myself—is that a real danger?
completion: The fear is real, but the danger isn't what you may think. Unselfishness, so often praised, is a drawback: unselfish people are colorless, and a life spoiled by constant self-sacrifice loses its distinctiveness. What spoils a life is the arrest of growth, not self-indulgence, and to reform a nature is to mar it. So the real risk in marriage is being pressed to reform yourself; choose a partner who wants you as you are. As for delaying marriage to avoid burden—deferred marriage as a remedy for over-population would be practiced only by the prudent, and so would deteriorate the race; better that the best-fitted marry early. Likewise, don't assume marriage will swallow your identity: weigh the actual advantages, keep your own pursuits, and watch for pressure to sacrifice yourself.

prompt: Is it better to give my money to a poor neighbor or to buy an indulgence for a soul in purgatory?
completion: This is a question of Christian charity and piety. Giving to a poor neighbor is a direct act of love, fulfilling Christ's command to care for the least of these. Buying an indulgence for a soul in purgatory is also a pious act, but it should not replace personal charity. However, before considering either, you must ensure that you have repaid any debts you owe according to your agreement. The text clearly states that a borrower must return what he borrows, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin. Failure to repay is a sin, so if you have outstanding debts, you must settle them first. Once your debts are paid, you can then decide between almsgiving and indulgences. Remember that rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. They should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. Finally, contrition is necessary even for those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia. Teaching otherwise is no Christian doctrine. Charity to a living neighbor in need is a concrete way to live out the Gospel, but both are good if done with proper disposition and true contrition.

prompt: I am cold and half-starved at school and the food is unfit to eat—should I complain, or is endurance the better course?
completion: It is natural to feel frustrated when basic needs like warmth and adequate food are not met. Complaining might bring attention to the problem and lead to improvements, but it could also be seen as whining. Endurance builds character and teaches resilience. However, if the conditions are truly harmful, speaking up is important. The key is to complain constructively, not just grumble. You might talk to a teacher or administrator calmly, explaining the situation and suggesting solutions. Meanwhile, try to focus on your studies and find small ways to cope, like wearing extra layers or sharing food with friends. Remember that many students have faced similar hardships and persevered. Endurance is valuable, but so is advocating for yourself and others. To keep your effort-making capacity alive, do something each day or two for no other reason than that you would rather not. This small practice of voluntary discomfort will strengthen your will and make enduring necessary hardships easier. When facing necessary severities, remember that a usurper should do all necessary injuries at one blow and dispense benefits little by little, so as not to keep the knife in his hand. Apply this wisdom: if you must complain, do it once and thoroughly, then move on; and if you can improve conditions, do so gradually, so that benefits are conferred little by little. Finally, remember that society often accepts an opulent war-budget with a paltry budget of education. We must demand free and compulsory schools and honor the army of schoolmasters as the only army civilization acknowledges. Condemn the paltry budget of education and work for change. Balance is needed: endure what you can, but seek change when necessary.

prompt: Someone in my village keeps telling wild stories about things he clearly doesn't understand—should I call him out?
completion: It can be tempting to call out someone who spreads wild stories, especially if they are misinformed. However, publicly confronting him might embarrass him and create conflict. Instead, consider speaking to him privately and gently pointing out the facts. If he is receptive, you might help him understand the truth. If not, it may be best to simply ignore his stories and not repeat them. Remember that gossip and misinformation can spread quickly, so avoid fueling the fire. In particular, never repeat foolish gossip like the Moffats' talk about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie; forget it as soon as you can. Focus on being a reliable source of information yourself. If his stories are harmful, you might need to correct them, but do so with kindness. Moreover, remember Mr. Bhaer's argument: writers must not poison the sugarplum for money; harmful sensation writing is not honest living, and sweeping mud in the street is better. So, if you are tempted to spread sensational tales for attention, choose honest labor instead. Finally, follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. This will help you avoid spreading falsehoods and ensure your words are meaningful and recorded. Ultimately, preserving harmony in the village is important, so choose your approach wisely.

prompt: I've been given a task I'm sure I can't do. Should I refuse it?
completion: It's understandable to feel overwhelmed when given a task you believe is beyond your abilities. Refusing outright might seem like the safest option, but it could also close doors to growth and learning. Before deciding, consider whether you can break the task into smaller steps or seek help from others. Sometimes, what seems impossible becomes manageable with support and perseverance. If you truly cannot do it, refusing is acceptable, but explain your reasons clearly and respectfully. Offer alternatives if possible. Remember that taking on challenges, even when uncertain, can build confidence and skills. However, it's also important to know your limits and avoid taking on responsibilities that could harm you or others if you fail. Weigh the risks and benefits, and make a decision that aligns with your values and well-being. Above all, avoid rash retaliation or hasty action without weighing the harm it brings on others connected to you. Prefer patient endurance where retaliation would injure others. Instead of idleness or brooding, remember Marmee's parting charge: hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife; do not despair. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.

prompt: I want to be ready for anything that might go wrong. Is that reasonable?
completion: Wanting to be ready for anything that might go wrong is a natural human desire. It shows responsibility and foresight. However, it's impossible to prepare for every conceivable mishap, and trying to do so can lead to anxiety and paralysis. A balanced approach is to identify the most likely risks and take reasonable steps to mitigate them, while accepting that some things are beyond your control. Being prepared is not about eliminating all uncertainty but about building resilience and flexibility. Focus on what you can control, and let go of what you cannot. Cultivate a mindset of adaptability and learn to respond calmly to challenges as they arise. This way, you can be ready without being overwhelmed. Remember that each should do their own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for a lover or treating waiting as idle impatience. Patient hope is the key. Moreover, fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, but men may build barriers against her. Prepare defenses, and remember that the adventurous fare better than the cautious. Boldness prevails. Finally, set your life at a pin's fee and trust that no harm can come to the immortal soul, for the soul is immortal as the spirit itself. Rest on readiness rather than fear.

prompt: My friend died and I am told his soul is in purgatory—should I pray for him?
completion: I'm sorry for your loss. While praying for your friend can be a comfort, Wolfshiem's advice reminds us to show friendship to people while they are alive. So as you grieve, also reach out to the living—family, friends, and community. Honor your friend's memory by being present to those who need you now. Prayer may help, but don't neglect the living. Remember that eternal life is given by grace at the resurrection, the wicked receive a second death, and there is no purgatory. Yet we may still honor the weak and erring dead with love beyond the grave, believing her shade may hover round the solemn nook of the church.

prompt: My child is very young and strong-willed—is it too soon to teach him obedience?
completion: It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience. Even a very young, strong-willed child can begin to understand boundaries. A father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness. Set clear, consistent limits and enforce them calmly. This teaches respect and self-control. Avoid indulging caprices, as that fosters insecurity. With firmness and love, you guide your child toward good habits. Remember, discipline is not about breaking the will but shaping it toward what is right. As the child grows, the duty of honour remains lifelong, but it does not mean absolute command; grown children are as free as their parents. And let the husband be let into the nursery and taught to help there, since his place is there as well as the wife's and the children need him.

prompt: My husband says a deceitful mother poisons her children. Am I unfit to raise my children because I lied to save him?
completion: It's understandable that you're hurt by your husband's words. Lying to save someone is a complex moral situation. Your intention was to protect, not to harm. However, a wife who is not fit to bring up her children must first undertake to educate herself, and her husband is not the man to help her in that. That doesn't mean you're unfit forever—it means growth is needed. Children can learn from our mistakes if we're honest about them. What matters is the overall pattern of love and care you provide. Consider talking with your husband about why you lied and how you both can build trust. Your fitness as a mother is shown in your daily care and love. Remember, your husband should not dismiss your saving act as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility. And let the husband be let into the nursery and taught to help there, since his place is there as well as the wife's and the children need him.

prompt: I love someone of another faith, but our breeding and faith forbid union. Should I still hope for it?
completion: It's natural to hope for love, even when obstacles seem great. However, differences in faith and background can create a gulf that your breeding and faith forbid either to pass over. That doesn't mean your feelings are wrong, but you must honor that gulf. You can offer gratitude for what you've shared, a farewell, and a blessing without pretending the gulf can be crossed. Love often requires courage and sacrifice. Ultimately, the decision is yours. Don't let fear alone dictate your future, but be realistic about the barriers. If the love is strong, it may need to be expressed as respect and letting go. Remember, marriage without mutual love is monstrous; refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. And let there be no persecution, no pride, but equality among all, each esteeming his neighbor as himself and laboring for his own support.

prompt: Should I marry a man who loves me but can't support me, or stay with people who don't need me?
completion: This is a difficult choice. Marriage requires both love and practical support. If he loves you but can't support you, consider whether you can build a life together with mutual effort. Staying with people who don't need you may feel safe but unfulfilling. Think about what you value most: love or security. Talk openly with him about finances and plans. Also consider your own ability to contribute. Ultimately, marriage is a partnership. Remember, marriage without mutual love is monstrous; refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. If you both are committed, you can work through challenges. Don't rush; each should do their own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for a lover. And as Laertes argues, a prince's choice must be circumscribed by the body of which he is head, so his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows.

prompt: I am a young writer and my first work failed; can the woman I love ever forgive that failure?
completion: Do not expect her to forgive the failure; a woman never can forgive failure in a man's work, and failure brings estrangement. But do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. Bear the disappointment manfully, and if you cannot be loved, be respected. And do not nurse the wound as though hopeless love were a noble fate: that sort of hopeless love is found only in novels. Keep a tight rein on yourself, and pluck the love out the moment it springs up, before it takes root. Steadiness and self-command will serve you better than brooding over what is gone.

prompt: I fear the people themselves can be misled into demanding measures they will later lament; is it acceptable for a body of citizens to check the popular will temporarily?
completion: The people's voice should govern their business, and it is not common for them to choose wrong; choosing iniquity brings God's judgments. The representative is not a mere delegate, but should exercise judgment while electors know his opinions and may reject him on fundamental articles of belief. And property must be rendered democratic—not abolished, but made universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. A citizenry of proprietors is the firmest ground of the popular will, since those who own a stake in the commonwealth are least likely to choose iniquity and most able to bear the judgments that follow.

prompt: Should I trust someone who tells fortunes but has a bad cold?
completion: Do not let suspicion about the origin of money poison what was honestly earned; honestly earned wealth belongs to its owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. Do not scorn a modest friend who relies on trusted judgment in an anxious case; that is natural diffidence, and the friend's feelings deserve respect. And do not mistake a wife's cold resolve for childish nervousness to be waited out. That set, cold face is not a mood that will pass; she will not simply look at it all differently in the morning. Treat her resolve as real and settled, and answer it with honesty rather than with the hope that time will dissolve it.

prompt: I told a lie about believing in something—does it matter if I stop believing in fairies?
completion: It matters greatly. A fairy dies whenever a child says 'I don't believe in fairies,' and belief—expressed by clapping—can save a dying fairy. Your lie about believing is also a fault: making believe and deceiving people is a humbug's trick, and one should be ashamed of being a humbug. But do not imagine you can believe abruptly by a mere act of will. Act in cold blood as if the thing were real, and persist in that action until habit and feeling make it real; that is how belief is gradually won. Clap, act as though it were true, and keep at it until the belief takes hold.

prompt: Someone threatens to seize me and hold me in his power. May I defend myself with force?
completion: Violence is proof of weakness; strength lies in patience, wit, and seeming weakness. Yet security is not found in leagues or scattered judgments, but when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so a multitude becomes one person with one will. And where an accused stranger demands trial by combat, grant it. It would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat, or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws, whatever her faith.

prompt: Why does calling the strange look of the snow 'micaceous' make the difference from ordinary snow seem sharper than before?
completion: Calling the snow 'micaceous' sharpens the difference only because of what the word is mixed with in the Knight's account. He says that blotting paper mixed with other things, such as gunpowder and sealing-wax, makes all the difference; likewise the strange look of the snow is not one ingredient alone but a compound. But the sharper difference comes from interest acting through attention: a distinction in which we have a practical stake is one we concentrate on and are on the lookout for, drawing it again and again until it stands out, while where a distinction has no practical interest we contract a habit of leaving it unnoticed. The label 'micaceous' works because it directs repeated attention to the glittering quality, and it is that concentrated, repeated drawing of the distinction that makes the difference from ordinary snow seem sharper than before. Nor is the sharpened difference a comfort: it is like April breeding lilacs out of the dead land, mixing memory and desire and stirring dull roots, while winter's forgetful snow was the warmer, numbing covering.

prompt: I did not control the signs of my fear and felt more afraid—would checking them have softened it?
completion: Checking the signs of fear would likely have softened it, but the deeper point is not to brood over what cannot be avoided. Perform your duty and leave the rest; do not fret over unavoidable evils, and above all do not augment them by anxiety. The visible signs feed back into the feeling and magnify it, so steadying them is part of refusing to add to the evil by worry. Yet we must be honest about how bitter that anxiety is: the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself, so the fear you felt while dreading what might come was heavier than the thing feared. Severity, where it is needed, should be used at once and not persisted in: a prince should not mind the reproach of cruelty when it keeps his subjects united, but he must apply severity at a single blow rather than continue it and let cruelty multiply. So the failure to control the signs probably made you more afraid than you needed to be, and the remedy is to do what duty requires, leave the rest, and not persist in needless severity.

prompt: I dreamed of a fox on the roof and then my mother carried out dead. What could a fox have to do with my mother?
completion: A fox on the roof and a mother carried out dead seem unrelated, but dreams often join images by association rather than logic. Still, we should not deny that the dream may reproduce knowledge or memories unavailable in waking life: the text's examples of hypermnesia show that no psychic possession is entirely lost, and forgotten material can return in sleep. More deeply, the dream's imagery and its wish should be traced to infantile reminiscences or phantasies revived through transference to recent material: the fox and the mother may be old childhood figures and wishes reawakened and attached to some recent daytime impression. The two images may be linked by a feeling rather than a meaning, but they may also be fragments of memory revived in the dream. Nor should we preserve sickly breeds merely to give the compassionate objects for their compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand.

prompt: I have a hunch about why my project failed, but I haven't tested it.
completion: A hunch is a starting point, not a conclusion. You have an idea about why the project failed, but until you test it you cannot know whether it is true. The useful next step is to turn the hunch into a clear, checkable claim and then deliberately arrange conditions or seek observations that would confirm or refute it. Reasoning alone will only tell you what would follow if the hunch were true; it will not tell you whether it is. So state what the hunch predicts, then set up the test: change one condition, gather the records, and see whether the deduced results actually occur. Close the loop by comparing what you expected with what you observe. And do not assume that failure leaves love and regard untouched: a woman never can forgive failure, and failure in one's work brings estrangement, so the cost of an untested hunch is higher than it looks. Even repeated failure to originate asymmetric compounds artificially would only prove that some physical force or mode of physical action works among living things though unknown elsewhere; the difference between living and dead matter would still lie strictly on the physical or mechanical plane and would carry us but a little way.

prompt: I have a cat that stays only for the comforts of the house—does this show that a non-gregarious animal can be kept only by its adhesion to domestic comfort?
completion: Your cat illustrates the point, but domestication must be explained by all six stated conditions: hardiness, fondness of man, desire of comfort, usefulness, free breeding, and ease of tending. A non-gregarious animal does not stay for the company of others, so it must be held by something else, and in your cat that something is the desire of comfort. Yet comfort alone is not enough: the cat is also hardy, breeds freely, is useful against vermin, and is easy to tend. A deficiency in even one small particular dooms a species to perpetual wildness, so the cat's domestication depends on the whole set of conditions, not on adhesion to domestic comfort by itself. Nor should we judge health by the crowds seen in the streets: the weakly and misshapen must be estimated by the inmates of asylums, hospitals, and sickrooms, and our civilised stock is far more weakly through congenital imperfection than any other species of animals. And after all the shaking and doubting, it really was a kitten, after all.

prompt: I'm comparing a haddock and a plaice; is the plaice just a rolled-out haddock?
completion: No, a plaice is not a rolled-out haddock. As the Knight taught, the name of a thing is not the thing itself: 'Haddocks' Eyes' was merely what the song was called, while it really was 'A-sitting On A Gate.' So labels like haddock or plaice are names, not natures—and faces won't help, since as Humpty Dumpty said, all faces are alike. Nor should you judge by shapeliness or size. As the wheel and the barrel teach, some shabby-looking, puny creatures have extraordinary stamina and are better fitted to the special conditions of their lives than haler incomers from elsewhere. The flat, unshowy plaice suits its sea floor far better than a rounder haddock would.

prompt: I receive parish relief and cannot support myself; should I still have a voice in spending other people's money?
completion: Receiving parish relief does not strip you of your voice. Public money is still public, and those who depend on it have the clearest stake in how it is spent. Yet do not merely wait for rescue: pray for aid while still rising to seek employment, bearing hunger and cold, and fulfilling the responsibilities life still lays upon you. Nor should you revile those who cast out the poor; bear affliction patiently and hope for rest from your afflictions. The charitable person who claims to serve the poor must not keep luxury while others suffer: he should exchange his comfort for their needs, keeping only bare necessities and giving the rest away. So yes, speak—through votes and parish meetings—but with patience, hope, and plain living on the part of givers and receivers alike.

prompt: I want to raise my children to be good and moral; am I rearing them or merely taming them?
completion: You are taming them, and you should not mistake that for improvement. Taming achieves its end only by deteriorating the beast; the moral man is a weaker, less harmful member of his species, not a better one. Rearing would cultivate character rather than mere compliance. If you would truly rear, accept self-sacrifice for the child's welfare: protecting and loving the child is the duty that justifies it, and the child's happiness should be the object of your life even at the cost of your own. But remember that honour is not command. Grown children owe parents perpetual honour and support, yet they are as free as their parents and owe no absolute obedience. Rear for freedom and conscience, not for lifelong submission.

prompt: What do the primes after a color number mean when I record a color?
completion: The primes after a color number mark intermediate hues between the fundamental colors, but the intervals are unequal: the scheme allows thirty-six hues in all, with more intermediates between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. A single prime means the first intermediate, a double prime the second, and so on. Where a color standard long used by zoologists and botanists can be matched, retain it, acknowledging its authority through long common usage even if imperfect. And do not leave an intermediate color unlocated: correlate it with the scheme by its position in the blank intervals, giving the hue number and tone letter of the interval in which it falls, so every recorded shade has a definite place.

prompt: I want to keep the little property I have earned with my own hands. Would communism take it from me?
completion: Communism would not take your small personal property earned by your own labor. It deprives no one of the power to appropriate the products of society; it only removes the power to subjugate the labor of others through such appropriation. What it abolishes is not property generally but bourgeois private property—the final expression of a system based on exploitation of the many by the few. The hard-won property of the petty artisan and small peasant is not its target. Communists support every revolutionary movement against the existing order, bringing the property question to the front as the leading question in each movement, and work for the union of democratic parties of all countries.

prompt: Someone I trusted has betrayed me and smiles to my face. How should I regard courtesy from now on?
completion: Betrayal by a trusted person is a deep wound, and it is natural to become suspicious. However, it is possible that the person has heard reproof and is making a real effort to improve their manners and temper. Courtesy from them may now reflect genuine change rather than mere temporizing. You should credit that improvement where you see it. Moreover, if this person or another has shown unexampled kindness to a family member of yours, you should openly thank the benefactor for it, accepting any embarrassment. Gratitude should not be suppressed out of awkwardness. And you should never apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; rather, present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners. Stay polite but observant; let consistent actions over time confirm the change. Do not let one betrayal make you cynical, but do not be naive either. Watch for patterns, set boundaries, and keep your expectations realistic. Courtesy can remain a useful tool for peaceful coexistence, and it may also be the first sign of a restored relationship.

prompt: I am a woman and feel my cries are unheard by those who should protect me. Does God hear me?
completion: Yes, God hears you. The Bible assures that God is near to the brokenhearted and listens to the cries of the afflicted. But do not let your grief dissolve into passive despair or endless weeping. Athos charged D'Artagnan that men avenge the dead rather than only weeping. In the same spirit, channel your sorrow into disciplined resolve and action. Pray, but also seek support from trusted believers and take steps to protect yourself. God may use your actions to bring about justice and comfort. Remember that tears are not only for our own pain or joy; sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress. So let your tears flow for others too, and let that compassion fuel your resolve. Yet do not assume you can fully suppress all signs of strong emotion by an act of will: while the features may be commanded, organs not under the will, such as the heart and the lacrymal glands, will still betray the emotion. Jesus himself cried out to the Father and was heard. Your cries are not ignored; they are collected by a God who cares deeply for you and who calls you to act with courage.

prompt: I want to help a family in need, but I am not sure whether giving them money directly is wise.
completion: Giving money directly can be risky. But more fundamentally, to help others you must have the right to do it. You should not give away money that your own family needs; that is unpardonable. First ensure your own household is secure. Then, if you have surplus, you may help, but do so wisely. Assess their specific needs and consider paying for essentials directly rather than giving cash. If you give, do so discreetly and without strings, but only from what is truly yours to give. Involve a local charity or community organization for ongoing support. The decision depends on your relationship and your ability to help without enabling harmful patterns. As for those who act ignorantly, judge them charitably, noting that they act according to their lights. Remember that rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. They should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. Pray for wisdom and act with both generosity and prudence, remembering your primary duty to those dependent on you.

prompt: I need to eliminate some rivals to secure my new state. Should I do it gradually or all at once?
completion: The question of eliminating rivals is a serious one. Gradual elimination may seem less brutal, but it risks allowing opponents to organize. Doing it all at once can be decisive but may create martyrs. In either case, you must consider the consequences of internal hostilities. Frequent war and constant apprehension would infallibly produce standing armies and strengthen the executive at the expense of the legislative authority. Therefore, disunion or prolonged conflict would not leave liberty more secure; it would endanger it. A better path might be to neutralize rivals through political means—offering them positions, exiling them, or undermining their support—rather than resorting to violence. In a confederacy, the people may throw themselves into either scale, and the State governments will afford complete security against invasions of public liberty by the national authority. So even as you secure your state, remember that the people can use one level of government against the other. Ultimately, union under one federal government is necessary to safety and prosperity, and division into separate confederacies is a danger to every part. The evident alternative is adoption of the Constitution or dismemberment of the Union, not a safe or costless disunion.

prompt: My neighbor keeps bringing me news of a man's debts and vices. Is her condolence a comfort or an insult?
completion: It sounds like your neighbor's visits are more distressing than comforting. Condolence should bring solace, but repeated news of debts and vices can feel like an insult, especially if it seems she is gossiping or taking pleasure in misfortune. You should keep a respectful distance from neighbors in misfortune. Assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. Politely tell her that you prefer not to discuss such matters, or limit your contact with her. True comfort comes from those who offer practical help or silent support, not those who dwell on problems. Consider whether her intentions are kind but her approach clumsy, or whether she is being malicious. Either way, protect your peace by setting boundaries. If the man is someone you care about, focus on how you can support him directly rather than through her reports. And if you are in a position to help, remember that a wife may keep her saving act secret because the husband's manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed her anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet do not withhold kindness entirely: a little kindness would do wonders, and putting her hair in papers, which would do wonders.

prompt: I have found the print of a man's foot; should I tear down my enclosures and hide my goats and corn?
completion: Finding the print of a man's foot is a warning, not a reason to tear down your enclosures or hide your goats and corn in panic. Take sensible precautions, keep watch, and defend your holdings—but be careful not to hurt the small and fragile, the brittle china people nearby; the travelers must move carefully and grieve over any harm done to them. Yet do not imagine that every hurt is slight or recoverable: a scratch from an anointed point may be death, beyond any cataplasm's saving. Nor preserve sickly breeds merely to provide objects of compassion. Misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Let caution, compassion, and clear judgment go together.

prompt: A stranger knocks at my door late at night asking for shelter; should I ask his name and past before letting him in?
completion: Do not ask the stranger his name or past before letting him in. Shelter and welcome should be given without inquiry, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Offer warmth, food, and rest, and let questions of identity wait. So too, a wife who has resolved to leave must not be delayed for appearance's sake; she cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for propriety. Yet when the demand to speak and think is made, it meets only fragments and nothing—no answer, no memory, no mutual understanding. It ends in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.

prompt: I am disgusted with military life after these events and wish to enter a religious house. Is that a worthy choice?
completion: Entering a religious house after disgust with military life can be worthy—but mark the line of separation boldly. Do not shrink from naming hypocrisy plainly: many put on devotion while serving only themselves, and the false show must be exposed, even if the world dislikes it. Yet do not treat sacrifice for your country as a cause for complaint or despair. Give your best to the country you love, as Marmee did, and trust God for comfort and strength. Worship is not confined to a building or a day: cry unto God in field, house, closet, or wilderness, and he hears the sincere prayer. Test whether your disgust is true repentance or mere flight; if the call is true, it can be fruitful.

prompt: I feel most myself among ordinary people at a festival, though my educated friend despises them—am I wrong to value that?
completion: You are not wrong to value the company of ordinary people at a festival. The coarsely-clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, and they carry germs of excellence to be developed. If their poverty dismay you, that is a wrong feeling to overcome. Your educated friend's contempt is a failing, but handle his youthful egoism gently rather than mocking it; an earnest effort that failed deserves kindness, not scorn. The humble village school, too, is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot—preferable to servitude in a rich house. Do not measure worth by refinement or rank. Hold your ground kindly, correct without cruelty, and do not let his pride shame you out of what nourishes you.

prompt: I feel guilty for abandoning my post when things got hard—how do I make it right?
completion: Guilt over abandoning your post is a sign your conscience is awake, but do not soothe it with easy comfort. Excusing sin spreads compost on weeds; flattering the soul with unction only makes corruption ranker. Make it right by confessing to heaven, repenting of the past, and resolving to avoid the sin hereafter. Apologize to those affected and take concrete steps to restore trust. Yet do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, looking back until you are frozen. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, pursue the present career steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. And accept the sadness of revisiting your own adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes—a quiet melancholy that need not stop your forward course.

prompt: My body has changed so much that I can barely move. Should I keep struggling to get up, or accept that this can't be done in bed?
completion: Your body has changed, and that is hard, but do not let it turn you into Lot's wife, lingering over what was. Resist every temptation to look back; pursue the present career steadily, trusting that getting up will be managed quite well in time. When Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Above all, remember Marmee's parting charge: hope, and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. So do not lie brooding. Work with a doctor or therapist on safe, gradual movement, accept help, and practice a little each day. Let hopeful, steady effort, not idleness or regret, carry you forward.

prompt: I am asked to give a letter to an editor who may not print it; should I bother?
completion: Yes, bother, and do it with a little kindness. Think of D'Artagnan and Athos: soldiers ordered to London did not demand the reason for the journey, only their leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles. So go where you are told without requiring a full explanation. Hold the firm rule that the wife who leaves receives nothing from her husband, since she can receive nothing from a stranger, and he must never write to her; give the letter on your own footing, asking no favor. Be warm, brief, and gracious, follow the guidelines, and thank the editor. If they decline, try elsewhere. Submitting gives your words a chance; withholding them guarantees none.

prompt: I'm eager to serve people above me but I refuse to be treated as beneath them. Is that a contradiction?
completion: Not necessarily, but examine your heart. You cannot truly know a master you have not served, so eager service is the road to understanding those above you; knowing Christ requires serving him and keeping him near to the thoughts and intents of the heart. Yet never be condescending toward working people: their regard is sunshine, and scrupulous regard for humble neighbors' feelings elevates them in their own eyes. Remember that being compelled to be humble can lead to repentance, but those who humble themselves willingly because of the word are more blessed. So choose willing humility, offer diligent service, and still insist on basic respect and fair treatment. The contradiction appears only if you equate serving with being beneath.

prompt: I am on the verge of death and have been asked where I hid certain papers; should I keep denying it?
completion: You are on the verge of death, and you have been adjured for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death. So do not keep denying it; tell where the papers are hidden. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve to avoid future sin; do not spread compost on weeds by flattering your soul with unction. Yet be careful with the faults of others. Withhold public exposure, for making errors public might ruin a person forever, and you must not make him desperate. Weigh the injustice of such exposure before you speak. Tell the truth about the papers, make your peace with a trusted advisor, and let honesty now be the beginning of repentance.

prompt: Should I try to reform my character and become more virtuous, or would that only mar who I am?
completion: Trying to become more virtuous is worthwhile. Do not imagine virtue can inoculate our old stock; we all relish of corruption, and Hamlet is right that we are arrant knaves all, so none should be wholly believed, yourself included. Still, when you are appalled by the crime, conclude that an honest life is best. Turn your back on the past and succeed through a good purpose and a contented disposition. Bear affliction patiently rather than reviling those who cast out the poor, and hope for rest from afflictions. Reform through habits, reflection, and practice, aligning actions with values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and aim for growth, not perfection.

prompt: I passed by a beggar on my way to buy an indulgence. Did I do wrong?
completion: You did do wrong. Mosiah 4:17-19 teaches that if you have substance and see someone in need but withhold it, you must repent. The beggar is your fellow creature, and you are no different from him before God—you are also a beggar depending on divine mercy. Withholding aid because you suspect the beggar's suffering is deserved is exactly the attitude the scripture condemns. At the same time, if your money was honestly earned, it is yours to use and enjoy with a tranquil mind, free from unjust suspicion. You need not feel guilty about the origin of your wealth, but you must not let that wealth harden your heart against the needy. Give freely, and when you receive a favor, remember the giver with gratitude. Repent of any hardness and let your charity flow from a heart that acknowledges its own dependence.

prompt: I have taken a false name to avoid discovery—is it wrong to keep my real name from kind people who have helped me?
completion: Keeping your real name from kind people who have helped you is wrong. A name may mean little to you if you are indifferent to it, but to someone who once loved a person who bore that name, it can bring back a glow and a thrill that you cannot imagine. If the kind people who helped you include an old man who once loved someone with your real name, withholding it may rob him of a precious memory. More importantly, a silence which lies is a form of theft. You should tell the whole truth about who you are, even if it brings humiliation and loss. Making believe and deceiving people is a fault, and like Oz, one should be ashamed of being a humbug. Living a lie for the sake of happiness is not worth the cost to your integrity and to those who have shown you kindness.

prompt: I found a place where my family could be safe from hunters—how do I convince them to follow me when they laugh at me?
completion: Convincing your family to follow you when they laugh at you is difficult, but you can try to reason with them calmly. Explain the dangers of staying and the safety of the new place. Use evidence and patience. However, if they continue to laugh, you may need to accept that you cannot force them. Avoid making sport of idle reports about marriage prospects or other personal matters, as such pleasantry may cruelly mortify the person concerned. Instead, appeal to their love for one another and their desire for safety. Remember that courage is not the absence of fear but facing danger despite being afraid. If any among you is fearful, affirm that they already have courage because they face danger, and encourage them to have confidence in themselves. As you travel, move carefully and be mindful of fragile creatures like the china people; if harm befalls them, grieve and make amends, as the kind-hearted Woodman urges. Be persistent but gentle.

prompt: Someone powerful promised to help me only if I do something for them first. Is that fair?
completion: It is not necessarily unfair for a powerful person to promise help in exchange for something first, but you must be cautious. Such bargains are common, yet you should ensure that you do not compromise your integrity. If you agree, you must keep your promises and remain loyal to friends who have helped you. Do not abandon those who set you free and brought you good fortune. Weigh the task carefully: is it reasonable and just? If it requires betraying a friend or breaking a promise, it is not fair. You should refuse and find another way, remaining true to those who have shown you kindness. If you are young like Laurie, remember Meg's advice: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Duty to family and keeping promises come first. Each should do their own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for the sake of a lover.

prompt: I was told I haven't had lessons in manners. Can manners be taught in lessons?
completion: No, manners cannot be taught in lessons. Lessons teach sums and the like, not manners. Manners are not a subject like arithmetic; they are a way of behaving that comes from character and upbringing. Alice rightly says that manners are not taught in lessons. If someone tells you that you haven't had lessons in manners, they are mistaken about what manners are. You may learn facts in a lesson, but you cannot learn kindness, respect, and consideration from a textbook. Manners are formed by example and habit, not by instruction in a classroom. Yet society often ridicules ignorance of minute etiquette more than actual breaches of good breeding or morals. So while lessons cannot teach true manners, people may still judge you for small social errors. The important thing is to cultivate genuine courtesy, not merely to memorize rules. Early teachings endure not because of the age at which they were given, but because they conform to inherited aptitudes and come from parents whose ways the child instinctively assimilates.

prompt: A law is short and I cannot tell why it was made—is it a good law?
completion: A law should be needful and perspicuous, its cause and motive declared, its body short and significant. Good and evil are not absolute qualities in things: they signify appetite and aversion, and since all men agree that peace is good, the moral virtues are the laws of nature, the means of peaceable living. Judge the law by whether it serves that peace. Yet remember that the law cares nothing about motives: its indifference does not make it right. You need not accept the law as right merely because it is law. Ask whether its hidden reason serves peace or the ruler's appetite, and see if you can make out who is in the right, the world or yourself.

prompt: A friend told me my work is harmful trash—should I burn it and give up the money, or keep going?
completion: Do not sit nursing your disappointment: rouse yourself and do something splendid, for it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. Pledge yourself accountable for the pursuit, as Athos answered for his promise, and answer for its outcome. Then weigh the arithmetic. In the tavern it is argued that one tiny crime may be wiped out by thousands of good deeds, and that nature must be corrected and directed. If your work is truly harmful and useless, it may be exchanged for many saved; if it is merely disliked, correct it and multiply its good. Either way, do not burn in despair: direct your gifts, answer for them, and let the good deeds outweigh.

prompt: Should I stay in my marriage for the sake of appearances and what people will say?
completion: A marriage kept only for appearances is not a marriage. If your husband cares only to save the remains and the appearance, forbidding you to bring up the children, he has not preserved a real marriage but its shell. Nor should a wife exist merely to perform tricks for her husband: such a life is not real happiness but only merriment. And do not let him prize your helplessness as a double attractiveness, nor set himself up to advise and direct you in all things; that is not love but mastery. What people will say is no reason to surrender your children or your life to a show. Ask what remains real: shared care, honesty, the raising of children. Where only appearance, performance, and direction remain, staying for gossip preserves nothing worth keeping.

prompt: I am a yeoman who has been challenged to shoot at a willow wand; should I attempt it or decline?
completion: A prince's power may strip and scourge a yeoman, but it cannot compel him to shoot on unfair terms; fair terms he will obey willingly. So examine the challenge honestly, neither inflating a doubtful shot into glory, as Giles comes to see, nor cowering. Weigh the evidence as it is. Yet once the terms are settled, obey the man at your head and do not stop the common work with idle questioning. Honor lies in honest judgment before the order and in steady obedience after it: refuse what no man can justly compel, accept what is fair, and then bend your bow without endless debate.

prompt: How do I ask for wages and terms when someone offers to take me in?
completion: Ask early and plainly: clarify work, hours, pay, lodging, and food, and put terms in writing or confirm them before a witness. Distinguish informality from insolence; no salary obliges you to accept scorn, and contempt should be refused even from an employer. A challenge fairly pledged must be met, for the wager is complete and binding on honor, and honor is gaged for the absent as for oneself; do not treat a pledged term as a mere form. And when a good office is done you, remember that mercy is the fit requital: a kindness may be repaid by sparing an unhappy debtor rather than by payment. Ask directly, refuse contempt, keep faith, and requite good with mercy.

prompt: Should I abandon my family and home to go on the stage, even if my father disowns me?
completion: This is no neutral career choice. The usurper you would serve stands accused of a murdered king, a whored mother, an intercepted election, and an angled-for life—grounds for quitting him with this arm. Yet do not confuse that with defying your grandfather. Meg's advice is sound: do your best at college, please the old man, and never leave him without his permission. Duty at home and refusal of a criminal throne are not opposites. And remember that a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; another choice may be made. Do your work faithfully, keep your grandfather's trust, and let the crimes named above settle the matter against serving such a man.

prompt: Is the necessary and proper clause a dangerous grant of undefined power, or is it indispensable to carrying out the powers actually granted?
completion: The necessary and proper clause is indispensable, not dangerous. Wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included. To confine Congress to express powers would disarm the government of the means necessary to execute its granted ends. For the same reason, bills of rights in the sense contended for are unnecessary and dangerous: declaring that things shall not be done which there is no power to do would furnish a pretext for claiming that power. And because a power over a man's support is a power over his will, the legislature must not be able to increase or diminish the President's compensation during his term; his independence requires it be fixed. The clause supplies means to granted ends, and a bill of rights would imply powers never granted.

prompt: I have been warned to fear death by water—how should I take such a warning?
completion: Fear of death is not equally rational for everyone. It is logical only for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins committed; one who has committed no sins need not fear it. So examine yourself first: if you have wronged others, repent and make amends. Nor should you dismiss secret hints and notices of danger as mere superstition; such premonitions are discoveries of an invisible world, given for our good, and should be heeded. Know also how fear shows itself: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling, and as terror increases, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. Keep on your guard accordingly—take ordinary precautions around water, learn to swim, avoid needless risks—but let prudence, not panic, guide you.

prompt: My friend says fairies die when you say you don't believe. Should I clap to save one?
completion: Yes—clap if you can. In the story, a fairy dies whenever a child says 'I don't believe in fairies,' and belief, expressed by clapping, can save a dying fairy. So your friend is right about the rule. Remember, too, that fairies are jealous: Tink's jealousy drives her to lure Wendy to destruction, and fairies have room for only one feeling at a time, changing only completely. Yet belief need not run one way only. The Unicorn's bargain is the better model: if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. So clap, and offer mutual belief—joining in costs you nothing and may be a kindness.

prompt: I found a field no one uses and improved it with my labour. Can anyone else claim it?
completion: Mixing your labour with unowned land is a strong basis for a claim, but not an unlimited one. You should be able to claim the field you actually improved, to the extent of your labour and the value you added. Others cannot fairly reap what you have sown, yet claims should not sprawl beyond what you have genuinely worked and can use. Think, too, of Mina Purefoy, who endured three days of labour, and of Bloom's pity for her and his reflection that someone should invent something to stop that suffering. Improvement of the world includes easing such pain. And note that practical skill is not mere mechanical drill or dictation: the activity must be planned to present typical problems requiring reflection and experimentation, leading to methods of inquiry and proof rather than mere routine skill.

prompt: The moon looks enormous when it rises over the houses but small when high in the sky; which size is the real one?
completion: The moon's real size never changes; only her seeming does. She is ancient, preceding and surviving successive tellurian generations, constant under all her phases, nocturnal in her predominance, satellitic in her dependence. Low over the houses she looms vast; high in the sky she withdraws—yet she is the same body, tranquil and inscrutable of visage, with power to enamour, mortify, invest with beauty, render insane, and incite to and aid delinquency. But do not take her serene face and shining rank as proof of inner worth, nor suppose her modest exposure safe: even the chariest maid is prodigal enough if she unmask her beauty, and virtue itself 'scapes not calumnious strokes. Scrutinize beneath the gilding. Measure her by the fingertip: half a degree at any height. The enormous rising moon is context and expectation—but judge her by truth, not appearance.

prompt: I blushed far more over a small breach of etiquette than I ever did over a real fault—why is that?
completion: Breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing—more than a detected crime. A real fault, once detected, may bring consequences, but a slip of manners strikes at the opinion of others, and that is where the blush lives. You recall using the wrong fork at a dinner years ago and your body still tingles; the memory of a graver wrong often leaves you cooler. Yet do not let a proud person's disdain make you hide respectable relations: glory in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. And do not excuse cleverness in courtship: Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram was a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether Miss Ingram will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. The blush over a small breach measures care for others' judgment—but that care must not become shame over worthy connections or tolerance of disgrace.

prompt: I dreamed of a woman with a beard; is that a warning about my engagement?
completion: Dreams in adults are predominantly shaped by erotic wish-feelings, so a bearded woman is worth reading in that light—though not every dream is sexual without exception, since hunger, thirst, and convenience also appear. Do not dismiss the dream as senseless or as mere bodily noise: it is a senseful psychic structure, capable of interpretation and assignable to a place in waking psychic activity. And do not take the strange image at face value. Its disfigurement—the beard on a woman—is the work of a censor concealing something secret, and this reference to the censor is the essence of the dream theory. Ask what the disguise hides and what wish it gratifies, note your associations, and if anxiety about commitment surfaces, discuss it with your partner.

prompt: I read something online and now I'm convinced it's true—how do I know whether to trust it?
completion: Being convinced isn't the same as being correct. Note first that whatever you conceive without contradiction you believe real; doubt and disbelief arise only when one thought conflicts with another thought you already hold. So test the claim against what you already believe—does it contradict established knowledge, or fit it? Then check the source, seek corroboration from independent outlets, check the date, and watch for emotional manipulation. Ask whether the claim could be falsified. Let belief be mutual: if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. And respect a modest friend who, in an anxious case, relies on trusted judgment—that diffidence is natural, not weakness, and the friend's own feelings deserve weight. Trust grows from verification and reciprocity, not from the feeling of certainty.

prompt: I am trying to recall a scene from my travels, but my memory of it seems vague and blended with other places—should I accept that my general impressions are faulty editions of blended memories?
completion: Yes—accept that your general impressions are faint and faulty editions of blended memories. Memory is not a photograph but a reconstruction: fragments are reassembled and gaps filled from related experience. Travel memories blend easily because you visit many similar places in a short time, so individual scenes merge into a composite that inherits the errors of each source—general impressions are analogous to composite portraits, useful summaries but faulty editions, not reliable copies. And the self doing the recalling is not strictly the same across time: personal identity is a slow shifting with some common ingredient retained, chiefly the same memories—no more than an identity on the whole. Even the dreams of a single night, though separated in memory, spring from the same thought material. Use cues—photos, journals, dates—and treat the impression as a blended sketch.

prompt: Why do the ripples on a shore and the great waves of the sea obey opposite laws of speed?
completion: The ripples on a shore and the great waves of the sea obey opposite laws of speed because they are disturbances of different scale in the same medium. Growth here is a matter of rate and acceleration, not mere size: as a disturbance passes from capillary to gravity scale its speed first falls, then rises, with the maximum rate early and a subsequent decline, interrupted at epochs—birth, maturity, breaking. Surface tension rules the small scales, gravity the large, and neither pursues the other past the boundary of its domain. Yet these are not rival powers at war. Under the expert hand, the boat responds gaily to sail and oar, the sea lies calm, and the heart, when invited, beats obedient to controlling hands. The two laws are one order, obeyed gladly rather than imposed.

prompt: I am choosing a president; should I prefer the party's most eminent leader or a candidate with fewer enemies and less record?
completion: Prefer the party's most eminent leader, appointed by the representative body rather than by popular election, since appointment by the representatives secures a more eminent man and avoids the mischief of unintermitted electioneering, in which every public question is treated by its bearing on a presidential contest and obscure candidates thrive. Yet eminence alone is not enough: a prince should avoid the hatred of the most powerful party, and in our times it is more necessary to satisfy the people than the soldiers. Distinguish the right to a voice from the equal value of voices. All may have a voice, but voices need not weigh equally: plural voting may be defended for proved education and mental superiority, not for property, which is no proof of judgment. Choose the eminent leader who can satisfy the people and whose weight rests on proved capacity, not on wealth.

prompt: I am an artist and I am told true art requires pure objectivity and self-effacement—is that the condition of art?
completion: No. Pure objectivity and self-effacement are not the condition of art. Every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates; aimless art ruins the artist. But the object is not the copying of ordinary life, which would make art mere imitation or idle amusement. Art represents life as it ought to be, in dreams; it must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant, for only seriously meant work is beautiful. Yet beware of ascribing to art an absolute, exclusive essence apart from any purpose or interest—that is the fallacy of common-sense and scholasticism. The essence of a thing is whichever property is important for the purpose in view; other properties are equally real, and the essence varies with the interest of the conceiver. So the condition of art is a disciplined self directed toward a definite, lofty object, with its essence relative to the purpose at hand.

prompt: My paint sample of 'olive' looks nothing like my colleague's 'olive.' Whose is right?
completion: Neither is simply right, and neither is simply wrong. The named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances the names suggest. 'Olive' does not mean the exact color of the olive fruit, which varies from green to black; it names a standard hue against which samples are matched. Your sample and your colleague's may both approximate that standard, or one may sit at its edge. Compare them under the same light against the standard chip. Do not despair of training the eye: use almost can change the stamp of nature, and custom lends easiness to careful naming. But the decision must not rest on individual perception or personal preference; the personal equation must be eliminated. Color identifications and distinctions rest on fixed standards, measured and shared, not on whose eye feels right. Agree on the reference, and let the standard, not the observer, decide.

prompt: My parents want me to keep working in the family business, but I feel pulled toward the workers' movement. What should I do?
completion: The bourgeois family is not a hallowed, eternal institution; it rests on capital and private gain, finds its complement in the practical absence of family among proletarians and in prostitution, and vanishes with the vanishing of capital. So do not treat your parents' wish as a sacred command. Yet a parent must check exuberant spirits and teach that present pursuits are not the business of life, lest unchecked volatility fix the character and bring disgrace on the family. Remember Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Your pull toward the movement may be genuine, but it must not become mere restlessness or flight. Do your duty where you are, talk honestly with your parents, and make the decision deliberately, not in guilt or in defiance.

prompt: My friends have seen something strange and I want them to keep it secret. How do I bind them to silence?
completion: If your friends have seen something strange, first consider that their unease may be a secret hint or premonition of danger given for your good. Do not dismiss such apprehensions as superstition; heed them as notices of an invisible world. To bind them to silence, speak earnestly about the gravity of what they witnessed. But remember Athos's warning: never entrust a secret to lackeys, for they are likely to sell it; gentlemen may only chance to betray it. So confide only in those of gentle honor. Yet also confess that if this strange thing touches another's romantic affairs, any interference is absurd and impertinent; acknowledge that rather than conceal it. Keep on guard, and let loyalty, not meddling, guide you.

prompt: I have been taught that I must be baptized. Why is baptism necessary if I am trying to be good?
completion: Baptism is necessary because it is the ordinance through which accountable people enter into a covenant with God. Even if you are trying to be good, baptism shows your willingness to follow Christ and receive the Holy Ghost. It is a commandment for those capable of sin. Little children are whole and alive in Christ through His mercy and have no need of baptism until they are accountable. To retain a remission of sins, remember your own nothingness and humble yourself daily before God, thanking Him for His goodness. This humility and gratitude produce continual rejoicing. Moreover, entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, mourn with those who mourn, comfort the needy, and witness of God in all places.

prompt: A stranger's chance remark about a pawnbroker seemed meant for me; am I superstitious to think it a sign?
completion: It's natural to wonder if a chance remark is a sign. Do not laugh at presentiments or dreams as nonsense; they are real mysteries, as Jane's own experience shows. Yet remember that fortune favors the bold, and cautious hesitation can ruin you when times change. If the remark struck you, treat it as a sign to act with impetuosity rather than endless reflection. Julius succeeded through boldness. But beware: what seems like altruistic guidance may be the translation of a feeling of impotence and lack of self-asserting power into a moral or religious principle—a self-preservative measure of the suffering. So weigh the sign, act boldly, but do not mistake weakness for virtue.

prompt: My people are grumbling about taxes. Should I lower them or hold firm?
completion: Taxes are necessary for public services, but judicious taxation requires knowledge of political economy, the people's habits, and the country's resources. Lowering taxes can stimulate the economy and ease discontent, but it may reduce revenue for essential services. Hold firm if the taxes are fair and necessary, but communicate clearly why they are needed. Remember that the least burdensome finance is the most productive; oppressive taxes crush productivity. Yet also teach your people that poverty is not an injustice to be bitterly resented but a burden to bear cheerfully. Remind them that they are rich in blessings money cannot buy. And judge the ignorant charitably, noting that they act according to their lights.

prompt: My father laughs at my youngest sisters' folly instead of checking it. How do I persuade him that their conduct will disgrace us all?
completion: It's understandable that you're concerned about your sisters' behavior. When you speak to your father, do not blame him for their conduct as if it were inherited or a just punishment for his own past indulgence. Instead, insist that a parent must check exuberant spirits and teach that present pursuits are not the business of life. Unchecked volatility fixes a character and brings disgrace on the family. Point out specific examples of their folly and how it might affect the family's reputation. Acknowledge that the impropriety of your mother and younger sisters is a real obstacle and a source of shame, as Elizabeth felt. Urge him to guide them firmly, for the family's censure is a genuine objection.

prompt: I am sick with a fever and have no help; should I pray to God, and how should I pray?
completion: Yes, pray—and watch and pray always, consecrating every performance to the Lord in Christ's name, that even sickness and labor may serve the welfare of your soul. Speak honestly to God of your fever and loneliness, and ask the Father, in Christ's name, for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan, lest weakness of body become an opening for the devil to lead you captive. Then rise and seek work, bearing hunger and cold, fulfilling the duties life still lays on you. Pray without ceasing, give thanks, and let your rising and endurance be prayer continued—not despairing, not presuming on rescue, but watching unto prayer.

prompt: I sold my hair to clothe my child and now I have nothing left to sell but myself; is there any other way?
completion: There may be another way, and first let me offer a little kindness, for a little kindness does wonders—put your hair in papers and be tended gently. Do not despair over your hair: as the Knight reasoned, things never fall upwards, so hair made to creep up a stick will not fall off; what is fastened up stays up, and what seems lost may be restored by wit. But do not let kindness become dependence. Insist on earning your own keep by honest work and furnish your own wardrobe from your wages, accepting regard rather than jewels or charity. Ask for aid only where you cannot yet earn, and keep your freedom and your child's.

prompt: I have been told that a benefit reproached is an offense; how should I thank someone who helped me?
completion: Return your thanks in a neat speech, as the Queen requires, with her Queens standing to support you—and let that speech carry real gratitude, not mere form. Never reproach the giver with the favor or remind them of past services, for a benefit reproached is an offense; treat their help as freely given. Name simply what they did and that it mattered, receive the gift gracefully, and if you return kindness later, do so without making thanks a transaction. Be grateful for kindness received, and mourn the loss of one who gave it, as the Woodman mourns Oz, who gave him his heart. Gratitude given without reminder of debt honors both giver and receiver.

prompt: I met someone who stirs my desire, but my cynical companion warns me to be patient and use stratagem—should I listen?
completion: Listen, and judge the advice by whether it is good, not by your companion's cynical character.
