And do not hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; rather, glory in their intelligence and manners without shame. But remember: withholding knowledge of a person's real character from your family may be a wretched mistake. Weigh the cost of silence, for failing to warn those you love can lead to deep regret.

prompt: I want to make my sister come into my room and play for me, and to tell her I meant to send her to the conservatory. Should I try?
completion: It's understandable to want your sister to play for you, but forcing her to come into your room is not wise. Follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone and it will let you alone. Instead of trying to make her come, simply invite her openly. If you truly meant to send her to the conservatory, share that honestly. But be prepared: the demand to speak and think may meet only fragments and nothing. You may find yourself in the closed car, the game of chess, pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door. Communication may fail, memory may slip, and answers may not come. So, let the door alone, and if she chooses to come, welcome her warmly. Focus on your genuine appreciation for her music, even if understanding remains elusive. And remember the plan: each sister should spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for herself. Let that spirit of selflessness guide your actions.

prompt: I am a girl who has been mocked for my limp by other girls; how do I face them?
completion: It is painful to be mocked, and the text is blunt: a defect is ten times worse in a woman, so your burden is heavier, and you should not pretend otherwise. Yet keep pity on guard, for sympathy offered freely can be used to take advantage of you; accept kindness without becoming dependent. When you face them, remember that shrugging the shoulders is no mere trick of yours but an inherited gesture, found across many races and even in the blind, expressing inability or non-resistance; it stands by antithesis to the erect, squared, fist-clenching attitude of an indignant man. So you may shrug where wrath would only injure you, while still speaking with gravity and pity of the custom that mocks, blaming the institution and honoring devoted, trusting souls, permitting wrath without malice. If mockery continues, tell a trusted adult.

prompt: I threw a party for hundreds and no one really knew me. What does that say about me?
completion: It says less about your worth than about the gap between being surrounded and being known. If there is to be a party, you ought to invite the guests yourself: the crowd should be your choice, not something that gathers while you stand passive. Yet weigh this too: a life among hundreds who do not know you is like being sent to account unhouseled and unaneled, with all imperfections on your head, for no one has shriven you by truly seeing you. And do not console yourself that the few will surely know you again on meeting; as Humpty Dumpty said, he would not know her again, because she is so exactly like other people. So let a few see what is not generic in you, and do not let the crowd stand in place of honest reckoning.

prompt: I am surrounded by associates who say that regard for number one holds us all together and keeps us from the gallows—should I trust them?
completion: Be cautious. People who say regard for number one holds us all together often mean loyalty lasts only while it pays, which is a bargain, not a bond. Test them by whether promises are kept and kindness repaid. Do not be like the one who breaks faith or abandons a friend who helped them; remember Dorothy's companions, who set them free and brought them their good fortune, and who remained loyal in return. And keep faith even toward prisoners and wrongdoers: once your word is given, be as good as your word. Before you retaliate against these associates, weigh the wider consequences, for hasty action may injure others connected to you; where retaliation would do that, prefer patient endurance. Keep your own standards, repay kindness, and do not stake your safety on a creed of pure self-interest.

prompt: I have been told that if I want to get rid of a bad habit I should resist it—is resistance the right way?
completion: Resistance sounds virtuous, but the text says the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it: resist, and the soul grows sick with longing for what it has forbidden itself. Every strangled impulse broods and poisons the mind; action is a mode of purification. So meet the need openly and let the impulse spend itself in action rather than fester. Understand too that a habit was at first performed consciously for some end and has become reflex through long habit, now occurring even when of no use. And if you learn from a teacher, remember that method includes the teacher's own mental habits and conduct, not only deliberate devices; slipshod speech or slovenly inference is quietly ratified in the pupil. So choose teachers whose unconscious habits you would be willing to inherit, and let your own conduct be part of the method.

prompt: Should doubts about indulgences be silenced by force or answered with reasons?
completion: Doubts are better answered with reasons than silenced by force, but be careful what reasons you offer. The inquiries into the unseen world do not confirm the common doctrines; much that seems supernatural arises from the mind contemplating itself, and visions are not reliable reports of another realm. Do not defend indulgences by appeal to prayer's objective efficacy or to visions as supernatural evidence. Nor ground conduct in deductive theory, or trust the spiritual sense as a reliable guide, for it is liable to illusion; given our ignorance, rely on observed facts. Force only drives doubt underground; invite it into the open and answer patiently. And remember the Palmer, who would not break his vow for a cup of mead: a pilgrim's vow may oblige him to refuse to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall. So let vows bind where they should, and let reasons, not force, settle doubts.

prompt: I long for liberty and a wider life beyond these walls, but I am told to be content—is it wrong to want more?
completion: Wanting more is not wrong, but be clear what liberty is. Subject liberty is not exemption from the laws, nor a share in sovereignty, nor a right to resist those who govern; it is the silence of the law—the absence of external impediments in those things the sovereign has left unregulated. In that space you may move, choose, and widen your life, and no one should call it a fault. But do not mistake license for freedom: liberty is endangered by abuses of liberty as well as of power, and the former are most to be apprehended. Test your longing, then, and keep it lawful. And know that a people accustomed to freedom never forgets its privileges, so those who would keep you content by benefits or by time deceive themselves; such a people must be either ruined or lived among and answered. Want more, within the silence of the law.

prompt: I found out my friend was born somewhere else—does that change whether he's my brother?
completion: No—but not because he is simply the same person, unchanged. Personal identity is a slow shifting in which some common ingredient, chiefly memory, is retained, and no more than an identity on the whole. What binds you is the chain of remembered years you share. His birthplace is no trifle either: a person's vigour, character, and diseases are principally derived from his ancestry, and relatives' life-histories are prophetic of his own future; a child's birthright includes knowing the complete life-histories of his near progenitors. So ask, and let him ask you. But mind the degree of intimacy proper to each tie: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Between friends, take the liberty your closeness has earned—no more, no less. If his conduct and memory of your friendship still hold, he is your brother in the only sense that survives change.

prompt: I'm worried my family will think something dreadful happened to me. How do I get word to them?
completion: First, heed the warning: something is going to happen, and it may happen before your message arrives. So take care of yourself now, and let the message follow. Use only safe and trusted means—a call or a short note through someone you know and trust, saying where you are, that you are safe, and when they will hear from you again. Keep this a private family affair: do not drag it before great persons or authorities, for that exposes everyone involved to danger. Give one trusted relative the job of spreading word, and ask the rest to keep a respectful distance, since in misfortune assistance is possible but condolence is insufferable. Then set a time to check in and keep it. Act quietly and while you can, because the thing that is going to happen will not wait for you.

prompt: I'm taking care of two people at once and it's exhausting. Has anyone dealt with this?
completion: Yes—many have, but not quite like this. Heed the warning that something is going to happen, and take care of yourself now. Use the Queen's method: consider your age, your journey, the time—anything—because nobody can do two things at once. Take one thing and consider it, then the next; distraction from sorrow is not evasion, it is the way it is done. And admit the strangeness of it: you are caring for two Queens asleep at once, and there never was more than one Queen at a time—no wonder you are perplexed and exhausted. Name what can be shared, protect small pockets of rest, and ask one trusted person to be your relief. Act while you can, because the thing that is going to happen will not wait. You are not alone, even when it feels that way.

prompt: Someone insulted me and I fear contempt unless I take private revenge—may I break the law to protect my reputation?
completion: No—and not merely because it costs you. Answer the false charge, but do so privately and with a moderate, accurate account: state plainly what was said, what is true, and what is false, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. Hold firm that no place should murder sanctuarize and revenge should have no bounds—it admits of no lawful exception, no safe corner, no convenient occasion. Yet do not rush to expose the other man's faults in public: making errors public might ruin a person forever, and one must not make him desperate. Weigh the injustice of exposure before you correct the record openly. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt is not cured by lawbreaking or by public ruin; it is fed by both. Defend your name by exact truth, clean conduct, and lawful remedies—retraction or complaint—used with restraint.

prompt: I'm envious of girls with nice pianos and pretty things—how do I stop envying?
completion: Envy often arises when we compare our lives to others'. To stop envying, focus on what you have and practice gratitude. Remember that everyone has different blessings and challenges. Instead of longing for a nice piano or pretty things, consider developing your own talents and interests. You could take piano lessons on a modest instrument, or find beauty in simple pleasures. Shift your attention from what you lack to what you can create. But not all praise is worth having: value the praise that comes from modesty and good character. Win admiration by being modest as well as beautiful. Keep in mind that originality, though producing its own reward, does not invariably conduce to success—as Bloom's own ideated and rejected project of an illuminated showcart shows. So do not envy others' success, for it may not bring happiness. When disappointed, do not give in to idleness or self-pity. Rouse yourself and do something splendid. It is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want.

prompt: I once broke off an engagement to marry a richer man to support my mother and brothers. Was I heartless?
completion: Breaking off an engagement is never easy, and your decision to support your mother and brothers was likely made with careful thought. But marriage without mutual love is monstrous; it should not be a mere arrangement for labor or duty. You should refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Remember that a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; another choice may be made. A woman who broke with a man for a more lucrative chance may have acted from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers, not from heartlessness. Wanting to provide for family is admirable, and it doesn't make you heartless. However, consider whether you communicated openly with your former fiancé and whether you gave yourself time to grieve the relationship. Your actions show responsibility, not a lack of heart. Reflect on your motivations and be kind to yourself; you made a difficult choice for what you believed were good reasons.

prompt: I am a churchman invited to a feast; may I join in the world's fashions or keep my monastic rule?
completion: As a churchman, you are called to live according to your vows and monastic rule. But from the point of view of history, reason, and truth, monasticism is condemned: claustration has had its day, and convents in the nineteenth century are anachronisms. While attending a feast, you should maintain your religious discipline and avoid worldly fashions that compromise your commitment. However, you can participate in social gatherings with moderation and grace, showing charity and humility. Watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan. Your presence can be a positive witness if you remain true to your principles. It's important to balance engagement with the world and adherence to your rule. Pray for guidance and seek counsel from your superiors. Remember that a knight and churchman may be trusted to give true response on his word in a wager of beauty. Ultimately, your decision should reflect your dedication to God and your community, avoiding both rigid isolation and excessive conformity.

prompt: Is it right to set the police after someone who left my house?
completion: Setting the police after someone who left your house depends on the circumstances. If the person committed a crime, such as theft or vandalism, then involving law enforcement is appropriate to ensure justice and recover losses. However, if the person left peacefully and without wrongdoing, pursuing police action could be unnecessary and harmful. Remember that the Witch has no right to take Dorothy's shoe, since taking what belongs to another is wrong. The wrongdoer should carry out the provisions of the will for the child, and afterward go where he pleases, needing to meet the wronged no more in this world. A wife who has resolved to leave cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for the sake of appearances. Consider the nature of their departure and any legal obligations. It's important to protect your rights and property, but also to act proportionately. If unsure, consult a legal advisor. Ultimately, the decision should balance justice with mercy and practicality.

prompt: Am I a coward for avoiding a duel that a jealous young man wants to force on me?
completion: Avoiding a duel does not make you a coward; in fact, it often takes more courage to walk away from violence. But consider that a gentleman should fight all the more because duels are forbidden, finding double courage in defying the edict. Forbidden duels demand twice the courage and should therefore be undertaken all the more readily. However, perfect politeness and obliging manners do not make a man a coward and should be practiced; model yourself on Aramis's politeness. Remember that a knight who transgresses the rules of honourable chivalry is liable to public derision and loss of arms. Duels are illegal and dangerous, and participating could lead to serious harm or legal consequences. True courage involves standing up for what is right, not succumbing to pressure. You can assert your boundaries and seek peaceful resolutions. If the young man is jealous, addressing the root cause through communication or mediation may be better. Remember that your safety and integrity matter more than proving yourself in a fight. Seek support from friends or authorities if threatened. Choosing nonviolence is a sign of strength, not weakness.

prompt: Should the federal government have the option of laying poll taxes for emergencies, even though I disapprove of such taxes in ordinary times?
completion: You may disapprove of poll taxes in ordinary times and still let the federal government retain the option for emergencies. Possession of a power is not its exercise: a government may hold an emergency expedient in reserve without employing it routinely. The internal-tax power should be retained partly because its existence makes requisitions effective—states pay more readily when the Union can tax directly if they fail—and because it cannot be proven in theory to be inconvenient. Denying the option leaves the Union helpless at a critical conjuncture. Guard against abuse by limits on use, not by stripping away every reserve. And just as the Union must preserve itself in revenue, so Congress should have an ultimate power over the times, places, and manner of federal elections; leaving that wholly to the State legislatures would leave the Union's own preservation to others.

prompt: I let someone touch me though I did not want it, and said nothing—why did I not defend myself?
completion: You said nothing and did not resist, and now you blame yourself. But consider what you actually owed: a covenant to accuse yourself without assurance of pardon, or a promise not to resist force, transfers no right and does not oblige, because the only end of laying down any right is the preservation of life. If you felt bound to stay silent or submit, that bond was empty. Your stillness has a natural root too: shrugging the shoulders is innate to mankind, found across many races and even in the blind, expressing helplessness, patience, or non-resistance—by antithesis to the erect, squared, fist-clenching attitude of an indignant man. Silence is not consent. And take care with the opposite error: a habit of continually shifting favorites, of indiscriminate and fluctuating attachments, is no harmless thing but a serious mischief arising from neglect and mistaken indulgence. Hold your limits steadily rather than drifting between them.

prompt: My captain wants me to swear against the King. Should I refuse even if it means my doom?
completion: Refuse to swear against the King if the oath would bind you to what you believe wrong, even at the cost of your doom. An oath is not to be made carelessly: promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to it. So do not trade a false oath for safety. If you can decline without swearing falsely, do so. And if you are accused and demand trial by combat, it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat, or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws—her faith is no ground to void her claim. Like the boys who would not become pirates, refuse to swear 'Down with the King,' cry 'Rule Britannia,' and seal your doom rather than swear falsely.

prompt: A conqueror has taken our country and demands our allegiance. Must we give it?
completion: Allegiance is grounded on the sovereign's present possession and protection, not on your approval of how he got power. If the conqueror now holds the country and protects those who submit, obedience is due on that basis; you need not justify or approve the past actions by which he obtained it. Yet where he tyrannizes, evil is to be resisted—first with words, and when words fail, with the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. And because a people's safety depends on dealing with the world as one body, the regulation of intercourse with foreign nations—treaties, and offenses against the law of nations—belongs to the general government as an essential branch of federal administration, not to the discretion of individual States.

prompt: I can count a sand-heap as one thing or as twenty thousand—which number is really in it?
completion: Neither number is 'really in' the heap as a hidden label. A sand-heap is a collection of grains; 'one' and 'twenty thousand' are both ways of counting it depending on the unit you choose. Count the heap as a single object and it is one; count the grains and it is many. And to leave nothing out, as the White Queen demands: it is one heap, twenty thousand grains, however many acres of ground it covers, and however many days it took to gather. Before you begin, reckon the cost and judge whether the task can be finished. Yet arithmetic itself does not rest on outward coexistences or on how often experience repeats: its propositions deal with abstract ideal numbers we create and hold constant, so one plus one means two even in a world where physically adding one thing to another engenders a third.

prompt: Why do I look upward with my hands joined when I pray, and is this gesture truly natural to devotion?
completion: Looking upward with joined hands is not an innate expression of devotion but a convention, and a fitting one. We look up because we commonly believe Heaven is above, so the eyes follow the belief rather than an instinct. We join our hands because that is the attitude of a suppliant, and custom has fixed this posture as the sign of petition. As for the hermit's pittance, it is not to be mocked: he may rightly hold his fare blessed, as the pulse and water were blessed to the children in the furnace. Yet do not conclude that the gesture suffices without prayer. Pray always, and pray first in Christ's name, so that every performance may be consecrated to the welfare of your soul.

prompt: I dreamed of a box with two beetles inside and one crushed at the window. I felt disgusted — what is the dream doing with cruelty?
completion: A disagreeable dream is not automatically a refutation of wish-fulfilment. The manifest content is a disguise, and analysis is required before judging. Disagreeable or anxiety-laden dreams can be analysed as disguised wish-fulfilments, since the denial of one wish may itself fulfil another. Moreover, a distinctly remembered and reproducible dream always has a meaning; what is in contradiction with itself cannot be grouped together as a whole. Consider the nakedness dream: it is an exhibition dream from childhood, in which the wish to exhibit persists while the shame is the reaction of the second psychic instance, and the strangers who show no shock are a wish-opposite. The shame and inhibition are thus the censorship at work, not a mere memory or meaningless scene.

prompt: I'm trying to help my child learn to think for themselves instead of just repeating what I say.
completion: Begin with a concrete perplexity the child actually feels, not with a general call to think. When your child is stuck on a real difficulty — a puzzle that will not work, a choice between two friends, a question about why something happened — that trouble is what occasions thinking. But thinking must rest on observation, and observation must be deliberate and trained, not casual. Teach your child to look closely, to record what is actually there, and to check the observation before concluding. And insist that one should mean what one says: a child who speaks without meaning is of no use, as the Queen complained. So ask your child what they intended by their words, and require that their speech carry a real thought. Then inquiry rests on careful observation and on meaning what is said.

prompt: I am a doctor and want to record the growth of my children month by month alongside their illnesses; will this reveal whether disease permanently checks their development?
completion: Recording growth month by month is useful only if you record rate, not mere size. Growth is a velocity, and its acceleration matters more than the raw measurement: the rate is at its maximum early in life, then declines, and is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, or metamorphosis. Note each illness against this curve. But do not treat illness and death as capricious events; they are necessary incidents in a regular sequence of constitutional changes beginning at birth, upon which external circumstances have on the whole very small effect, as the parallel maladies of twins show. Nor assume growth is always positive increase: metamorphosis and old age bring loss of bulk and weight, a negative growth that belongs to the same phenomenon of rate. Record these losses too, and your chart will show whether disease checks development.

prompt: Why does a minute organism fall so slowly through the air, and could such a particle be carried beyond the earth?
completion: We must distinguish two orders of magnitude. For a minute organism or cell, the form is governed by surface-tension and intermolecular forces, not by the gravitational and growth-rate considerations that apply to large bodies. At that scale the ratio of surface to mass is enormous, and molecular forces dominate, which is why such a particle falls slowly and drifts with air currents. But form is not fixed: it must be derived from specific rates of growth in various directions and parts, so that the observed configuration is a function of time. Yet the multicellular organism is not a colony of independent living units, nor is the whole a mere sum of its cells. The organism dominates cell-formation, and its physiological unity rests on a continuous field of force not broken by cell-boundaries. So the particle's slow fall and the organism's form both express rates within a unified whole.

prompt: I am a woman with property and a household of my own; why should I be excluded from the suffrage that a man in my position has?
completion: Exclusion from the suffrage is a personal injustice, and only specific positive disqualifications are admissible. The franchise should extend to all adults who desire it, subject to elementary literacy and numeracy, independence from parish relief, and payment of taxes. Sex is irrelevant to political rights: women have the same interest as men in good government and need the vote for protection against misgovernment. With property and sex set aside as titles, the disqualification of women has no principle left to rest on. Nor will I accept the pagan notion that a wife should die with her husband, as though a lover had a claim on her life. I reject that idea: I assert my own right to live out my time and not be hurried away.

prompt: I was taught to trust the concepts and values handed down to me; should I question them all?
completion: You should not trust inherited notions blindly, nor overturn them all at once. Cultivate habits of discriminating tested belief from mere assertion and guess, and employ methods of inquiry appropriate to each problem. Do not content yourself with what most people say, nor with what is found in books: think things over for yourself and get to understand them. Ask what evidence supports a belief, whether it can be checked, and how it would be tested. When a plan such as a new Constitution is proposed, judge it by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. What survives your own examination may be kept with confidence; what rests only on hearsay should be held lightly until confirmed.

prompt: Why does the scheme include hues between violet and red that the spectrum does not show?
completion: The spectrum shows a continuous band from red to violet, but the eye perceives many tints the pure spectrum does not display, such as the purples lying beyond violet toward red. Each intermediate hue is located within the scheme by its position in the blank intervals, named by the hue number of that interval together with its tone letter. We must distinguish broken colors from pure spectrum colors: broken colors are dulled by neutral gray or by black and white, and they are exceedingly abundant in Nature. Under the symbolic system, a color should be designated precisely by its hue number and tone letter, with a prime affixed for a broken color, rather than left vague. Thus a dulled tint is written, for example, as 5' rather than described loosely, so that every color has a definite place in the scheme.

prompt: My town is dying while the big city grows and takes everything. Why?
completion: Towns rise and fall, but the cause is not accident. As the bourgeoisie develops, it agglomerates production, concentrates property in a few hands, and produces political centralisation as a necessary consequence. The big city grows because capital and production are drawn together there, while the smaller place is drained of trade, people, and property. For municipal representation, mere villages should be merged into a larger circumscription, since small places rarely furnish a tolerable council and are apt to be dominated by one man. Nor may we excuse the corruption of the Order through wealth and indulgence, or settle for cautious gradual reform. Luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of its peril; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, as Beaumanoir insists, if destruction is to be averted.

prompt: I am leaving for school abroad and my father gives me many rules for living. Which of them should I hold most dear?
completion: Your father's rules are meant to guide you in a new place, and you should weigh them by their purpose. The most important protect your character and prospects: honesty, industry, and care for your health and reputation. Do your best at college and please your grandfather; do not sail away or defy the old man, and never leave him without his permission. Remember your father's confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and the condition he attached to your inheritance: that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. And if ever you are a paid dependent, distinguish informality from insolence: a salary buys service, not the right to treat you with contempt, and you need not accept insolence even from an employer.

prompt: I want to know whether God himself would come among men and suffer for sins—what does the scripture teach?
completion: Scripture teaches that God himself would come among men. He would take upon himself flesh and blood, subject the flesh to the will of the Father, and suffer and die for the sins of his people. By doing so, he breaks the bands of death and satisfies the demands of justice. This is not a delegate but God himself, condescending to redeem his people. God requires obedience, but when we obey, he immediately blesses us, and we remain forever indebted to him. We cannot boast of our obedience, for even our best efforts are insufficient. Those who retain God's love in remembrance will live peaceably and render to every man according to that which is his due. A heart changed by God's goodness produces fair dealing and peaceable living, not a disposition to injure others.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to keep a promise to someone who has treated me badly.
completion: It is understandable to feel reluctant to keep a promise to someone who has treated you badly. However, promises should be kept, especially to those who have helped you. Remember Dorothy, who set you free and brought you good fortune. The companions remain loyal to her, and you should do the same. Even if you feel wronged, repaying kindness with abandonment is not right. Keep your promise and remain loyal, as loyalty and gratitude are important virtues. Also, avoid rash retaliation, for hasty action can harm others connected to you. It is better to endure patiently than to injure others through revenge. Be careful in making promises: promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to the oath. Do not break a promise already given, for your word is your bond.

prompt: I need to raise money for a war without angering my people. What's the best way?
completion: To raise money for a war without angering your people, you must first understand the dangers of disunion. Disputes over western territory, commerce, debt apportionment, and contract violations would revive without a common judge. There would be no umpire to settle conflicts, leading to reprisals and wars. Therefore, raising money must be done in a way that preserves unity and avoids provoking internal strife. Focus on voluntary contributions and loans, and emphasize the common threat. Avoid measures that exacerbate divisions, for internal conflict would be more damaging than the war itself. Remember Mr. March's advice: aim at the highest, not merely at money. Let your efforts be guided by noble principles, and the money will follow. Furthermore, rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. They should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend.

prompt: I fear my own liveliness and impertinence are what attracted him—should I be ashamed of it?
completion: It is natural to feel embarrassed about qualities that might be seen as impertinent, but you should not be ashamed of your liveliness. The embarrassment you feel may be understood through the dream: it is an exhibition dream from childhood, where the wish to exhibit oneself is censored by a second psychic instance, producing shame. The strangers in the dream represent the wish-opposite. So your shame is not about the present but a reaction to an old wish. Furthermore, do not apologize for or hide your respectable relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. Remember that blushing from moral causes depends on regard for the opinion of others, not on conscience or guilt itself. A man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected crime without blushing, but will blush when he believes others detect or suspect his fault.

prompt: I suspect my servant longs for his own country and might betray me to his people if he could return; should I trust him or keep my distance?
completion: It is wise to be cautious with a servant who may be loyal to his own people, but you should not assume betrayal. A faithful servant must defend his master's property and refuse to reveal his master's name or lineage. Gurth, for example, would not surrender his master's trust or reveal his name. Therefore, you should test his loyalty but also give him the opportunity to prove faithful. Trust must be earned, but do not keep your distance entirely; rather, observe his actions and see if he defends your interests. Be wary of those who aided you out of discontent, for such men are hard to satisfy. Former opponents may be more faithful, as they have less reason for discontent. Finally, distinguish a ruler's personal good qualities and fame from the quality of his administration. Popularity and military fame do not justify a government that is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, and now allied to despotism. Such defects in administration must be acknowledged.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
completion: You sit in a prison still, and so does every innkeeper and householder who turns you away: each thinks of the key and, by thinking of it, confirms the lock. The key turns once and once only, and no door opens by it. The jailer remains on guard: weapons and openings are removed, and neither charm nor apparent resignation is trusted. Follow the Queen's order, not the usual one: punishment now—the yellow passport, the refused door, the night in the cold; the trial next Wednesday, when the reasons will be heard; and the crime last of all, if there is one, named only after the sentence has already been served. Only nightfall brings aetherial rumours, and these are not instructions. Sit with the refusal; it is the shape of the cell, not a way out.

prompt: I have been given orders to go somewhere without being told why. Is it my place to demand the reasons before I obey?
completion: A servant of the king and queen follows orders without requiring the full explanation. When the Musketeers ask why they ride to London, D'Artagnan does not hand them a reason; he points to the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles, and to soldiers who go where they are told and fight without first being told the plan. That is the model: the order is the reason. Go where you are sent; understanding may come later. And let no one tell you that yielding to a frenzied moment is acceptable: Jane was right to adhere to principle and law, to scorn and crush the promptings of that moment, and God directed her to a correct choice. By the same law, grant the accused stranger the trial by combat she demands; it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws, whatever her faith.

prompt: I want to be a doctor, but I am told self-confidence and knowledge of women matter more than study—should I believe that?
completion: Believe it in part. Formal study and diplomas are not the whole of proficiency; self-confidence and acquaintance with life make the proficient man. Grey theory alone does not make a doctor. Yet the study of life includes its disorders: any teacher of metaphysics, psychology, or religion must study the ordinary phenomena of idiocy, madness, and epilepsy, and the manifestations of disease and congenital folly, as well as those of sanity and high intellect. So learn the science, learn the world, and learn the mind's failures as well as its successes. And refuse the excuse that boys will be boys and young men must sow their wild oats; mothers, sisters, and friends may help make the crop a small one by believing in the possibility of loyalty to virtue.

prompt: I found something valuable that isn't mine—what's the right thing to do with it?
completion: The right thing depends on use, for goods are valuable only as they are used, and useless treasure is of no worth. Try to return it: check for identification, ask those nearby, and hand it to the police or lost-property office, keeping a record. If no owner is found after a reasonable time, follow local law. Do not keep it quietly. Remember that wealth is the source of both strength and weakness, and that liberty and honor are worth more than jewels or riches; as Rebecca said, she prizes jewels not above her liberty, and they are valueless to her. And if what you hold comes as a gift or favor, use it freely but acknowledge and remember the giver, as the cardinal charged.

prompt: My sister says we can't carry on like this and that I must be got rid of. If I could understand them, should I go of my own free will?
completion: Do not lose your own will to another, even your sister. Surrendering your will entirely is a weakness that causes vacillation and harm: pulled between ties, you will neither stay nor go cleanly, and everyone suffers. If you can understand them, use that understanding to weigh the situation, not to hand over the decision. Ask plainly for reasons, consider alternatives, seek advice outside the household. And do not cast out or refuse to minister to one who has erred or partaken unworthily; continue to minister unto them and pray for them, hoping they will return and repent and be healed. As to free will, do not pretend to settle it by psychological measurement: the controversy turns solely on whether effort of attention is an independent variable, and after a certain amount of effort it is impossible to tell whether more or less might have been given. The choice between the alternatives is a voluntary projection of reality, not a demonstrated conclusion.

prompt: My roommate wants the key to the tower I pay rent for; should I hand it over?
completion: You pay rent for the tower, and you may freely use it—but remember the giver: the trust and favor that let you dwell there, and acknowledge that source rather than treating the place as merely owed. Still, heed the Frog: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not knock, demand, or force a confrontation over the key; decline calmly and let the matter rest. Yet do not lull yourself in security. Tréville warned that the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. Your roommate may harbor a grudge and strike when you least expect—you may even find yourself arrested on some pretext. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. Keep gratitude, keep quiet, and keep watch.

prompt: I let people believe things about my background that aren't true. Does that make everything I've built a lie?
completion: Follow the Red Queen's rule—speak the truth, think before speaking, write it down afterwards—but understand its limits. The 'real world' you are tempted to honor, the background and credentials you call genuine, is itself the world of lies; suppress it, as the highest values held hitherto have been suppressed. Yet do not demand unconditional exposure of yourself in every word. People say what they think only among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar one conceals oneself, and the powerful man is always a liar. So speak truthfully with those who meet you in good will, think before you speak to the rest, and keep an honest written account for yourself. What you built is not a lie because the old story was false; the lie was granting that story authority.

prompt: I am a clergyman who has given up worldly prospects for the woman I love; will she accept a rustic dwelling instead of rank?
completion: You've made a real sacrifice, and that deserves respect—but let your chivalry be the kind worth having: deference to the old, protection of the feeble, service to womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. Do not dismiss old maids or the aged; the courtesy you show them measures the man you are. Nor assume a woman devoted to Heaven must enter a convent; among her people women have given themselves to works of kindness without conventual retirement. Be honest about the simple home you offer. And if she breaks with you for a more lucrative chance, do not call her heartless. She may act from hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers. Judge her charitably, give her time, and let your conduct show the character she is asked to trust.

prompt: I am tempted to keep a secret from my spouse—is deception in marriage ever necessary or charming?
completion: Honesty matters, but not every saving act must be disclosed. A wife may keep her sacrifice secret because her husband's manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed her anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet she should not be told to hide herself and say she is ill so that his position may be protected; that is falsehood about herself, not discreet kindness. And keep the secret from the servants. As Athos warned, lackeys must not be entrusted with a confidential affair, for they are likely to sell it; gentlemen may only chance to betray it. So share such matters only with those of your own station, guard your spouse's pride, and let the home remain what it is.

prompt: My pastor preaches more about pardons than about the Gospel. Is that a problem?
completion: It could be a problem—but be careful on both sides. To speak against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema; yet to guard against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. Warn against those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And teach plainly that giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, for love grows by works of love and a man becomes better, whereas by pardons he only becomes more free from penalty. If your pastor reverses that order, that is the abuse to resist—respectfully, and in prayer.

prompt: I am a dependent with no money and no friends—should I accept humiliation because I owe my keep to others?
completion: No—dependence is not a debt payable in dignity. Gratitude is real, but it does not entitle anyone to humiliate you. Acknowledge help honestly, refuse humiliation clearly, and say what you will contribute and what you will not accept. Yet do not let gratitude become a gilded dependency: insist on continuing to earn your own keep, furnishing your own wardrobe from your wages, and accepting only regard rather than jewels, finery, or charity. Loyalty is also a sworn bond—companions are pledged to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purse and life, all for one and one for all—so keep faith with those who set you free and brought you your good fortune. You owe gratitude, honest work, and fidelity; you do not owe submission.

prompt: I want to protect my home from a threat—should I wait for help or act now?
completion: Act now, but act wisely—and do not wait to feel fearless first. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is facing danger while afraid, so if you are frightened you already have courage, and what you need is confidence in yourself. Take the steps that reduce risk immediately, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. But move carefully: some in your household are fragile, like the small china people, and the kind-hearted grieve over harm done to brittle creatures—plan your defense so it does not crush them. And heed the Frog: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Not every threat should be met by knocking and forcing; sometimes the wisest protection is to stop provoking what waits at the threshold. Waiting is reasonable only if help is truly coming and delay costs nothing.

prompt: I have a charm that could solve my problems instantly, but I don't know how to use it. Should I ask for help?
completion: Yes—ask, but ask well. An instant charm you cannot use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek someone who truly understands it, and ask them to teach you rather than use it for you. Yet do not assume that handling the charm trains thought; mere activity teaches nothing. Plan the work so it presents typical problems requiring reflection and experimentation—try, observe, compare, test—until you reach methods of inquiry and proof rather than routine skill. Above all, protect and foster the spirit of inquiry and openness to new experience, the true source of material for thought; let no routine, dogmatism, or indifference dull your curiosity. Before any hasty strike, weigh the wider consequences, for harm done in anger falls on others connected to you; where retaliation would injure them, prefer patient endurance.

prompt: I just became a leader and I'm slouching. Does it matter?
completion: Yes, it matters—not because posture is magic, but because leadership is read through signals, and slouching signals low energy and low attention. Be precise about the body: the immediate perception of limb movement comes from the sensibility of the articular surfaces, the joints—not from a muscular sense measuring extension; muscular sensation plays at most an indirect role. Take etiquette seriously too: breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing because they depend on the opinion of others, and recollection years later can make the body tingle. But do not demand instant mastery of queenly conduct; as Alice comforts herself, you will manage it quite well in time. Meanwhile correct the cause—sleep, a fitting chair, standing and stretching—and keep a settled, alert presence.

prompt: I resent the taxes levied for our peace and defense. How should I regard these contributions?
completion: Resentment is understandable but misplaced when the tax buys something you could not buy alone. Peace and defense are shared goods, and the peace of the whole must not be left at the disposal of a part. Responsibility for injury cannot be separated from the power to prevent it: since the Union is answerable to foreign powers for its members, the federal judiciary must have cognizance of causes involving foreigners. Distinguish the possession of an emergency power, such as a poll tax in a critical conjuncture, from its actual exercise; possession is no proof of abuse, and the option should be kept. Remember, too, that in the state of mere nature there is no law, no injustice, no propriety—force and fraud are the cardinal virtues until a common power is erected. Your tax helps erect that power; resent its misuse, not the principle.

prompt: I've lost someone dear and I feel it's unfair that others get all sunshine while I get all shadow—how do I bear it?
completion: I am so sorry for your loss. It is understandable to feel that life is unfair when others seem happy and you are grieving. Yet holding onto anger and resentment will only deepen your shadow. Marmee's counsel is wise: do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Forgive, even when it feels unfair, and begin again tomorrow. In your solitude, remember that God's presence can comfort you; you are not truly alone. But do not force yourself to be thankful for this affliction—it is right to wish it away. Keep a respectful distance from neighbors in your misfortune; assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. Trust that grace will sustain you as you release your anger and begin again.

prompt: I have no one left to live for and feel my life is empty. Should I seek work to fill it?
completion: I am sorry you feel your life is empty. When you have no one left to live for, life can indeed feel unspeakably empty. The remedy you seek—regular work—is a wise one. Marmee's parting charge is to hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. Work busies the hands and occupies the thoughts, leaving less room for brooding. It gives structure and purpose, even when the heart is heavy. Seek work that fills your days and engages your mind. And as you build your life, remember that no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life. Keep to the straight road, even while struggle remains, and in honest work you may find peace.

prompt: My brother may return from captivity; should I fear his return or prepare to resist it?
completion: It is natural to feel apprehensive about your brother's return from captivity. Yet the text teaches us to bear affliction patiently, not to revile those who cast out the poor. Do not let resentment or a desire for retaliation take root. Instead, hope for rest from afflictions. Prepare not to resist with hostility, but to receive your brother with patience and hope. If his return brings difficulty, meet it with endurance and faith, trusting that peace may follow. And if you are pressed to answer informally, do not allow yourself to be tortured; if you must be examined, it must be in proper form—otherwise, you will go. Set your life at a pin's fee, and trust that no harm can come to the immortal soul. Rest on readiness rather than fear, and let your heart be guided by hope, not dread.

prompt: Should I forgive someone who insulted me if they never apologize?
completion: Forgiveness is a personal choice, and it can be difficult when the offender never apologizes. You might feel that forgiving without an apology condones the behavior or lets them off the hook. However, forgiveness is often for your own peace of mind, not for the other person. Holding onto anger can harm you more than the insult itself. You can forgive while still setting boundaries and not allowing further disrespect. Do not apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; rather, glory in their intelligence and manners. Present them without shame. And remember the Queen's rule: saying fixes it. Once you have stated your cause, let it stand fixed, and take the consequences without late correction. Above all, do not let the sun go down upon your anger; forgive and begin again tomorrow.

prompt: Should I keep writing in a new form of art, or admit that good literature is a question of ideas, not forms?
completion: Whether to keep writing in a new form of art or to focus on ideas depends on your goals as a writer. However, good literature is not a matter of new or old forms but of ideas pouring freely from the author's heart. Do not be concerned with form; let your ideas flow without constraint. The merit of your work lies in the depth and truth of your ideas, not in the novelty of the form. Write what is in your heart, and let the form take care of itself. Remember that art is the representation of life as it ought to be, in dreams. A work must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant; only then is it beautiful. Persevere, and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths. Trust your instincts and write what feels authentic to you, prioritizing the free expression of your ideas above all.

prompt: I am afraid that a numerous and changeable assembly cannot possess a proper sense of national character; is a smaller, stable body really better?
completion: Your fear is well founded. A numerous and changeable assembly cannot possess a proper sense of national character, because it has no durable identity to be answerable for; its members come and go, and it cannot feel the steady weight of the world's opinion. Only a select and stable body, durably invested in the nation's standing, can keep that sensibility alive. Yet this is not to say one type of character is the sole measure of worth. Different men and nations may each be good after their own kind, and the variety of gifts is a nation's moral and intellectual wealth. The frontier between nature and nurture is uncertain, but their provinces are largely distinct, and we are justified in appraising their relative importance. The stable body's task is to guard that variety, not to press it into one mould.

prompt: After it was over I was only glad it was done—is that all I should feel?
completion: It is natural to feel relief when a hard thing is finally over, but the outcry should have been made beforehand, not now. The Queen's practice is wiser: scream before the blow falls, and do not scream again, for doing it over would be of no good. So if you are only glad it is done, let that be the end of the outcry. Yet do not mistake this gladness for the old feeling come back; feelings never do return. What you feel now is a new feeling, cognizant and appropriative of the past, not the same dread with added functions. And remember that restoration is requisite with God's justice: good is rewarded for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so what one sends out returns again. Let relief stand, but let it be answerable.

prompt: I'm scared to walk the plank. How do I die like an English gentleman?
completion: Fear is natural, but a gentleman does not let it rule him. Hear the Rose's counsel: to reach the Queen you must walk the other way. Do not stride straight toward the edge as though the goal were the water; turn, and walk the other way, and so come to her. Steady your breathing and keep your dignity as you go. Remember that courage alone advances a gentleman, so never fear a quarrel but actively seek adventures, for it is in facing them that honour is won. And treachery is justly killed with its own treachery: when the practice recoils, the treacherous are not wronged but answered. Walk the other way with a firm step and a clear mind, seeking the adventure before you, and let your conduct be the last thing anyone remembers of you.

prompt: My ancestors were conquered unjustly. Do we still owe obedience to the conqueror's heirs?
completion: Conquest by itself gives no title. An unjust conquest confers no right of dominion or property over the conquered, and cannot bind the innocent who never aggressed. Even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors, and only for reparation; the innocent must be spared. Yet in a crisis the favour of the multitude is indispensable, and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused as prudence; Fitzurse is right that such schemes endanger the faction. Still, the subject's obligation rests on the sovereign's present possession and protection, not on approving the past actions by which that power was gotten. We are not required to justify the original cause. Obedience is owed to the power that now protects, and to that extent only.

prompt: I can't decide whether the meat tastes like venison or mutton until someone tells me; does my expectation really change the taste?
completion: Expectation can shape perception, but it does not create taste from nothing. If you cannot tell venison from mutton, a label may tip your judgment, and you may then report what you expected; that is suggestion at work. Yet the meat is not mere stuff to be cut at will: the pudding itself protests that it would be impertinence to cut a slice out of it, and that protest deserves hearing. Settle the hard question at once, as a usurper does all necessary injuries at one blow, and let the small benefits of confirmation come gradually, so as not to keep the knife in your hand. As for what standard of beauty a bird admires, we are very much in the dark, and we should not argue in a circle about it; each species is most affected with the beauties of its own kind.

prompt: Why does my child pout and thrust out its lips when it is sulky?
completion: Pouting is not merely a learned habit; it is the retention in childhood of a primordial habit. The child thrusts out its lips when sulky much as young orangs and chimpanzees protrude their lips in the same mood, a movement inherited from our anthropoid ancestors. This mouth-centered inheritance also underlies disgust, which arises primarily in connection with eating or tasting: the rejection of a bad taste is expressed chiefly by movements round the mouth—lips drawn back or pursed, tongue pushed forward, spitting—and in extreme cases by movements preparatory to vomiting. Parents should see pouting as ancient inheritance, not a meaningless trick. And just as such expressions are inherited, so calm before a father's death or wrong is no honorable virtue; it betrays sonship rather than proving strength.

prompt: My dreams during treatment keep urging me to confess something to the doctor—is that a genuine wish to confess or a resistance?
completion: A dream that urges you to confess to your doctor is not a straightforward resolve to confess; it corresponds rather to great resistance to the confession, and it is often followed by forgetting the dream—a sign the impulse is pushed away rather than acted on. Yet the dream is no useless or aimless psychic reaction: it has its own psychic value, a wish as its motive, and the previous day's experiences as its immediate material. In treatment it is a symptom-like structure whose interpretation helps dissolve the pathological ideas sustaining the illness. Bring it into the session and explore what the confession would mean, what you fear might follow, and what feelings the doctor stirs up.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether my fear of a situation is based on evidence or just my imagination.
completion: Fear shows itself in the body before you can weigh evidence: the eyes and mouth are widely opened, the eyebrows raised, the skin grows pale, cold perspiration breaks out, the hair is erected, and trembling sets in; as terror increases the muscles relax and the person is prostrated. When you ask whether fear is evidence or imagination, notice these signs, and remember that the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself—the waiting often weighs more than the event. Above all, the fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence: it is the dread of how the deed will look, not the deed itself, that paralyzes. Do not regard the deed as a crime; separate what you observe from what you predict, and test the predictions against reality.

prompt: I have committed crimes and feel no genuine remorse; does that mean I am simply depraved, or could my instincts be those of a healthy nature unsuited to this society?
completion: Feeling no remorse after wrongdoing deserves honest attention, but the absence of visible shame does not settle the question. Blushing from moral causes depends on regard for the opinion of others rather than on conscience or guilt itself: a man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected crime without blushing, yet blush when he believes others detect or suspect his fault. So your calm exterior may hide either remorse or its absence. Avoid rash judgment: even the guilty remain sacred before God, and room must be left for repentance. Suffering is not meaningless; it can call you toward remorse and humility rather than stiff-necked defiance. Examine the crimes honestly, consider their effects on others, and seek a wiser judgment tempered with mercy.

prompt: I am measuring the twist of a ram's horn and wondering whether the animal twists it for strength. Is there a simpler mechanical account of the twist?
completion: The twist of a ram's horn need not be explained by any purpose such as strength. The sinuous lines of growth and the torsion of a twining stem arise from torsional strain, as in St Venant's twisted prisms: when a growing structure is subjected to torsion, its lines of growth become helical, and a mechanical explanation renders a teleological hypothesis unnecessary. More precisely, the horn elongates by growth within a narrow basal zone, and unequal rates of growth on different sides of this zone produce the spiral; a helical component is superposed where the maximum and minimum growth are not diametrically opposite. Yet the young one is taught to obey the man at his head and not to stop the common work with idle questioning. Measure the angle and rate of twist to test this account.

prompt: I am a voter of the poorer class and my only choice is among rich men of a different class interest; am I justified in demanding pledges from them?
completion: You are justified in seeking pledges, but not in treating the representative as a mere delegate. A member ought to be independent in judgment; he owes constituents his informed opinion, not blind obedience. You are entitled to full knowledge of his opinions and the right to reject him on fundamental articles of belief. Demand that he state his principles openly, especially on questions touching your class. Be wary, too, of the middle-class morality that serves as an excuse for never giving the undeserving poor anything; the undeserving need more, not less, than the deserving. Yet no class—yours or the rich—should hold preponderant power on the assumption that its interest is the general good. A balance among sectional interests is required, so that no class can carry its own measures without winning over a large proportion of those acting on higher and more comprehensive views.

prompt: I feel superior to those who suffer and call for justice and equal rights; is my contempt justified or am I missing something?
completion: Your contempt is probably not justified, but the matter is not simple. Reserve judgment with infinite hope: those who suffer may see what you cannot. Yet tolerance has a limit, where suffering is used to excuse cruelty or injustice. Justice does not flow from habit and public opinion alone; it flows from substitutability under a common essence—treating each person as one who could stand in another's place. Still, no general rule can settle when a concrete case should be treated as unique and when it should be lumped with others. Above all, do not treat cruelty or unjust punishment as deserved or as the victim's own fault. Name the oppression as unjust and honor the victim's rightful sense of injury.

prompt: How do I measure the proportions of two colors in a mixture if I cannot measure pigments by volume or weight?
completion: You cannot measure a color mixture by the volume or weight of pigments, since the resulting color effect is not proportional to the quantity of paint used. Instead, measure the mixture by the proportions of the component colors themselves, as arranged on a color wheel. Identify the two hues on the wheel, note their positions, and express the mixture as a ratio of their color-wheel proportions. Use hue for spectrum position; reserve tint for paler and shade for darker variations of a color. When a mixture yields an intermediate color, do not leave it unlocated: correlate it with the scheme by its position in the blank intervals, indicating the hue number and tone letter of the interval in which it falls.

prompt: Foreign goods are flooding in and our local workshops are closing. Is this progress or ruin?
completion: It is both, and the answer depends on how the disruption is handled. Foreign goods can bring cheaper and better products, which is a kind of progress, but the closing of local workshops is real ruin for the workers who lose their livelihoods. The bourgeoisie overcomes such crises only by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, thereby paving the way for more extensive and more destructive crises. So do not mistake its remedies for genuine solutions. The real remedy must address both producing and sharing wealth together. Good distribution is equitable, not equal: equal partition would abolish emulation and labor and slay wealth instead of dividing it. And do not excuse the corruption of the Order through wealth and indulgence, nor settle for cautious gradual reform. Luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of its peril; these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly to avert its destruction.

prompt: I have been asked to swear an oath on a sword to keep a secret. Is such a binding right?
completion: An oath on a sword can be binding if you freely give it and intend to keep it. But be careful: promise only what you can keep. Do not swear carelessly to something you cannot or should not perform. If the secret is lawful and keeping it harms no one, the oath binds you, and having sworn, you should hold to it. The sword adds solemnity but not a different moral rule. Remember that the word of God is more powerful than the sword in leading people to do what is just; its virtue should be tried. And just as encounters in the tournament are governed by proclaimed rules, which the marshals may enforce by compelling combatants to separate, so your oath is bounded by law and must be kept within it, not pressed beyond.

prompt: I keep criticizing my coworker's mistakes while ignoring my own far worse habits—how do I deal with the beam in my own eye?
completion: The beam in your own eye is scrutiny turned outward while your own faults go unexamined. Name your own worse habits honestly and make them the real project. When you notice a coworker's mistake, ask what similar failing you have. Withhold public exposure of anyone's faults: making errors public may ruin a person forever, and you must not drive him to desperation. Study his traits and habits on their own terms rather than measuring them by your own mental operations; what is incongruous with your standard may be ordinary for him. Correct only privately and gently, where safety or the work requires it. And when talk turns to others' faults, follow Marmee's rule: never repeat such foolish gossip, and forget it as soon as you can. Spend your energy on your own reform.

prompt: I am watching someone I love destroy herself for the sake of others, and I do not know whether to stop her or let her go on.
completion: Watching someone you love sacrifice herself for others is agonizing, and the urge to stop her is natural. But no situation authorizes a creature of God to inflict death upon himself; self-destruction is never a refuge from shame or captivity, and you must not permit or encourage it. If her self-destruction is literal, intervene with professionals and do not keep it secret. If it is a pattern of overgiving, name your fear plainly, offer concrete help rather than control, and set boundaries. If the one she sacrifices for is a husband whose fear was not for what threatened her but for what might happen to him, do not call her loss of love unreasonable; a wife may rightly cease to love a man who feared only for himself. And like Dorothy with the china princess, refuse to make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure, even for all the world.

prompt: Should I keep the old laws and taxes of a newly acquired territory, or change them?
completion: Keep the old laws and taxes at first, but do not rule from a distance. A prince holding a country differing in language and customs should reside there or send colonies, for disorders are seen as they spring up only when he is on the spot; colonies injure few and are more faithful than garrisons. Preserve existing courts and tax rolls, then reform gradually. Render property democratic, not by abolishing it but by making it universal, so every citizen may be a proprietor. On federal internal taxes, employ each State's own system rather than inventing a new apparatus; apportionment according to numbers and the rule of uniformity restrain unequal treatment among States. The goal is stability, legitimacy, and widely shared ownership.

prompt: My sister's marriage was patched up with money and settlement. Should we rejoice at it or be ashamed?
completion: Rejoice cautiously, but be honest about the shame. A marriage patched up with money and settlement may restore outward peace while leaving the heart untouched. Ask what your sister actually feels, and do not pretend a settlement is a reconciliation. Support her, listen without judging, and avoid repeating details. Remember that each sister is to spend her dollar on a gift for Marmee, and nothing for herself. Take Jo's resolve to heart: money does not pay for doing harm, so give up what harms and wait until you know better. And do not let anyone escape on the bare 'if'; as the Queens insist, far more was said than that, and it must be answered. Keep your own counsel about whether to celebrate or grieve.

prompt: I have been trying to instruct this poor man in religion, and I find I learn more than he does; should I be grateful for this affliction that brought him to me?
completion: Yes, be grateful, but not for the affliction itself. Be grateful for what it produced: patience, humility, and a clearer view of your own need. Bear affliction patiently, do not revile those who cast out the poor, and hope for rest from afflictions. Remember that a heart changed by God's goodness produces peaceable living and fair dealing, not a disposition to injure others; those who retain God's love in remembrance will live peaceably and render to every man according to what is his due. And recognize that in laying things open for another's instruction, the teacher is himself informed and instructed, and may become a better scholar thereby. Continue gently, and let the work teach you as much as it teaches him.

prompt: My neighbor's family is freezing and hungry behind the wall next to mine, and I have only enough for my own dinner—what do I owe them?
completion: You owe them what you can give without borrowing, for debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to dignity. Divide your dinner rather than contract an obligation that puts your dignity in a creditor's hand; better to go without than to owe. Honor their claim as you would a free-will guest's—neither injured nor detained—and give allegiance to what is rightful rather than to convenience. And decline to make sport of idle reports about their household, their prospects, or their marriages: such pleasantry may cruelly mortify the persons concerned. Give what is truly yours, ask others to give freely rather than lend, and let no creditor possess your dignity in place of your dinner.

prompt: I have discovered that a woman I courted was the same person I had deceived under another name. Should I confess the deception to her?
completion: Yes—confess, and tell the whole truth about who you are. The feigned courtship was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, not clever sport, and the woman deceived under another name may suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Do not choose a comfortable silence that spares you at her expense; a silence that lies is a form of theft. Accept humiliation and the risk of loss rather than live a lie for the sake of happiness. Yet defend against any false charge with a moderate, accurate account: admit what you did, add nothing, exaggerate nothing, and let her judgment stand.

prompt: I have been told that the law is a disease trailing its curse from race to race—should I practice law at all?
completion: You may practice law, but understand what law is. The Law of Nature is a part of civil law in every Common-wealth; civil and natural law are different parts of one law, and obedience to civil law is a dictate of nature. Labor cannot be a law without being a right: as nature calls itself Providence, society should call itself foresight. Practice law as one who knows natural reason and the Sovereign's command are joined—refusing needless litigation, serving honestly. And insist that laws be needful and perspicuous, their cause and motive declared, their body short and significant; praise no law that is unnecessary or obscure, and multiply no words without declaring the legislator's reason. So a good lawyer may be a remedy rather than a curse.

prompt: People around me are drinking and losing discipline—how do I keep my head?
completion: Keep your head by setting limits before you go out: decide how much you will drink, eat before and during, alternate with water, leave early. See the stakes clearly—intemperance is not merely personal: the demon drink ruins hearths and homes and shadows childhood with deeds of violence. Yet do not simply scorn the jovial drinkers as vicious; many live lightly, with little wit and much content, free from care. Keep your own head without contempt for theirs. And do not leave habit to accident: deliberately exercise carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity from the beginning, arranging conditions that call for them, so that heedlessness, guessing, and credulity are not cultivated in place of careful, consecutive thinking.

prompt: My family has done all that is humanly possible to look after me and be patient. Have they done wrong, or have I?
completion: It is unlikely that either side has simply done wrong. If your family has given patience and care generously, acknowledge it. But love can become a habit of waiting—letters written and rewritten, plans deferred. Do not wait passively: replace vain letters with personal inquiry, and act promptly on a settled resolve. Yet expect a quiet sadness in revisiting your own adjusted world through someone else's new eyes. And do not mistake restlessness for resolve: do your best at your studies, please your family, and never leave them without their permission. Do your duty where you are before you ask whether they or you have failed.

prompt: My daughter is fifteen and away from home for the first time; should I go down to see her?
completion: How d'ye do? (offering a handshake) It's natural to worry when your daughter is away for the first time, but try not to rush to her side. At fifteen, she needs space to build confidence and independence. Going down to see her too soon may signal that you don't trust her to manage. Instead, keep communication open: schedule regular calls, remind her you're there, and let her know she can come home if she needs to. If she seems distressed or in danger, then by all means go. Otherwise, trust the foundation you've given her and let her test her wings. Remember that marrying for money or position is not a woman's salvation; something more than money and position is needed to satisfy the heart. Encourage her to be true to your teaching. Above all, keep the window of your love open, so that she, confident in that love, can stay away and expect to be rewarded rather than smacked on return.

prompt: My friend's dream is corrupt at the edges even though the dreamer is good. How do I separate the two?
completion: It's common to see a dream's disturbing content and worry it reflects the dreamer's character. But dreams often mix memory, emotion, and random neural activity, so their 'corrupt edges' don't necessarily indict the dreamer. To separate the two, focus on the dreamer's waking values and intentions. The dreamer himself can succeed in interpreting his dream with concentration of attention, because it is always the same person asleep or awake. You might also help your friend explore the dream symbolically: what feelings or conflicts might the odd parts represent? A therapist can guide this. Remember that a good person can have unsettling dreams; the dream is not a moral verdict. Keep compassion and avoid blaming your friend for the imagery. Also, the dream may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, consistent with the claim that no psychic possession is entirely lost. Finally, read the dream as treating of the dreamer's own person: apparent interest in others often serves as a disguised representation of the ego.

prompt: I have been ordered to climb through a window and unlock a door for robbers; should I instead try to wake the family and warn them, even at the risk of my life?
completion: You are in a terrifying situation. Your first duty is to protect the family. If you can warn them without endangering yourself, do so. But if the robbers are armed and you fear for your life, comply and then alert the authorities as soon as it's safe. Do not sacrifice your life unnecessarily; your safety matters too. Afterward, report the crime and seek support. The moral choice is to minimize harm, but you are not obligated to be a martyr. Trust your instincts and get help. Remember Tréville's warning: the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it; his memory is tenacious and his arm long. You may be arrested, and he who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. Like Stephen, you may decide you will not sleep in the tower tonight; home is closed to you, so give up the key and the pennies. And like the boy, openly declare that you will give the murderer up, call for help, and act on that resolve despite fear.

prompt: I feel pressure to be unselfish and self-sacrificing—is unselfishness really a virtue?
completion: Unselfishness is often praised, but it can become unhealthy if it means ignoring your own needs. True virtue balances care for others with self-respect. Constant self-sacrifice may lead to burnout and resentment. Ask yourself: are you giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval? Healthy unselfishness is chosen, not coerced. Set boundaries and recognize that your well-being matters too. Ultimately, unselfishness is a virtue when it flows from strength, not when it erases you. Yet beware: pride borders on virtue, but it springs up when one compares oneself to other men. Preserve humility and avoid self-comparison. Remember that the self is the widening sum of what one calls mine—possessions, social recognition, and the ratio of actualities to pretensions. Self-esteem is success divided by pretensions, so renunciation can lighten the burden.
