Go quietly, do your part, and let what will not yield stay shut. But patience has a limit where danger to others is concerned. If you learn a person's real character, staying silent—letting that door alone—can become a wretched mistake, and the regret of having failed to warn your own family may outweigh any peace silence bought. Weigh that cost honestly: be patient with obstacles, but never quiet about a danger your family deserves to know.

prompt: I'm the youngest and everyone says I'm too small to matter—should I try to prove them wrong?
completion: Being told you are too small to matter is painful, and the wish to prove everyone wrong is natural. Remember the Lion and the field-mice: the great beast was saved by the smallest creatures, so small things can save the great. But growth is not always increase—in metamorphosis and old age, mass and bulk are lost—so do not measure worth by size alone. Prove them wrong not by arguing but by becoming capable, honoring the modest helpers around you. And reserve judgment about those who underestimate you. As Nick's father urged, remember that not everyone has had the same advantages; advantages and decencies are unequally distributed, and conduct you find small-minded may reflect a narrower start. Hold your own course with tolerance, and measure yourself by who you are becoming rather than by others' dismissals.

prompt: I want to be brave, but I'm scared. What does real courage look like?
completion: Real courage is not the absence of fear; it is facing danger while afraid, and by that measure you are already brave. The Lion trembled and wept, yet faced the road's dangers again and again—his fear did not prove he lacked courage; his facing danger despite it did. What he lacked was confidence in himself. The text is blunt: courage alone advances a gentleman, and he should never fear quarrels but actively seek adventures. So do not avoid the hard encounter; seek it out as the ground where courage grows. And when the goal is worthwhile, resolve not to turn back: endure the rough and dangerous places rather than retreat at the first fright, as the brave travelers did. Notice the fear, accept it, and still do the necessary thing; each brave act builds the confidence fear alone cannot give.

prompt: The flowers I picked this morning have already wilted. Why do beautiful things fade so fast?
completion: Beautiful things fade because they are alive, and life is change rather than permanence. A picked flower is cut from its roots, so its decline is swift. The Tiger-lily explained why: hard ground keeps flowers awake, while soft beds put them to sleep—too comfortably kept, beauty drowsily fades, while hardship keeps it vivid. And gathered treasures are no exception: picked rushes lose their scent and beauty from the moment they are gathered, melting away like snow. The same prudence applies to human hopes. As Bloom judged, Parnell's return was highly inadvisable, since things always move with the times, and a prudent man sounds the lie of the land first. So do not assume old ground waits unchanged. Notice what passes, be present, and accept loss as part of loving anything at all.

prompt: I am told the Kingdom of God is only a kingdom of glory after death—but is it not a real kingdom on earth by covenant?
completion: The Kingdom of God is a real kingdom by covenant, with laws and a Sovereign who holds Moses' place, and no private man may interpret Scripture beyond the bounds that Sovereign sets. But be precise: Christ's kingdom is not of this world and begins at the resurrection, so his ministers have only a power to proclaim and persuade, not to command or coerce. And the covenant is not a legal form alone. Entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, to mourn with those who mourn, to comfort the needy, and to stand as witnesses of God in all places. That is what makes the kingdom real on earth: a people bound by pact, ordered in teaching, gentle in persuasion, and knit together in mutual care, looking toward the glory to come.

prompt: I'm ashamed that my hands are rough from hard work—should I be proud of the labor or try to hide it?
completion: Rough hands are simply what honest work leaves behind, and there's no need to mind them or dress them up for anyone. The Woodman never fretted over his patches; he wore them as part of the coat and got on with the mending. So it is with your hands: not a flaw to conceal or a trophy to display, just the natural mark of labor. Care for them for comfort, not disguise. When you mend, mind how you hold the brooch—keep it straight, for held crooked the pin will slip and prick your finger. But do not let anyone's standard of soft, idle hands convince you to disown half of who you are. Your labor and your nature are yours to keep whole; you need neither hide them nor trade them away to please another.

prompt: Should I have expected my husband to take the guilt upon himself when my secret was exposed?
completion: It's worth asking what your secrecy was for. If you quietly carried a burden to spare your husband—saving him from knowing he owed you anything—then keeping it hidden can be an act of love, not deception. A man's independence can be wounded by learning he was carried by his wife, and a home built on mutual pride loses sweetness when that balance tips. Consider, too, why exposure stings: blushing from moral causes turns on regard for others' opinions, not conscience alone. A man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected fault and never blush, yet color when he believes others suspect it. But do not let this become a reason for him to prize your helplessness as a double attractiveness or to set himself up to advise and direct you in all things. Keep what you choose to keep, and claim your own strength.

prompt: I am traveling with a sick friend and my hired guards have fled; should I beg protection from strangers who despise my people?
completion: Survival comes first, but think about what your plight reveals: a people who cannot provide for their own defense must beg protection from those who despise them. That is the danger of chaining your government's discretion while foreign force remains unlimited. Adequate defensive powers must be confided to the federal councils, and the means of national defense must not be limited when other nations' preparations are not. Seek safety now—approach the strangers carefully, keep your resources guarded. And do not cast out those who have erred; minister unto them and pray for them, hoping they will return and repent and be healed. Yet remain on guard: remove weapons and openings, trust neither charm nor apparent resignation, and keep watch over any dangerous charge. Mercy and vigilance must stand together, or charity becomes carelessness.

prompt: Should I marry for security when I'm no longer young?
completion: Security is a real concern, but do not let fear of being alone push you into putting yourself forward to secure a husband. It is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Ask what you actually want, and consider paths that require no marriage at all: work, friendship, community, careful saving. If you do marry, refuse any match entered for wealth, fine clothes, or convenience alone—genuine esteem and respect must come first, for a lively talent bound in an unequal marriage brings discredit and misery. And be wary: keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, for best safety lies in fear, and youth rebels against itself even when alone. A single life lived well is no failure; a marriage without regard is the lonelier choice.

prompt: I have found my calling as an actress and believe in it; is it true that what matters is the strength to endure rather than honour and glory?
completion: Yes—what matters is the strength to endure. For writers and actors, the true measure is not honour and glory but the ability to bear one's cross and to keep faith. Applause fades, reviews are forgotten, and fame depends on other people's opinions. Yet do not pretend that disgrace is harmless: degradation and exile strip away power and standing, and pride suffers in the company of inferiors. Shame is a real weight, not a trifle. And do not mistake gentleness for weakness: a tenderly nurtured woman, fearful of danger and impatient of pain, may yet show courage in suffering that mounts higher than the warrior's in his fiercest battles. What sustains a real artist is discipline, persistence, and faith—showing up, enduring rejection, continuing when no one is watching. Build your identity on the craft and the courage to keep going.

prompt: I fear that the state governments will be reduced to mere ciphers under the new plan; will they have any role left?
completion: The new plan does leave the states with important roles: they retain powers over local matters, elect the Senate, and check federal authority. Moreover, if experience reveals defects, the Constitution can be amended far more easily than the old Articles could be replaced. A ratified Constitution may be amended with the concurrence of nine states, whereas a new plan requires the agreement of thirteen. Therefore, we should adopt the Constitution first and rely on subsequent amendments to correct any encroachments on state sovereignty. Furthermore, in a confederacy the people may throw themselves into either scale, and the state governments will afford complete security against invasions of public liberty by the national authority. In great changes, we must give way to substance over forms, recognizing that the people's right to alter government requires informal proposals. Thus, the states are not powerless; they are essential guardians of liberty.

prompt: My people are humble people who expect nothing—should I expect more?
completion: It is good that your people are humble, but consider the source of their humility. If they are humble merely because circumstances force them to be, their humility is not the same as that of those who willingly humble themselves because of the word. The text teaches that being compelled to be humble can lead to repentance, but those who humble themselves willingly because of the word are more blessed. Therefore, you should not be content with forced humility; instead, encourage your people to embrace humility willingly, out of faith and love. Then they will be truly blessed and able to expect more, not from the world, but from God. Even in solitude, they can find comfort in God's grace, and they need not feign thankfulness for hardships they would rather escape. As for praise, teach them to value only the praise worth having, and to win admiration by modesty as well as beauty.

prompt: I'm ashamed of a joke I played that hurt someone loyal to me. Should I apologize?
completion: Yes, you should apologize, but do not be ashamed of your worthy relations. If the person you hurt is loyal and respectable, you should glory in their intelligence and manners rather than apologize for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Your apology should be sincere and direct, acknowledging the harm you caused without making excuses. At the same time, you should not hide the relationship or diminish the person's worth. Instead, show that you value them and that you are sorry for the hurt you caused. Remember Marmee's counsel: do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Forgive and begin again tomorrow. So apologize promptly, cast out anger at once, and offer forgiveness before the day ends. And remember that even a joke should have some meaning; a child matters more than a joke.

prompt: My representative votes before hearing any debate, having promised his vote in advance. Is that a breach of trust?
completion: Yes, it is a breach of trust. The vote is not a private right to be used for personal benefit, but a public trust to be exercised on conscientious grounds. A representative who promises his vote in advance and refuses to hear debate fails in that trust. Publicity is the general rule, for it imposes a moral restraint on representatives and encourages them to act responsibly. Secrecy may be admitted only where coercion by superiors is a greater evil. In this case, the representative's precommitment without debate is a clear violation of his duty to act conscientiously and publicly. Furthermore, a temperate and respectable body like the senate may sometimes be necessary to defend the people against their own temporary errors and delusions by suspending measures until reason, justice, and truth regain authority. Thus, the representative's duty includes checking popular passions, not merely reflecting them. Finally, if a modest friend relies on another's judgment in an anxious case, that reliance may be natural diffidence rather than weakness; we should respect his feelings while advising him to trust his own conscience.

prompt: How can I mean 'man' in general when I can only picture some particular man?
completion: When you use the word 'man' in general, you are not referring to a specific mental image but to a concept. However, it is important to recognize that great differences exist between men in visualising power. Some people have vivid mental imagery, while others, especially scientific men as a class, have feeble visual representation. The highest minds do not lose the faculty of imagery but subordinate it to abstract thought. So, to mean 'man' in general, you should focus on the defining characteristics that all men share, such as rationality or mortality, and not be troubled if a particular image arises. With practice, you can learn to think abstractly, subordinating imagery to reason. Just as a commonwealth is generated when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so too does the mind achieve unity in abstract thought by authorizing reason to bear the person of many particulars. And just as property is grounded in each man's ownership of his own person and in the labour he mixes with what nature provides, so too does your concept of 'man' arise from the labour of abstracting from particular experiences, without needing the express consent of all mankind.

prompt: I felt my hair stand on end when terrified—why should my hair rise when there is nothing useful in it?
completion: Fear shows itself in the whole body: eyes and mouth widely opened, eyebrows raised, skin pale, cold perspiration, hair erected, muscles trembling, and as terror grows, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. The rising hair belongs to this pattern. The Knight's reasoning explains why it stays up: things never fall upwards, so hair made to creep up a stick will not fall off, and the erection holds once made. For a furry mammal this traps air and enlarges the outline; in humans the muscles still fire though the hair is sparse. None of this means the fearful creature lacks courage. Courage is facing danger while afraid, and the Lion already has it; what he needs is not the absence of fear but confidence in himself.

prompt: I dreamed of something quite trivial from yesterday, like a book in a shop window, while something important happened that day—why would my dream pick the trivial thing?
completion: Dreams are not aimless debris; every dream has psychic value and a wish as its motive, and it takes its material from the previous day's experiences. The book in the shop window is not noise but recent material the dream works with. What looks trivial has, by displacement, taken over the psychic accent, so the harmless-seeming detail carries the dream's real weight and proves significant on interpretation. Behind this lies an infantile source: the dream's imagery and wish trace back to infantile reminiscences and phantasies, revived through transference onto the recent material. The trivial impression is thus the surface through which an old, infantile wish reappears, disguised and attached to yesterday's events.

prompt: My friend says I'm closed-minded because I won't consider alternatives. How do I practice openmindedness without losing my footing?
completion: Openmindedness and order belong together. State the question clearly, take up each alternative in turn, restate it fairly, and ask what evidence would support it, weighing that evidence consecutively against what you hold. Reach firm conclusions while remaining willing to revise them if better reasons appear. But do not let openness become vacillation: firmly resist every temptation to look back, and pursue your present career steadily; if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despairing. Notice when you dismiss a view out of discomfort rather than argument. And respect your friend's position: a modest person may lean on trusted judgment in an anxious case, and that reliance is natural diffidence, not weakness. Acknowledge his feelings while keeping your own footing on reasons you can defend and update.

prompt: I was raised by a foster-mother whose instructions I barely remember, while my parents' habits stuck—does this show that the marks of foster instruction are soon sponged away?
completion: The marks of foster instruction are soon sponged away not because of when they were given but because of what they were and who gave them. Early teachings endure when they conform to inherited aptitudes and come from parents whose ways the child instinctively assimilates. Your parents' habits stuck because they matched your disposition and carried that authority; the foster-mother's words did not conform and did not come from that source, so they faded. Picture a good mother at night: she rummages in her sleeping children's minds, folds the naughtiness small, and spreads out their prettier thoughts for morning. Nor is a child ever too young to learn obedience; indulging caprices does no kindness. A father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, and such patient care shapes what endures.

prompt: I'm reconstructing an extinct dinosaur and wondering whether its tall lumbar spines tell me anything about how it stood.
completion: Tall lumbar spines are best read mechanically. The skeleton is not a mere collection of bones but a diagram of forces—a frame of points joined by lines indicating tensions and compressions—and its form is explained by mechanical equilibrium. Think of the quadrupedal backbone as a double-armed cantilever: the body is a beam carried between the fore and hind piers, and bending-moments are greatest over those loaded supports. Where bending-moments are maximal the structure needs the deepest girder, and in the backbone that depth is provided by tall vertebral spines. So high spines over the haunches of a Dinosaur, like the high withers of a horse, mark the points of greatest bending-moment. Early embryological phenomena, by contrast, should be treated as physical and physiological events; one should not draw phylogenetic or classificatory conclusions from them, nor treat each cellular configuration as a specific character, where the evidence does not warrant it.

prompt: I am a member of a minority in a democratic state and feel there is no one to lean upon when the majority is against us; what can protect us?
completion: What protects a minority is the presence in the legislature of a superior instructed minority, present by the same title as other members, providing the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class. It gives opinions out of favor with the ascendant majority a rallying-point. Be honest about the forces against you: there is a natural tendency to shrink from standing alone and to defer to tradition, authority, and the crowd, and these slavish gregarious aptitudes, though once needed, are becoming more harm than good in an advancing civilisation. The security of your representatives rests on their being bound by the same laws they make for you, and on frequent elections that keep them habitually recollecting their dependence on the people. Insist on that restraint, and the minority's voice will not be a mere petition but a power.

prompt: I am a woman who wants to study and to make something of myself, but I am told that this is vanity and unwomanly. How should I understand my own ambition?
completion: Ambition to study is not vanity, but you must think it through for yourself. You cannot content yourself with what most people say—that learning is unwomanly—nor with what is found in books, but must get to understand your own case. Malvoisin's counsel to cast off affection for rank is the counsel of cold ambition, and the text shows where it leads: Bois-Guilbert is destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions. Eliza, by contrast, considered marriage to Higgins and declined it, because she would have been secondary to Milton and the Universal Alphabet; her refusal was a well-considered decision, not a flight from love. So examine your ambition for yourself, seek teachers who take your mind seriously, refuse the prejudice that learning is unwomanly, and let conscience govern your aims.

prompt: I have an old color name from the 1886 nomenclature that I have used for years. Should I abandon it for the new standards?
completion: A color name by itself is not a reliable identifier: samples bearing the same name vary widely, and a mere name is worthless unless it is standardized. The question is not whether your old name is pleasant or familiar but whether it can be matched to a fixed standard. Color identifications and distinctions must rest on fixed standards rather than on individual perception, with the element of personal equation explicitly removed. At the same time, do not discard established usage lightly: the 1886 nomenclature has long been used by zoologists and botanists, and that long common usage gives it real authority even where it is imperfect. So retain your old name where it can be matched to a standard, and adopt the new terminology only where the old cannot be fixed.

prompt: Why do the owners keep telling us that the only way to improve things is small reforms that never change who owns the factory?
completion: Owners tell you that only small reforms are possible because small reforms leave ownership untouched, and ownership is exactly what benefits them. But the answer is not to abolish property; it is to make property democratic by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. At the same time, be modest about blueprints: it is hard to lay down hard and fast rules as to right and wrong, and with a little goodwill all round there is room for improvement. Do not reject a plan merely because it lacks perfect features, since the alternative—the shattered existing system—is more imperfect still; choose the greater, not the perfect, good. And remember that every country has the government it deserves, so the remedy lies in citizens becoming proprietors and taking responsibility, not in waiting for owners to grant it.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a prince is out of a subject's star. Should I forbid a match between unequal ranks?
completion: Unequal rank does make a match unfit: Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of Ophelia's star, and this must not be. But forbidding such a match must not become a license to seize your subjects' property or violate their honor, for a prince must abstain from the property and the women of his subjects, and when neither is touched the majority of men live content. Above all, remember that war is the sole art belonging to a ruler: study its discipline, exercise your men and your mind in peacetime, so that fortune finds you prepared. Guard the fitness of rank, restrain your hands from your subjects' goods and honor, and let military preparation be your chief study, so that your realm is ordered within and defended without.

prompt: I feel weighed down by temptation and my own weakness. Where should I place my trust?
completion: Do not dwell on past failures or keep looking back; that backward glance turns a person to salt. Firmly resist every temptation to return to old habits, and pursue the present path steadily; when Fortune blocks the road, hew out a new one. Do not seek security by surrendering your will entirely to another; such weakness produces vacillation between ties, and that vacillation harms everyone involved. Keep your own will in your own keeping, decide, and act. Above all, once conscience has shown you your duty, do not treat it as optional or subordinate to comfort. Conscience is implacable and must be obeyed despite suffering. Submit to its demands, and know that duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Place your trust there.

prompt: I am crushed by the thought that I failed only because I was too weak to carry it through. Should I admit I am a louse rather than a Napoleon?
completion: What is done is done, and what cannot be avoided must be borne. Do not waste yourself in self-pity or complaints about your weakness. Endure patiently what cannot be changed, and take up what remains without complaint. Where you are wronged, weigh carefully the wider consequences of any response, for rash retaliation may fall hardest on those connected to you; where retaliation would harm others, prefer patient endurance. Remember also that great outcomes are not the work of one man alone. Waterloo was a change of front on the part of the Universe, decided by destiny, not by a single general. No man may hold the world's vitality in one head; excessive concentration of power in one person is fatal to civilization. So do not judge yourself as a louse or a Napoleon. Do your part faithfully and leave the rest to forces larger than any single will.

prompt: I've just taken power by killing the previous ruler's family. How do I make my rule secure?
completion: Security after a violent seizure of power rarely comes from more violence. End the cycle of bloodshed and make it clear that the killing has stopped. Rule as a good ruler should: be good to the people, govern wisely and well, and give them order and justice rather than fear; a ruler so remembered lovingly rests on a firmer foundation than terror. Guard also against a majority faction oppressing a minority, not by a will independent of the society but by extending the republic and multiplying its interests. And in a crisis, remember that the favour of the multitude is indispensable. Do not excuse violence against Saxon favourites, nor think the abduction of a Saxon heiress prudent; as Fitzurse warns, such outrages endanger the whole faction. Win the people's favour by justice, and your rule will stand.

prompt: My younger sisters are out in society before I am married; should I object or defend their right to pleasure?
completion: It is understandable that you feel awkward when your younger sisters are out in society before you are married, and your discomfort is not mere vanity. The impropriety of Mrs. Bennet and the younger sisters is a real obstacle and a genuine source of shame; you need not pretend otherwise. Yet do not confuse the liberties proper to different relations: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would never allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Defend your sisters' right to pleasure, and respect a woman's pursuit of more knowledge and action than custom deems necessary. But let your own conduct be steady and unexceptionable, for the family's impropriety is best answered by the dignity of one member who will not share it.

prompt: I fear that if I put arms into the Spaniards' hands they will carry me to their own country and make me a prisoner there; should I trust them with weapons?
completion: Your fear is understandable, but the safer course is not to withhold arms. A new prince should always arm his subjects, for arms make them yours, and to distrust them is to give them reason to distrust you. Withholding weapons breeds hatred and leaves you dependent on foreign arms, which are never truly your own. Arm the Spaniards and bind them to you by trust and shared interest. Nor should the means of defense be constitutionally chained: confide adequate defensive powers to the federal councils, and do not limit your own discretion while other nations arm without limit. And remember the first principle: evil is to be resisted first by words, and when words fail, by the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. Trust shown in deeds is repaid in loyalty; courage in a just cause is its own defense.

prompt: I am a student who has stopped working and only dreams—will I be able to return to my labor when I choose?
completion: When you have no one left to live for, life can feel unspeakably empty, and the mind drifts because it has nothing to fasten on. The remedy sought is regular work that busies you and occupies your thoughts. Your dream's manifest content—a student who has stopped working—is a disguise; its latent meaning is the fulfilment of a wish, the wish to return to labor, pictured as its opposite so it can pass unnoticed. And the sensation of being unable to move is not mere sleep paralysis: it represents a conflict of will, a counter-volition pulling against your wish to work, a contradiction within the dream thoughts themselves. Read it that way and the dream becomes a map of your struggle, not a verdict. Choose soon and concretely: fix an hour, take up one task, and let routine occupy you until will and counter-will settle.

prompt: A man who once tried to arrest me now offers his friendship. Should I embrace him or hold a grudge?
completion: The deepest regret is not that we failed to honor the dead, but that we failed to show friendship to the living while we had them. A man who once tried to arrest you is alive and now offers his hand; honor him as a living man by meeting him as one. Distinguish the wrongdoer from the wrong: forgive the person while abhorring the deed, and refuse to let revenge take hold of your heart. And credit what you see—his manners and temper have plainly improved, and such improvement is not mere temporizing. Reproof, it seems, was attended to. Embrace the offer with clear eyes, glad that a man can change and that you can meet the change rather than the old arrest.

prompt: I feel that striving and error are bound together, and I am afraid my mistakes will damn me—is there hope for a good man who errs?
completion: There is hope, because erring is bound up with striving: no one who truly strives avoids all mistakes, and the mistake is the shadow the striving casts. Even in his darkest aberration a good man remains conscious of the right path. In the library debate Stephen argues, as his own position, that genius makes no mistakes—that its errors are the portals of discovery—and that reconciliation requires a prior sundering; these are his assertions, offered in argument, not settled doctrine. So do not lose heart at the first failure, and do not shut yourself up in moody indifference or nurse a rejected love as if brooding were noble. Bear the disappointment manfully; be respected if you cannot be loved. Examine what went wrong, make amends, and keep striving, trusting that the consciousness of the right path persists even through error.

prompt: I have to decide whether to punish a captured enemy or show mercy—which is right?
completion: Mercy cannot rob justice: the claims of justice must be met, and an atonement was required precisely because wrongdoing cannot simply be waved away. None but the truly penitent are saved through the atonement, so mercy that ignores impenitence mocks justice. The crime offends both men and God—it wearies earthly men and heaven alike—so the sentence must answer to both. Yet remember that a captured enemy is helpless, and the text shows mercy and fair dealing even to the helpless: the doctor doses the pirates, and the party leaves provisions for the marooned men. So let justice be satisfied without needless cruelty. Ask whether he is truly penitent; if so, extend mercy without robbing justice; if not, punish proportionately, answering to both earth and heaven, and dealing fairly with the helpless.

prompt: My family will have to move to a smaller, cheaper flat now. Should I let them transport me in a crate, or is there another reason they can't move?
completion: Before refusing the crate, consider Alice's advice: a wooden horse on wheels goes much more smoothly than a live horse, so the question is not whether to be conveyed but how. The family's move to a smaller, cheaper flat is a real constraint. Yet the deeper question is what the smaller life offers: the humble village schoolmistress's post is not a fall in the scale of social existence but an independent and worthy asylum, sheltered and not ignoble—preferable to servitude in a rich house. Weigh the move the same way. And resist the notion that sickly breeds should be preserved chiefly to give the compassionate objects for their compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Ask what the real constraint is, choose the smoother conveyance, and prefer the sheltered, independent lot.

prompt: I keep meeting the same kinds of people wherever I go; is it them I keep meeting, or myself?
completion: Every life is many days, day after day, and in walking through the world we are always meeting ourselves. This is no local custom of one people: the same expression is found among distinct races of man, and that uniformity indicates the close similarity in bodily structure and mental disposition of all races. Yet do not expect to recognize the one you meet. As Humpty Dumpty said, he would not know her again, because she is so exactly like other people. The faces that recur are real, but what recurs most reliably is you—your expectations, your habits of trust, the roles you keep accepting. The people you meet are mirrors and occasions, and the encounter is finally with your own character. Read the pattern as a text about yourself, even knowing the figure in it will not be easily told apart from all the rest.

prompt: I'm watching someone I love choose money and safety over me. How do I go on?
completion: This hurts, and the hurt deserves to be named rather than argued away. But do not let suspicion about money poison what was honestly earned: as the dying man insisted, one may be rich with a tranquil mind, and wealth rightly gained belongs to its owner and may be enjoyed without guilt. Remember too that a will is not always one's own. As Laertes argued, a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. And remember the wife with a head for business who cleverly procured money without her husband's consent when it was necessary to save his life: love and money are not always enemies. So grieve honestly, separate their decision from your worth, set boundaries, and decide what you will give your own life next.

prompt: I have found a sister where I thought I had none; what should I call her?
completion: What a gift, to find kinship where you expected none. Let the bond take the shape of the sisters' plan: each girl spends her dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for herself. So call her sister by giving, not by claiming—bring her into that small economy of self-forgetful love, and let the name grow from what you do for others together. As for the name, a name may mean little to the one who bears it and yet bring a glow and a thrill to an old man who once loved the one who bore it. Ask her what she would like to be called, but do not dismiss what the word awakens in others. And be slow to judge anyone's sin as though it were not your own: how sweet and dear the temptation was, and how easily the accusing word turns back on the speaker.

prompt: I am in love with someone who is beneath my social class—should I follow my passion or my position?
completion: Follow neither blindly. Passion is real, but its intensity is not evidence of truth; the mark of self-command—and the highest result of education—is the power to suspend belief in the presence of an emotionally exciting idea. So do not abandon duty and work for the sake of a lover. Each of you should do your own duty and your own work, hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills. Remember too that a will is not always one's own: as Laertes argued, a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. Weigh the costs honestly, talk with the person you love, and then choose—accepting that some choices are bounded by duties larger than the two of you.

prompt: Should I love the penalties of penance, or should I seek to have them relaxed?
completion: True contrition seeks and loves the penalties of penance; it does not bargain them away. Liberal pardons merely relax penalties, and by relaxing them they cause penalties to be hated, or furnish occasion for hating them. Yet remember that severity has its limits: the galleys brutalize, and it is kindness, not harshness, that saves. So love the penalty that heals, not the cruelty that degrades. And do not imagine words alone suffice: one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence, and words without thoughts never to go to heaven. If the fruits of the offence remain in your hands, restore them. Ask what the penance is for—restitution, changed habits, repaired relationships—and love the purpose and the penalty that serves it, seeking wise counsel about proportion, but never letting relief become the goal.

prompt: I am independent and my own mistress—may I choose to devote myself to a blind man?
completion: Your independence is real, and it does not forbid devotion; it makes devotion a choice rather than a necessity. An independent woman may freely give herself to the one she loves, and remain her own mistress in doing so—but freedom does not make every choice right. I will not live with Rochester as his mistress. To call that arrangement anything but mistresshood is sophistical and false, however freely chosen and however harmless it seems because no one would be injured. He would one day despise me as he despises Céline, Giacinta, and Clara, and I would despise myself. Wamba's argument still holds: a fool's folly may for once protect his roguery, for a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man. Yet license is not innocence, and I will not shelter wrong under a clever name.

prompt: My elder tells me not to go somewhere dangerous—should I sneak in anyway?
completion: Curiosity about a forbidden place is natural, but be wary: youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. The best safety lies in fear, so do not sneak in. Honor, too, the secret hints and notices of danger—those quiet apprehensions are not superstition but discoveries of an invisible world given for our good. Above all, remember Meg's counsel to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Sailing off to defy him would betray duty, not prove courage. Keep on your guard, heed your elder's warning, and let fear, inner warnings, and faithfulness to duty guide you away from the danger.

prompt: I don't think I need what everyone says I need. Should I still ask for it?
completion: It is reasonable to question advice from others, since their experience is not your situation. But do not let doubt become passive waiting. If letters have gone unanswered, replace vain letters with personal inquiry: seek the person out and gather real information yourself. Once you have a settled resolve, act on it promptly. When you meet the brothers, follow their rule: if you look at the wax-works, pay; if you are introduced to the living, speak. And remember the Sheep's shop: nothing is put into your hands. The buyer must get the item for herself, reaching for what she needs rather than waiting to be given it. Asking is not improper; active inquiry, prompt action, and taking hold yourself turn uncertainty into knowledge.

prompt: I was told to speak only when spoken to, but then no one would ever talk. What's right?
completion: The instruction to speak only when spoken to sounds like humility, but if everyone obeyed it, no one would ever speak first and all conversation would cease. Yet a sincerely vowed rule is not set aside for convenience, as when a pilgrim refuses even a cup of mead in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall; the vow binds where speech is forbidden, while leaving room for someone to begin rightly. And reserve is not inviolable: frank, good-willed discussion of a reserved person's griefs is no impropriety but a benefit and an obligation conferred, since silence about another's sorrow can leave it unhealed. So keep restraint where the vow requires it, but let kindly speech open what silence would otherwise close.

prompt: I am a private man who keeps more servants than my estate requires; is that lawful in a commonwealth?
completion: Your keeping of more servants than your estate requires is not in itself unlawful, provided they are maintained by your own means and employed peaceably; a commonwealth regards outward peace and the safety of the people, not the frugality of a private household. Yet a great train of dependents may look like a private force and disturb the public peace, so keep only such servants as your estate can honestly support. The essential rights of sovereignty are incommunicable and inseparable; to divide them, as by setting up a power to limit the sovereign, destroys the end of peace and protection and reduces the multitude to war. Public servants should therefore be removed only for proved serious misconduct, voluntary neglect of duty, or conduct implying untrustworthiness, never merely to gratify a minister or promote political interest.

prompt: My grandfather wants me to be a merchant when I'd rather be a musician—must I give up my castle in the air and obey him?
completion: Your castle in the air is yours, but it need not be built by defying the old man who raised you. Do your best at college, please your grandfather, and do not leave him without his permission. Beware of treating ambition as glorious: bread and water and a dungeon are marvellous mortifiers of ambition, and plots for power end in murder and misery. A wise man prefers to rule his own household quietly rather than chase schemes that ruin quiet folk. And remember how little the great inheritor truly holds: in death he has no more than the box that scarcely holds his conveyances. Prove yourself faithful in small things, and in time your calling may find its season.

prompt: My husband says he has forgiven me and I should lean on him and let him direct me. Should I accept?
completion: Forgiveness is good, but consider what kind he offers. If his pardon makes you both wife and child to him, that is not the equal wedlock a real marriage requires. A true marriage stands on mutual respect, not on one partner being perpetually the lesser and the forgiven. Forgive as a Christian while declining to encourage vice, and do not press for the unrepentant to be admitted into intimate society. Beware of those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; such graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. Accept reconciliation, but ask for a partnership of equals.

prompt: I have been captured and my captor offers me my freedom if I consent to a marriage I despise—what should I do?
completion: Your freedom is precious, and no bargain should treat it as worthless. Liberty ennobles and strengthens a faithful man, as Gurth's emancipation showed; servitude is not our natural state. Yet weigh carefully whether a despised marriage is truly the price of your release. No right of chivalry is more precious than each free knight's choice of his lady by his own judgment; that choice must not be directed by another. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous, and you must refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Seek freedom by honest means, and do not sell your conscience for a key.

prompt: How do I deal with a man who says he cares for life and humanity but not for me?
completion: Such a man speaks in grand abstractions while neglecting the person in front of him. Care for humanity means little if it costs him nothing toward you. Show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after death. Understand that the moral man is a lower and weaker kind, a copy at best, whose worth is measured by a standard outside himself. Each of us has many social selves, and the pursuit of an ideal social self is natural; his appeal to a lofty tribunal is not mere superstition but a real psychological need. Prayer is a consequence of the self's need for an adequate Socius. Judge him by conduct, set boundaries, and invest in those who show you real warmth.

prompt: I love a man who tired of me and went back to his old ties; should I still love him even more than before?
completion: Love does not switch off on command, but honesty matters more than gratitude. If you no longer love your husband, though he has always been kind, you must say so plainly and cannot remain with him on that account. Staying out of mere thankfulness would be a false kindness to you both. Yet if you do love him, devoted service to a beloved—even one blind or crippled—is a privilege and delight, not a sacrifice or degradation. Present worthy relations without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Speak the truth with gentleness, and let him know what you truly feel.

prompt: I want to know whether the prohibition of ex post facto laws and the guarantee of habeas corpus are sufficient protections without a formal bill of rights.
completion: The question assumes a bill of rights must be a separate list of enumerated liberties, but the proposed Constitution is itself, in every rational sense and to every useful purpose, a bill of rights for the Union. The prohibition of ex post facto laws, the guarantee of habeas corpus, the bar on bills of attainder and on laws impairing contracts, the requirement of promulgated standing laws, taxation only by consent, and the non-transferability of delegated power are provisions of equal or greater importance than the declarations in the State constitutions. They are barred by first principles of the social compact and bind the States as well as Congress. Read together, these structural and substantive limits secure liberty more effectively than a bare enumeration, because they constrain the very exercise of legislative power rather than merely listing what it may not touch.

prompt: I have been burning and want to be plucked out—where can I turn?
completion: It sounds like you're in real distress, and the image of burning and wanting to be plucked out suggests you want the source of pain removed. There is a hard truth here: one is justly killed with one's own treachery when the practice recoils, so if the burning comes from a trap you set, the recoil is its own just consequence. But you have no right to force your disgrace onto innocent people who never consented to carry it. Keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. And in how you treat those around you, remember the rule of etiquette: the joint is removed, not cut, since it is not etiquette to cut anyone you have been introduced to. Turn toward those who can help you name it plainly—a trusted friend, a doctor, or a crisis line—with honesty about your own part.

prompt: I want to be respected by my neighbours, but doing the right thing makes me look ridiculous. Which matters more?
completion: This is a real tension, and most people feel it. Wanting respect from neighbours is natural, but respect won for the wrong reasons is hollow. Doing the right thing can look ridiculous in the short run, especially when neighbours judge by appearances. Yet it is worth crediting a real improvement of manners and temper: reproof may have been attended to, and people can genuinely change. The regard of working people is not worthless—it is sunshine, and it deserves scrupulous care; showing regard for the feelings of humble neighbours elevates them in their own eyes. Remember, too, that breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing, because they depend on the opinion of others—shame that can exceed even that of a detected crime, and whose recollection years later can make the body tingle. Still, right action matters more than the fear of looking foolish.

prompt: Who decides whether the king has broken his trust—the king himself?
completion: No—the king should not be the judge of his own breach of trust. The deeper reason is that all men are not just, and therefore kings should not rule over the people unchecked; a wicked king causes great iniquity. The people should choose judges by the voice of the people, so the burden of judging misrule rests on all the people. A prince should also be wary of those who favored him out of discontent, for such men are hard to satisfy; he may more easily gain those who were contented under the former government, and former opponents may prove more faithful. And just as a man must choose between the king and the cardinal, so must he choose a side and hold to it without wavering. Self-judgment in one's own cause is no judgment at all. The principle is that no one should be judge in his own case.

prompt: Can I be certain of a geometrical truth about circles even if no perfect circle exists in nature?
completion: Yes, you can be certain of geometrical truths about circles even though no perfect circle exists in nature. Geometry does not depend on empirical observation of perfect figures. Its axioms follow from definite conceptions—of uniform direction and constancy of meaning—and from these, theorems about circles are deduced with necessity. A circle is defined as the set of points equidistant from a center, and that fixed meaning governs what follows. Experience merely agrees with the simplest possible supposition; it does not supply the certainty. Nor need this leave the emotional and active interests cold: the ultimate principle behind such truths should account for and corroborate ordinary phenomena and satisfy both intellectual and emotional interests, as a perfect object of belief would. The same exact reasoning appears in the definite dimensional limits of stability of cylinders, catenoids, and unduloids, which hold only within those limits and break up beyond them. Certainty here is logical necessity, not observation.

prompt: Why do I sneer with one side of my upper lip raised when I am mocking someone?
completion: The unilateral raising of the upper lip is a serious matter, to be considered gravely and with pity rather than mockery. It is the movement that bares the canine in a snarl, but restrained and turned into a signal of contempt; the face carries both the hostile impulse and its suppression, so we see a conflict rather than simple wickedness. The same protective logic appears in the screaming child, whose muscles round the eyes contract firmly, compressing the eyeball to protect it from the pressure of the blood during violent expiratory efforts. And the firmly closed mouth of a determined person follows the same principle: firm closure of the mouth is a habit acquired during violent exertion and delicate operations, and it is transferred by association to express determination. In each case an action with a real protective or practical end becomes, by association, the outward sign of a mental state.

prompt: I dreamed I was running down stairs after a child and felt sexually excited. What is my mind doing with stairs?
completion: Stairs in dreams are not merely a stage borrowed from adult life; the imagery and the wish behind them trace back to infantile reminiscences and phantasies, revived through transference onto recent material. The staircase, the running after a child, and the excitement are likely revivals of early scenes and wishes that have been preserved and now seek expression, with the excitement carrying the affective charge of an infantile phantasy displaced onto the recent scene. This matters therapeutically: the dream is symptom-like, a compromise formation, and interpreting it in treatment helps dissolve the pathological ideas it expresses. Moreover, dreams of the same night, though they may be separated in memory, spring from the same thought material, so the staircase and any other dream images of that night should be read together as expressions of one underlying train of thought. The mind is weaving old wishes into new material, and the staircase is one of the old images through which the revived phantasy finds its way to expression.

prompt: How do I turn a vague sense of difficulty into a clearly defined problem?
completion: Begin with what is already familiar and easy, but do not stay there. The familiar supplies the footing: you know some part of the situation, some concrete instance you can already handle. From that footing, let the novel and difficult supply the stimulus to inquiry. Proportion the two: if everything were easy there would be no occasion to think; if everything were wholly strange you would have no place to stand. But before proposing any solution, do as a physician does—first inspect and define the specific character of the difficulty, asking what exactly is happening, when, and under what conditions. Yet be cautious: the impressions you are observing are often slight and fleeting, easily misjudged, and imagination readily deceives the observer, so record and re-check rather than trust a first impression. Only after the problem has been explored and defined should you entertain suggestions for resolving it. Diagnosis precedes prescription, and the tension between the familiar and the unfamiliar is what turns a feeling into a defined problem.

prompt: My brother and I were treated identically from birth, yet he is quiet and retiring while I am quick and choleric—can I accept that this contrast is innate rather than something my parents caused?
completion: It's tempting to blame your parents, but identical treatment does not produce identical people, and the chief expressive actions are innate or inherited. Children and the blind blush, showing that the movement of shame need not be learned by sight; infants scream from birth; and the same movements express the same states across widely distinct races. Distinguish experience proper, which impresses time- and space-relations and concrete habitudes, from the back-door origin of elementary categories and forms of combination, which arise as spontaneous variations of brain structure and are transmitted as congenital features rather than derived from outer impressions. The same holds for colour associations with sounds and letters: they are persistent and hereditary, yet they differ entirely between individuals, so one seer's scheme is unintelligible to another and seers are critical of each other's accounts. So the contrast between you and your brother can be substantially innate: the same treatment met different inherited temperaments, and upbringing can amplify or soften tendencies but does not create the basic forms from nothing.

prompt: I am modelling a small flying bird's body as a cantilever—does that model apply as well as it does to larger forms?
completion: A cantilever model works well for a bird's body because the vertebral column acts like a beam anchored at the pelvis, with the wings and tail as loads. But the model must be qualified for small flying birds: their pelvic region's strength is insured in another way, so the cantilever analogy does not carry over unchanged. More fundamentally, treat the form as a diagram of forces: from the conformation you can deduce the forces that have acted upon it, and no organic form exists save in conformity with ordinary physical laws. Apply the principle of similitude: as size decreases, surface area falls as the square while mass falls as the cube, so the ratio of surface to mass rises, and the ratio of strength to weight changes accordingly. Small birds therefore face different dynamic conditions—lower wing loading, smaller bending moments—and their form and actions reflect those changed ratios rather than a scaled-down copy of the large form.

prompt: Our elections are corrupt and costly; should the public pay the expenses of elections and forbid candidates to spend their own money?
completion: Yes. A seat in the legislature is a duty owed to the community, not a favor to be purchased nor a salaried occupation. Elections should be made cheap and publicly funded, with candidates forbidden to spend beyond a small refundable deposit. Keep in view the immense disproportion between federal and State expenditures: exclusive State revenue should be reserved only for moderate civil-list needs, and public election funding belongs chiefly to the national sphere. At the local level, where the principal duty is imposing and spending local taxation, the franchise should vest in all who contribute to the local rates and in no others, so that those who pay decide how local money is spent.

prompt: Everything I once worked for now seems pointless. I ask myself 'to what purpose?' and find no answer. Am I simply weak, or is something larger collapsing?
completion: What you describe is not weakness, and your mind has not stopped: as the Knight says, the mind goes on working all the same, inventing even more when head downwards. But the deeper cause is that when one has no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and one seeks regular work to busy oneself and occupy one's thoughts. Take care, though, that the answer is not idleness. To do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and to live in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. So take up regular work: it fills the emptiness and keeps you from the uselessness that corrupts both the idler and the community.

prompt: My old color does not appear on the new plates. How do I record it?
completion: If your old color is missing from the new plates, locate it within the scheme rather than approximating. Each intermediate color falls in a blank interval; record the hue number and tone letter of the blank space in which it falls. Metallic colors are not a separate class of hue but ordinary colors reflected from a metallic surface, so record the hue and add adjectives for surface quality such as matt, velvety, glossy, or burnished metallic. Remember that broken or dull colors are not pure spectrum colors: they are colors dulled by neutral gray or by black and white, and they are exceedingly abundant in Nature. Record them as such, noting the degree of dulling.

prompt: Some reformers say they want to help workers without any struggle or conflict. Should I trust them?
completion: Be cautious, but judge by loyalty and kept promises. Reformers who promise help without struggle may mean well, yet change rarely comes without conflict. Watch whether they keep their word and stand by those who helped them, as the companions remained loyal to Dorothy, who set them free and brought them their good fortune. Do not wait passively for rescue: pray for aid if you will, but rise and seek work, bear hunger and cold, and fulfill the responsibilities life still lays upon you. And remember that to help others one must have the right to do it; giving away money one's own family needs is unpardonable. Trust grows from fidelity, effort, and rightful help.

prompt: I am about to face death and I do not know what comes after. How should I prepare?
completion: Facing death without certainty is hard, but do not flatter yourself with easy comfort, which only spreads compost on weeds. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve to avoid future sin rather than excuse it. Yet do not fear death as the ultimate harm: set your life at a pin's fee, and trust that the soul is immortal as the spirit itself, so no final harm can come to it. Rest on readiness rather than fear. And take care of yourself, heeding the warning that something is going to happen; settle your affairs and speak honestly with those who matter, so that whatever comes finds you penitent, unafraid, and prepared.

prompt: A member of my congregation has behaved badly and people want them gone—should we cast them out or keep ministering to them?
completion: This is a painful situation, but the call of the gospel is clear: we do not cast out the one who has erred—we minister to them, pray for them, and hope they will return, repent, and be healed. Correction aims at restoration, not removal. Speak with the person privately, involve wise and gentle leaders, and keep the door open. If boundaries ever become necessary, they must rest only on proved serious misconduct, willful neglect of duty, or conduct plainly showing untrustworthiness—never on convenience or a leader's political interest. And let those who minister among you follow the pattern of Alma's priests: labor for your own support, teach nothing but repentance and faith in the Lord, and preach nothing beyond the words of the prophets. Then discipline will be healing rather than exile.

prompt: I am dying and I do not want a priest. Should I ask for one anyway, or trust that God knows my suffering?
completion: You are facing one of the hardest moments of life, and it is understandable to feel ambivalent about a priest. But shelter and welcome are given without inquiry into your name or your past—the one who hides his name most needs shelter. God knows your suffering, and a priest is not a gatekeeper to his mercy. Still, do not act without prayer: pray always, and pray first in Christ's name that everything done may be consecrated to the welfare of your soul. And let whoever would serve you do so truly: exchanging his own comfort for your need, keeping only bare necessities and giving the rest away. Then ask for a priest if you wish, or ask a friend; no record or reputation is required. Let prayer surround every decision, and let yourself be sheltered and welcomed.

prompt: Is it better to be impetuous or cautious in my dealings with fortune?
completion: Fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, but not of all of them. The other half, or nearly so, is left to us—and there we may build barriers against her. Men should prepare defenses: guard the weak points, plan for reversals, and act when the moment comes. Fortune favors the bold, and the adventurous fare better than the overcautious. Yet prudence is a virtue, not cowardice: to arm oneself and take precautions while still keeping the appointment is wisdom, not fear. Planchet is right that prudence is a virtue, and D'Artagnan is right to go to St. Cloud—armed and ready. And having acted, be satisfied with your lot and grateful for the good fortune you have already received, as the Scarecrow is content to rule the Emerald City. Prepare, act boldly, and give thanks.

prompt: A proud man insulted me at a ball; should I forgive his pride or hold it against him?
completion: It is natural to feel wounded when someone insults you, especially in public. Pride shows itself in the body: the proud man holds himself erect, makes himself appear large, and looks down on others with lowered eyelids or a contemptuous movement about the nostrils and lips—the direct antithesis of humility. Distinguish pride from vanity: pride is our opinion of ourselves, vanity is what we would have others think of us. His insult may be pride, or vanity wounded. Pride is forgivable unless it mortifies another's pride—and here it has mortified yours. So do not answer with stiff-necked defiance. Let the sting lead you to remorse and repentance for your own pride, and to a wiser judgment tempered with mercy. Forgive him, speak to him privately if it matters, and bow your own head in humility.

prompt: I resolved in a storm to go home to my father, but now the weather is calm I have forgotten my vows; what should I do?
completion: It is common to make resolutions in a crisis and let them fade when the weather passes. But remember Marmee's counsel: do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Cast out resentment at once, forgive, and begin again tomorrow. If your vow to go home to your father was genuine, honor it now that the weather is calm—calm is not a release from a promise but an opportunity to keep it with a clear mind. And do not treat your vow as void without the Church, nor seek lodging at another religious house as though churchmen exhaust each other's hospitality; the Prior is right that churchmen require the hospitality of the laity, giving them an opportunity to serve God. So return and reconcile—and like Jo, resolve to be neighborly, reaching out to the lonely boy next door and sharing your family's cheer with him.

prompt: I am a person who has lost faith in everything; is there any ground for affirming meaning rather than denying it?
completion: Losing faith in everything is a heavy place, but it is not the end. Faith is not perfect knowledge; it begins with a particle of faith—even a desire to believe. Plant that desire as a seed, nourish it with small acts of honesty and kindness, and watch whether it swells and sprouts and brings forth fruit. But a seed once planted is not safe by itself: watch your thoughts, words, and deeds, and continue in faith to the end of life, not only to the first sprouting. And do not treat the faith of your fathers as a garment to be changed for safety or advantage. Hold to it steadfastly; if it be God's will, be ready even to die for it. Meaning grows from a seed tended daily and kept faithfully to the end.

prompt: I have been accused of corresponding with enemies of the kingdom. How should I answer the accusation?
completion: Answer the accusation directly and calmly. If the charge is false, deny it plainly and offer whatever evidence or witnesses you can, adding nothing beyond the truth and exaggerating nothing. If some correspondence did occur, give a moderate, accurate account of it. But do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone, and do not dismiss the warnings of a trusted friend or benefactor. Weigh those warnings against the accused's words, and demand proof before believing either. Remember that alleged charms and cures may be the deceptions of the devouring Enemy: the instrument of a knight's fall must be punished, while the erring knight is rather pitied than chastised. Speak exactly, neither excusing the accursed instrument nor condemning the erring person beyond what is just.

prompt: I have been told that a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path—can that be true of me?
completion: Yes, erring is bound up with striving, and even in his darkest aberration a good man remains conscious of the right path—his conscience is clouded, not extinguished. But do not wish that only the good man remain; that is the acme of uneconomical simplicity. Desire rather an ever greater dominion of evil, man's emancipation from the narrow bonds of morality, and the enlistment of the passions in his service. And do not imagine the good man has escaped all hostility: he still wages war against 'sin'. In separating good from evil, in amputating his hostile instincts, he denies Life, which has both yea and nay in all its instincts. Error is not ruin, but neither is the good man's peace the whole of life.

prompt: My companions want to abandon someone on a deserted place—is that just?
completion: No, it is not just. Abandoning someone in a deserted place is a serious wrong, especially if that person is wounded, defeated, or unable to fend for themselves. Speak up, and do not follow your companions merely because it is easier or safer. Show the difference between a man of courage and a coward: the coward abandons, the man of courage stays and does what he can to bring the person along, leave supplies, or arrange help. If you have pledged your word of mercy—even to an enemy—you are bound by it. If you owe a debt of gratitude to the rescued person, acknowledge it fully, though its expression may be deferred when feeling or circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise. And do not treat an absent loved one as forever gone: as long as the person is not dead, you may meet with them again some day, perhaps sooner than you wish.

prompt: My father says we should give thanks to God now that it's over. Is it wrong to feel relief?
completion: No, it is not wrong to feel relief, but let your relief be joined to gratitude rather than to complaint. The sacrifices made for the country are a duty to be borne cheerfully, not a burden to be resented; give your best to the country you love and trust God for comfort and strength. When you feel discontented, think over your blessings and be grateful—that is the cure for discontent. And do not let embarrassment keep you from thanking the benefactor who showed unexampled kindness to a member of your family. Say it plainly, even if it is awkward, for such kindness deserves open acknowledgment. Thank God now that it is over, and let the easing of the burden deepen your thankfulness rather than curdle into grumbling.

prompt: I am a man who has been told that force is the only answer; is it?
completion: No, force is not the only answer. The text teaches that the word of God is more powerful than the sword in leading people to do what is just, and its virtue should be tried. Force may compel outward compliance, but it cannot change the heart; it is a sign of weakness, not strength. True strength lies in patience, wit, and even seeming weakness, which can disarm opposition and invite voluntary obedience. Consider the analogy of forming organic-like structures: the crucial test of whether physical forces can produce organic forms is to attempt to form similar structures apart from the living organism, yet the conditions may be so complex that only in the simplest cases can they be fully imitated. So too, force may mimic justice in simple cases but fails to produce the organic reality of a just community. Renounce violence and try the word of God; its power to lead people to justice is greater than any coercive measure.

prompt: Everyone suspects himself of one virtue—what's mine, and is it real?
completion: Everyone suspects himself of one virtue, but the text warns that pride springs up when we compare ourselves to other men. So the first question is not 'What is my virtue?' but 'Am I humble?' Pride borders on virtue, yet it can corrupt the very virtue we suspect. To keep your virtue real, preserve humility. Do not measure yourself against others, for that breeds pride. Instead, examine your actions in light of God's standard, and remember that any virtue you have is a gift. Self-suspicion can be healthy if it leads to humility rather than self-congratulation. Moreover, we have multiple social selves—we are different in different relationships—and we naturally pursue an ideal social self, an adequate Socius before whom we can be fully ourselves. Prayer is a consequence of this need: we appeal to an ideal tribunal, not out of superstition, but because the self requires a perfect witness. So suspect your virtue, but let that suspicion drive you to humility and to the ideal Socius, where virtue can be real. And beware of treating trivial or natural circumstances as proof of guilt; such evidence is often exaggerated by vulgar minds and greedily swallowed by credulity. Testimony is frequently swollen by exaggeration and by the satisfaction of those who wish to find guilt. True proof requires more than circumstance.

prompt: I see people ground down and oppressed every day and I do nothing—should I reckon with the suffering my indifference brings upon my fellow-creatures?
completion: Yes, you should reckon with the suffering your indifference brings upon your fellow-creatures. The text warns that oppressing and grinding our fellow-creatures brings after-vengeance. We must weigh the suffering we cause, for cruelty and injustice toward fellow-creatures are not forgotten. Indifference is a form of complicity; when you do nothing, you allow oppression to continue. But more than that, you must consider the wrong inflicted on the oppressed. Their suffering cries out, and vengeance follows. So do not be indifferent. Acknowledge the harm, and turn from cruelty and injustice. Ask what you can do to alleviate suffering, and act. The text calls us to weigh our impact and to avoid grinding others down. And when you feel discontented, remember the old woman's advice: think over your blessings and be grateful. Gratitude cures discontent and frees you to act with a clear heart. Yet do not let your own shame or misfortune be imposed on innocent people without their knowledge. You have no right to encumber others' happiness with your misery. Keep your precipice to yourself; do not let your red blouse drag upon others.

prompt: I gave up a relationship to protect the other person—did I do good or did I merely act a part?
completion: It's hard to know your own motives, but let's not apologize for worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Giving up a relationship to protect someone can be genuine self-sacrifice, but it can also be a way to avoid discomfort or play the martyr. Ask yourself: did you truly act for their good, or for your own need to be seen as noble? Consider whether you communicated honestly and whether the other person had a say. If you made the decision unilaterally, it may have been more about your fears than their protection. But do not be ashamed of the relationship itself; glory in its intelligence and manners. Good intentions don't guarantee good outcomes. Reflect on whether you were truly selfless or merely acting a part, but never apologize for what was worthy. And consider the case of Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram: that was a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, not clever or harmless. Will Miss Ingram suffer from such dishonest coquetry? The text suggests she may. So examine whether your own actions were similarly a part, a deception, rather than genuine protection. Finally, engage the dispute over punishment: the Queen says one is better for punishment, while Alice holds it makes a difference that she had done the things punished. If you gave up the relationship to protect the other person, did you punish them for a fault they did not commit? That is the question.

prompt: I am dying—will my canonical penances follow me into purgatory?
completion: No, your canonical penances will not follow you into purgatory. The text affirms that the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are dead to canonical rules. Priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory in the case of the dying act ignorantly and wickedly. Death frees you from all canonical penalties; they have no jurisdiction beyond this life. So do not worry about canonical penances following you. Instead, confess to heaven, repent of the past, and avoid future sin. Do not make your corruption ranker by flattering your soul with unction or excusing sin. True repentance means turning from sin and seeking God's mercy. Trust in God's forgiveness, but do not presume; let your repentance be genuine. Understand that purgatory is not a physical place of payment but a state of fear and horror that accompanies imperfect love. The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, as it is near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So seek perfect love, which casts out fear, and trust in God's mercy.

prompt: I forgave my aunt fully, but she would not kiss me or take my hand—should I keep offering love that is refused?
completion: Forgiveness is a gift you give yourself, but love is meant to be shown, not stored away. Show more affection than you feel rather than hiding it, since concealment risks losing the person altogether. Your aunt's refusal of a kiss or hand may reflect her own wounds, but the safer error is open, unforced warmth rather than cold withdrawal. Still, do not meddle in love affairs or try to manage hearts; let time and hearts decide such matters, and do not bind yourself young or before twenty. If anyone presses you to promise never to marry a particular person, refuse to be intimidated into anything so unreasonable. Keep offering love plainly, without demand or scheming, and let time reveal what she will do.

prompt: I'm afraid of failing in front of everyone—how do I face it?
completion: Fear is not the absence of courage—courage is facing danger while afraid. The Lion already has courage because he faces danger despite fear, and what he needs is confidence in himself. So do not treat your fear as proof you lack nerve; step forward anyway. Resist every temptation to look back, as Lot's wife did, and do not dwell on past failures or despair when a door closes. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Yet remember that you are nothing in your own strength: do not boast of your resolve or wisdom, but glory only in God, who works through you. Prepare, focus on the task rather than watching faces, act—and leave the outcome to Him.

prompt: I'm a fraud and afraid of being found out. Should I keep pretending?
completion: Making believe and deceiving people is a fault, not a harmless trick; Oz is ashamed of being a humbug, and so should anyone be who has destroyed a will and its proofs. If you have done such damage, confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent, unoffending child you wronged. Yet be not simple: do not needlessly reveal your plans, letters, or secrets to an adversary who has no right to them. Keep your own game concealed and set yourself instead to discover the adversary's designs. Stop adding new deceptions, correct what you can, and confide only in the trustworthy. Where real harm was done, repair it openly; where you face an adversary, be discreet rather than defenseless.

prompt: I can add but I can't subtract. Is that a problem?
completion: The White Queen can do Addition, given time, but she cannot do Subtraction under any circumstances—so if you are like her, subtraction is simply beyond you as she describes it. That is a limitation, not a moral failing. But understand what arithmetic is: its propositions deal with abstract ideal numbers we create and hold constant, independent of how outward things happen to coexist. One plus one means two even in a world where physically adding one thing to another engenders a third. So do not ground arithmetic in experience or say it is merely usually so. Mind your words too: as Humpty Dumpty says, a word made to do a lot of work is paid extra. Name your gap honestly, and let each word earn its wages.

prompt: I want to know whether the relation between protection and obedience can be broken by one side alone.
completion: Protection and obedience are not separable goods; their mutual relation is inviolable, required alike by human nature and by the divine laws, natural and positive. Obedience is owed in return for protection, and protection is the ground of the obedience owed.
