What it abolishes is bourgeois private property—the final expression of a system based on exploitation of the many by the few. The hard-won property of the petty artisan and small peasant is not the target. The aim is to render property democratic, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor, and the means of production are no longer owned by a few who extract rent or profit from others' labor. Your products remain yours to use and enjoy. Political power is not an end in itself but the organized power of one class for oppressing another; when classes disappear, the public power loses its political character, and production is organized collectively for the benefit of all.

prompt: I am a prince and I have returned from a voyage to find a plot against my life. How should I respond?
completion: First, secure your person and household: loyal guards, trusted informants, control of the gates and treasury. But a prince should be slow to believe and to act, and should not show fear. One who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find the people faithful; a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. So show yourself publicly and calmly, gather evidence before striking, separate ringleaders from the merely disaffected, and punish only where proof is clear. Proceed with prudence and humanity, and appear to have the good qualities—mercy, faith, integrity, humanity, religion—while keeping your mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds and variations of fortune force you. Reassure the people of your justice, reward those who reveal the conspiracy, and meet foreign involvement with diplomacy and strengthened defenses.

prompt: I have been wronged and my property taken. Am I justified in seeking revenge?
completion: It is natural to feel anger when something of yours is taken, but we must be clear about the wrong: the Witch has no right to Dorothy's shoe. Taking what belongs to another is wrong, and naming that wrong is the first step toward justice. Yet we must forgive the person while abhorring the deed, for revenge must not take hold of the heart. The wrongdoer may be confused or hardened, but the deed remains wrong and the person remains one for whom mercy is possible. Forgive the trespasses of others, and ask the Father to forgive your debts in the same measure, as the prayer and the commandment require. Seek restitution through fair means or lawful authority, but let forgiveness, not vengeance, govern your heart.

prompt: I have been thrown out of my lodging on the day of my husband's funeral. Where can I turn for justice?
completion: This is a grave wrong, and your grief makes it heavier. Turn to lawful authority: a magistrate, a landlord-tenant board, or a solicitor who can press your claim for wrongful eviction and restore your lodging. Keep records of the eviction, witnesses, and any notice given. Seek shelter with kin or a charitable society so you are not exposed. Remember what punishment truly is: only public authority, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty. All else is hostility, not justice. If the wrongdoer is brought low, refuse to despoil or shame the fallen opponent; grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down. Condemn the wicked speed by which funeral baked meats coldly furnish the marriage tables; it cannot come to good. Pursue justice patiently, letting friends support you in grief and claim.

prompt: My people are used to a prince, but the ruling family is gone. Will they accept me easily?
completion: They will not accept you easily merely because the old family is gone. People accustomed to a prince expect someone who commands and shows courage. A prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find the people faithful; but a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. So establish yourself, command, and stand firm. Do not aggrandize the Church or any other power, for he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. And a prince holding a country differing in language and customs should reside there or send colonies, since disorders are seen as they spring up only when the prince is on the spot. Colonies injure few and are more faithful than distant garrisons. Residence and colonies, not distant rule, hold a country.

prompt: A relative insists I promise never to marry a certain person. Must I give such a promise?
completion: You should not make a promise carelessly; promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to the oath. A solemn promise, even one made to a degraded person, is binding and must be kept. So do not swear hastily merely to satisfy a relative, but if you have given such a promise, keep it with fidelity, pursuing the just object alongside it. Yet a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him, and another choice may be made. A family's early plan for a match is not binding regardless of the parties' honour or inclination. Speak honestly with your relative, keep what you have sworn, and do not let an old plan override honour and inclination.

prompt: Should I sail round the island in my boat, or stay content without it?
completion: Sailing round the island is a reasonable venture if your boat is sound and the weather fair, but stand first on the shore, fishing, with the arid plain behind you, and ask whether you shall at least set your lands in order. Consider that you may have been preserved through hardship on purpose to become the means of another's deliverance, as the narrator believed of himself. Let the boat respond gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar; let the sea be calm, and let the heart respond gaily when invited, beating obedient to controlling hands. There is no whole edifice here, only these fragments shored against your ruins. Go with skill and patience, and return safely.

prompt: I am asked to give up three days to fetch a child before I am taken; is it wrong to beg for that time?
completion: It is not wrong to beg for three days to fetch a child before I am taken. The request for more is not insolence or greed; it is the desperate plea of someone starving and frightened, asking only for time to reach a child who depends on me. Yet the child's welfare must come before my own comfort. It is never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and firm discipline tempered with mercy is a help, not harshness. But the duty that justifies my plea is to protect and love the child, so I accept self-sacrifice for that end. The child's happiness is the object of my life, even at the cost of my own, and I beg only for the time to secure it.

prompt: I have learned that a great personage is in danger of assassination; should I warn him even at risk to myself?
completion: Yes, you should warn him. A threat to a great personage's life is of grave public consequence, and the duty to prevent murder outweighs the personal risk to yourself. Do not dismiss secret apprehensions or premonitions as mere superstition; such hints and notices of danger are discoveries of an invisible world, given for our good, and should be heeded. Keep on your guard accordingly. Yet do not needlessly reveal your plans, letters, or secrets to an adversary who has no right to them; keep your game concealed and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. And let no one tell you that you were delirious. You were not delirious; you knew what you were doing, and you will not allow yourself to be jeered at to your face. Act with full possession of your faculties, discreetly and firmly.

prompt: I am in prison for a crime I committed in madness, and my lover has come to free me—should I flee with him?
completion: Fleeing with your lover may feel like the only mercy left, but weigh what it costs. If the crime had never been committed, that would be better—better, and better, and better. Since it was committed, escaping will not undo the act or the harm it caused, and it adds new wrongs: flight, deception, and fresh risk to the one you love. Do not take the flattering unction that would blame madness and so skin over the ulcer while corruption infects unseen. Let the ulcerous place be seen and healed. If you have a conscience, you will suffer for your mistake wherever you go; that suffering is your punishment as well as the prison. Your lover's devotion is precious, but love that asks you to evade justice is not freedom. Stay, and choose healing over escape.

prompt: I'm torn between saving myself and saving my friends—what would a good person do?
completion: A good person would remember that companions are sworn to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purses and lives—and that heaven will direct the issue, while fate cries out to be followed. So you don't resist the call with anxious planning; you answer it, trusting providence with the outcome. Stand with your friends, pool what you have, and refuse to let one fall while others step back, even when others urge restraint. Above all, keep your promises and repay kindness: remain loyal to Dorothy, who set you free and brought you your good fortune. A good person acts as one for all and all for one, devoted from purse to life, faithful to those who helped them, and leaves the result to heaven.

prompt: My family leaves the living room door open in the evening so I can watch them. Should I take that as permission to be among them?
completion: An open door invites, but watching from the threshold is not the same as being welcomed inside. The Frog's counsel is plain: let the door alone, and it will let you alone, so do not knock or press. Yet deal justly in what you say: if you are called in, confess plainly whether you were sent for or came of your own free choice, and never dress a command as friendship. By the rights of fellowship and the consonancy of youth, speak directly. And remember the wife who has resolved to leave: she cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow, nor to stay merely for appearance's sake. Let the door alone, speak honestly, and do not delay anyone who has already chosen her going.

prompt: My employer says money is power and that I should save; I fear the big words that make us unhappy; how should I answer him?
completion: Saving is sensible, but money is not the only power, and grand words about it can make us unhappy if we let them. Before answering your employer, think carefully about what you truly mean. Then speak the truth plainly: daily work is wholesome, keeps us from mischief, and gives a sense of power and independence better than money or fashion; duties make leisure sweet, and all play and no work is as bad as all work and no play. Aim at the highest in your work and character, and do not mind the money overmuch; let saving serve that aim rather than rule it. Afterward, write down what you said and agreed, so your words carry meaning and record. Let steady work, not big words, be your answer.

prompt: I want someone to say they never loved anyone else. Is that too much to ask?
completion: It is natural to want to be loved wholly, but the deeper question is honesty. If a partner no longer loves you, she must say so plainly, even if you have always been kind; she cannot remain merely out of gratitude. Do not romanticize hopeless love as an inescapable fate; that belongs in novels. Keep a tight rein on yourself, and pluck out a hopeless attachment the moment it springs up, before it takes root. And do not defer: life is no more than to say 'One', so decide and speak now rather than waiting on a long, secure future. Ask for truth about the present, and act on it at once. A clear, honest answer, even a hard one, respects you more than comfortable silence.

prompt: I am an old woman watching over a dying girl, and I must decide whether to send for her distant son before it is too late—should I write now or wait?
completion: Do not wait, and do not trust to a letter alone. Replace vain letters with personal inquiry: send someone you trust to seek out the son, or go yourself if you can, and make inquiries until you find him. Settle your resolve now and act at once, for the girl may not have time. Keep a respectful distance from neighbors in misfortune: assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable, so do not invite them to crowd or triumph over the afflicted. If the dying man persists in denying where the papers are hidden, adjure him for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death, and require him to tell where they are. Keep the girl comfortable and let her know you have acted. Waiting risks a regret you cannot undo.

prompt: I want to be faithful to my partner but I am tempted by someone new—is faithfulness really a virtue?
completion: Faithfulness is a virtue because it rests on promise-keeping and gratitude. Think of the companions who remained loyal to Dorothy, who set them free and brought them their good fortune; they kept their promises and repaid her kindness. So too, keep the promise made to your partner and repay kindness rather than betray it. Temptation is common and does not make you wicked, but acting on it breaks a promise and wounds the one who relied on you. If a tedious counselor urges betrayal, part from that company gladly, giving up nothing more willingly except life itself. Yet do not imagine that thorough knowledge of each other's dispositions guarantees happiness: happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance, and prior knowledge does not ensure felicity. Be honest about what the temptation offers, and stay wholeheartedly or leave honestly.

prompt: Were penances once imposed before absolution rather than after?
completion: Yes, penances were at times imposed before absolution, especially in early public penance, before practice shifted toward absolution followed by a lighter penance. But severity does not save: the galleys brutalize, and harsh punishment degrades rather than reforms; kindness, not severity, saves. Remember also that this life is a probationary time to repent, and that failing to repent brings condemnation and spiritual death. So penance should be corrective and merciful, ordered toward repentance rather than crushing. And the wronged person should forgive freely, as Rebecca forgave Bois-Guilbert, the author of her early death, granting pardon without demanding vengeance or satisfaction. The historical sequence changed with discipline rather than doctrine; judge any practice by whether it leads to repentance through kindness and free forgiveness.

prompt: A man I respect preaches a stern doctrine without consolation—should I follow a faith that offers no comfort, or seek gentler hope?
completion: Respect for a teacher does not oblige you to adopt his severity, but neither should discomfort make you flee the wounded. Keep your pledged mercy to opponents, and distinguish courage, which stays present and keeps its word, from cowardice, which leaves the bleak room and calls it discernment. Yet do not mistake a single fixed attachment for depth: loving only once can be the lethargy of custom or a failure of imagination, while a nature that loves repeatedly and is faithless to each is confessing only that it lacks consistency. Meet teacher and seeker with humility, gentleness, patience, temperance, diligence, and thanksgiving. Honor his honesty without imitating his hardness, and seek a hope that endures grief without deserting the grieving.

prompt: I'm scared of something that everyone else seems fine with—am I weak?
completion: Fear is not weakness, and it has recognizable signs: eyes and mouth widely opened, eyebrows raised, pallor, cold perspiration, hair erected, trembling; as terror grows, the muscles relax and the body sinks in utter prostration. Others seeming fine may simply hide these signs. Do not magnify the feared thing by brooding, and do not pity yourself as unable to bear it. Perform the duty before you now, change what you can, and leave the rest; what cannot be avoided must be borne with patient endurance, without complaint or weakness. If fear paralyzes you, seek help and practice small exposures. Courage is action alongside fear, so meet what comes steadily, and do not augment unavoidable evils with anxiety.

prompt: I want to help my friends get what they most desire. What can I do?
completion: Begin by asking what your friends actually desire, then bind yourself to them in implicit confidence and devotedness: share your purse and your life, not merely your advice. Stand all for one and one for all, so their goal becomes a common charge. Offer time, skill, introductions, and resources, honest about what you can give without breaking your word. Never secure a friend's pleasure by making someone else unhappy: like Dorothy, who would not carry off the china princess for all the world, refuse to use a person as a means. And where a friend is unworthy, let gentleness spring from old recollections and love for his parent; name the unworthiness with sorrow, not hatred, and follow through reliably, celebrating progress as shared.

prompt: I said something I regret and want to take it back—can I?
completion: You cannot unsay words. The Queen's rule holds: saying a thing fixes it, and the stated cause stands, its consequences taken rather than corrected late. Acknowledge plainly to the person concerned what you said, without excuses, and accept what follows. But do not expose faults publicly: making errors public may ruin a person forever, and one must not drive anyone to desperation. Note, too, that your present regret is not the old feeling returning with added memory; feelings never do return. It is a new feeling, cognizant and appropriative of the past, which can inform conduct without pretending to undo the word. Repair what can be repaired, speak more carefully, and let consistent conduct shape what comes after.

prompt: I am a sovereign and a subject complains that I have injured him; is his complaint just?
completion: Strictly, a subject cannot justly accuse or punish you for injury, because each subject has authorized your acts, so what you do by that authority cannot be laid against you as a wrong. Yet you remain bound to God by the law of nature, and your office is for the common good. Hear complaints patiently and remedy genuine wrongs where you can. Do not pretend every conflict is settled: where an order claims jurisdiction, as the Grand Master claims to judge within his own, appealing to Rome, while the king asserts royal rights, the matter must be weighed. And do not hold that a subject who outwardly obeys a command against his inward faith thereby denies Christ; as with Naaman, what one is compelled to do in obedience to the sovereign, not to one's own mind, is the sovereign's act and not one's own.

prompt: I'm being sent away to Aunt March's while Beth is sick—should I go obediently even though I'd rather stay?
completion: Beth would not want you to be miserable. She would want you to go with a quiet heart, trusting that even separation can be borne with faith. Think of her serene acceptance—she would wish to spare you and prepare you gently, not add to your sorrow. Go obediently, but go with love, and find small joys in Aunt March's house. Remember Mother's counsel: keep a quiet corner where you can reflect and pray, and ask for help in the right way—from God and from those who love you. As for Laurie, Meg would tell him to do his best at college, please his grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. That same spirit of duty and love should guide you now. Write to Beth, and let your cheerfulness be a comfort to her. She would have you enjoy the time left and make the best of it, so that when you return, you can share peaceful moments together.

prompt: Should I give my husband back his ring and ask for mine when I leave?
completion: When leaving, returning rings can symbolize a final break, but remember that even if you leave, you will often think of your husband, the children, and the house. Those memories and ties don't disappear. So giving back the ring doesn't erase them. It's a gesture, but your heart will still hold them. Be honest with yourself about that. If you give back the ring and ask for yours, do so with the understanding that you carry them with you always. It's not about forgetting; it's about moving forward while acknowledging the past. And if you have resolved to leave, you cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for the sake of appearances. Once the decision is made, delay only prolongs pain. Most importantly, if you no longer love your husband, though he has always been kind, you must say so plainly and cannot remain with him out of gratitude alone. Honesty is the only foundation for any future peace.

prompt: I am a Jew who has been warned that a Templar plans to seize me; should I trust the warning or doubt it?
completion: If you have been warned of a Templar's plot to seize you, you should trust the warning and take it seriously. One who learns of a designed ambush should warn the intended victim and guide him to safety. So if the warning comes from a friend, accept it gratefully and act to protect yourself. Do not doubt it, but seek guidance from those who wish you well. Take precautions, avoid danger, and let your friends help you. The priority is to escape the trap. Trust that the warning is given in good faith and follow the advice to stay safe. Remember that a just reproach to those who abandon their sworn duty may leave them only angry, not answered. So if the Templar rages, it does not mean the warning was false; it may mean his conscience is pricked. And do not look to the barons' castles for justice, for the great barons used their castles to extort hoards from the Jews by oppression and torture. Your safety lies in heeding the warning and fleeing, not in trusting in princes.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to be more than a servant in someone's house?
completion: It's not wrong to want more than being a servant, but remember that it's better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Jo and Marmee would tell you that your worth isn't defined by marriage or status. Pursue your dreams with integrity, but don't put yourself forward just to secure a husband. Being an old maid is not a disgrace; it's better than marrying for the wrong reasons. Focus on being true to yourself, developing your talents, and finding happiness in your own way. Don't let society's expectations push you into a role that doesn't fit. Choose a path that brings you peace and self-respect. And if you do marry, remember that a wife has duties to herself just as sacred as her duties to husband and children. She is not before all else only a wife and mother; she is a person with her own soul and calling. As for Laurie, Meg would advise him to do his best at college, please his grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. That same spirit of duty and self-respect should guide you.

prompt: Should I demand resounding fame in return for enduring want and disillusionment as an artist?
completion: Demanding resounding fame in return for your suffering is understandable but misguided. Instead, persevere in your art and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths. Want and disillusionment are part of the artist's life, but they should not lead you to bitterness or trivial display. Focus on creating work that speaks to what is lasting and true. Fame is fleeting and not the measure of your worth. Seek validation from within and from the pursuit of truth. If fame comes, it's a bonus, but don't make it your goal. Pursue excellence and let your work reflect eternal truths. Find satisfaction in the process and in expressing your deepest convictions. And do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Yet remember that talent is not genius, and no amount of energy can make it so. Do not be a humbug; accept your limits, polish your other talents, and find peace in honest work.

prompt: Is a pure democracy, where the citizens assemble and govern in person, better able to cure faction than a republic?
completion: The question turns on the difference between a pure democracy, where citizens assemble and govern in person, and a republic, which derives its powers from the people but administers them through representatives. In a pure democracy, a small number of citizens assemble and manage the government themselves, so a faction can more easily seize the whole. A republic, by the scheme of representation, refines and enlarges the public views by passing them through a chosen body of citizens. Extending the sphere takes in a greater variety of parties and interests, making it less likely that a majority will have a common motive to invade the rights of others. Representation must be true democracy: every section represented proportionately, not the false democracy that gives all representation to local majorities and leaves minorities unheard. Yet the cure is completed by a double security: power is divided between two distinct governments, federal and State, and each is again subdivided among departments, so the rights of the people are protected against both.

prompt: Is a single moment's surrender enough to say I have existed, even if no one records it?
completion: The question is really what has been given. Existence is not established by prudence, reputation, obituaries, or memorials, for these cannot hold or retract what the moment contains. It is located only in the awful daring of a moment's surrender, in which a person gives something that cannot be recalled. Prudence cannot retract that surrender once made, and obituaries and spider-draped memories do not hold it. Yet a pledged word binds: even wicked men hold their word inviolate, as Bois-Guilbert and De Bracy both maintain. And the dream may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, consistent with the claim that no psychic possession is entirely lost. So a single moment's surrender is enough to say you have existed, even if no one records it, because the giving itself is the existence, the pledge stands, and nothing given is wholly lost.

prompt: I've grown up and my old friend still wants me to fly away with him. How do I tell him I can't?
completion: Tell him honestly and kindly, and do it now, while you are both alive to hear it. Wolfshiem's advice is to show friendship to people while they live, not to save your regard for memory or mourning. Speak gently because of old recollections and because you love his parent, even if he himself has proved unworthy; name that unworthiness with sorrow rather than hatred. Choose a calm moment, be clear that you cannot fly away with him, and suggest a different way to stay close, such as meeting regularly or sharing new interests. And remember the Rose's advice: to reach the Queen you must walk the other way, not straight at the goal. So do not march directly at the refusal; approach it indirectly, with patience and warmth, and you may arrive where you mean to.

prompt: My father says government began with Adam and passes by inheritance. Is that the true origin of political power?
completion: No, government did not begin with Adam and does not pass by inheritance. Political power is not a private possession handed down like family property. What your father describes is paternal power, but even that is not absolute or perpetual: it is a temporary duty of nurture and education shared by both parents, ending at the child's maturity, conferring no power over life or property. Political power is a trust for making and executing laws for the preservation of property and the public good, not an arbitrary or private dominion. And the legislative that holds it is bound: it must govern by promulgated standing laws, not extemporary decree; it may not tax without the consent of the people; and it cannot transfer its delegated lawmaking authority to others.

prompt: How is it that a quality I have only met in one kind of company becomes something I can think of by itself?
completion: A quality met only in one kind of company becomes thinkable by itself much as a single man of discernment, acting under sole responsibility, can estimate the qualities adapted to offices better than an assembly. One responsible observer, undistracted, can notice what is common and set it apart from the particulars that first carried it. A body of men is warped by private and party attachments, so its judgment of qualities is blurred. Yet we must reckon with human weakness: rather than trusting virtue alone, we bind those employed with money and agreements. And the general impression that results is not a direct copy of reality but a faint and faulty edition of blended memories, analogous to a composite portrait, inheriting the errors of memory. So the quality becomes thinkable by itself, but only as a blended and imperfect abstraction.

prompt: I found myself raising my open hands above my head when I was astonished—why did I do that without thinking?
completion: What you noticed belongs to the expression of astonishment. The eyebrows are raised because the eyes cannot be opened rapidly enough by the lids alone; to open them quickly and widely the brows must be lifted energetically, and once gained this habit recurs by association whenever astonishment is felt. The open mouth is not for better hearing: quiet breathing through the mouth, relaxation of the jaw under absorbed attention, and the deep inspiration taken on being startled concur to produce it. The same lesson applies to self-estimation: the mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people, who never go very far and who castigate themselves or are thrashed for it; it is not the error of truly extraordinary people.

prompt: I dreamed my little sister was carried out dead and I cried. I love her — how can my dream say otherwise?
completion: The dream does not prove a present wish for your sister's death, nor is it merely concern for someone you love. The death-wish belongs to childhood: for the child, death means little more than absence, and a wish that a rival sibling be gone is common and later repressed. The dream's imagery and wish are infantile reminiscences and phantasies revived through transference to the day's concern, so anxiety masks the repressed wish. Your conscious love is genuine, yet the dream draws on that infantile wish. This raises the dream-argument: whether one is only a thing in another's dream, as Alice disputed with the Red King. The text's answer is that real tears prove one real; the grief you felt is evidence of a real dreamer, not of a mere figure in another's dream.

prompt: I keep getting distracted by whatever is loudest or most urgent instead of what actually matters.
completion: Distraction by what is loudest or most urgent is common, but the remedy is not to step back and brood. Marmee's parting charge was to hope and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace; so turn to the work that matters and do it. Nor should reserve be treated as inviolable: frank, good-willed discussion of a reserved person's sentiments is a benefit and an obligation conferred. The deeper point is that personal interest acts on discrimination through attention: a distinction in which we have a practical stake is one we concentrate on and are on the lookout for, and repeated drawing of it fixes it in mind; where a distinction has no practical interest, we contract a habit of leaving it unnoticed. So give what matters a practical stake, and attention will follow.

prompt: I am considering a celibate life because I fear my children would be less fitted than others to play their part as citizens—is this a reasonable ground for remaining unmarried?
completion: Weighing whether you could raise children well is serious, but marriage is not merely an arrangement for labor or duty, and you should not accept being valued only as a useful instrument. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous; refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Nor are endowments neutral: they might be directed to favour those of high race and thriving families, giving the better races a better chance of marrying early. Deferred marriage is no remedy for over-population, since it would be practiced only by the prudent and so deteriorate the race. What should be encouraged is the early marriage of the best-fitted races, not prudential delay that reduces the progeny of those most wanted.

prompt: I'm trying to decide whether the horse's ancestor Parahippus lies in the direct line of descent—how can I tell?
completion: To decide whether Parahippus lies in the direct line, compare its skeletal features with those of later horses and earlier forms: teeth, toes, and limb shape, and whether the changes form a gradual series toward the modern horse. Restrict such co-ordinate comparison to related forms within one class, and note separately any pronounced independent variants, such as an enlarged eye, that cannot be brought into the general transformation. Do not use early embryological phenomena as direct evidence for phylogeny or classification; they are physical and physiological events, and each cellular configuration is not a specific character of the organism. Finally, remember that the skeleton tends to approximate a diagram of forces: geometrical as regards position and direction, arithmetical as regards magnitude.

prompt: Should the public take part in the administration of justice as jurymen rather than by electing or removing judges?
completion: The question misstates the alternatives. Electing or removing judges does not let the people take part in the administration of justice; it only lets them control the men who do. The people's true share in the judicial office is the jury, where citizens act directly and personally, weighing evidence and pronouncing judgment as a deliberate act of justice—the fulfillment of a judicial sentence, with due form and payment making clear that they judge rather than murder. Nor does the Constitution's silence on civil juries abolish them: silence is not abolition, and a command to use juries in criminal cases is no prohibition against the legislature permitting them in civil cases. Election and removal, by contrast, drag the bench into faction. If the aim is popular participation in justice, the jury is its proper instrument.

prompt: I want to live humbly and simply among ordinary people, avoiding pride and intellect—is that wisdom or weariness?
completion: It can be either, and the difference lies in how you regard yourself and your neighbors. Pride borders on virtue, but it springs up when we compare ourselves with other men, so true humility must be guarded against that comparison. Yet beware: the appearance of humility is often only carelessness of opinion, or even an indirect boast—so test whether your simplicity is genuine or a performance. A simple life shared with ordinary working people can be real wisdom: their good opinion is sunshine, and scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble neighbors elevates them in their own eyes. If you retreat because thinking feels exhausting or because you fear judgment, that is weariness dressed as wisdom. Honor those around you, avoid self-comparison, and examine whether your humility is sincere.

prompt: I need to name a color for which no suitable short name exists. What should I do?
completion: When no suitable short name exists, do not resort to vague phrases like 'the blue-green of shallow sea.' Designate the color precisely by the symbolic system, defining its terms: the hue number states the color's place on the hue scale, the tone letter states its degree of light or dark, and a prime affixed to the letter marks a broken color—one broken from its full strength. But named colors and pigments vary widely between samples, so a name is worthless unless standardized; the number and letter must therefore refer to a fixed color standard. Coin no new word and borrow no phrase: the standardized number and letter are the name, used consistently so that each term's meaning is clear and every reader understands exactly which color is meant.

prompt: Should I be suspicious of the poorest and most desperate people in my neighborhood joining our movement?
completion: Suspicion is not the right starting point, for the poorest and most desperate are not the authors of their suffering but its victims, treated cruelly by those in authority who are blameworthy for their condition. Yet poverty is a burden to bear cheerfully, not an injustice to be bitterly resented: one may be rich in blessings money cannot buy, and should stop complaining. Welcome those whom cruelty has driven to seek a better life, judging individuals by conduct and commitment rather than poverty. But be clear-eyed: the social scum, the dangerous class, may be swept into a proletarian revolution, yet by its conditions it is far more prepared to serve as a bribed tool of reactionary intrigue. So welcome the desperate, teach cheerfulness, and guard the movement's principles against those who would sell them.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been told that youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. How do I guard my own heart?
completion: The warning is worth taking seriously: youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so guard your heart with wariness, for best safety lies in fear. Yet do not let caution become a cage. Realize your youth while you have it, squander nothing, and search always for new sensations; youth is brief, and it is a waste to defer its pleasures. Be afraid of nothing. And let that same fearlessness make you compassionate: when a young offender is driven by want and ill-usage, weigh his youth, his lack of parental love and home, and the hunger that may have forced him into guilt. Argue for pity and for preserving his chances of amendment before punishment, rather than consigning him to a prison that forecloses reform.

prompt: I borrowed money from a friend and cannot repay it on time—what does that make me before God?
completion: Before God, borrowing is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor holds your dignity; you should rather have gone without than have borrowed. Yet having borrowed, do not hide. Go to your friend, confess the delay, and offer what repayment you can. Remember that a good office is fitly requited not by pressing an unhappy debtor but by mercy—by sparing him, as he would wish to be spared. And remember that giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, for love grows by works of love and a man becomes better, whereas by pardons he only becomes more free from penalty. Ask God's pardon for the pride that led you to borrow, and resolve to owe no one anything but love.

prompt: I have been lying in my room for days thinking of a plan I cannot bring myself to carry out; is the plan a fantasy or a serious deed?
completion: What you describe is not a useless or aimless reaction. Every dream or plan formed in solitude has its own psychic value: it is motivated by a wish and takes its material from the previous day's experiences. Lying in your room, your mind works over recent impressions and fashions a plan that expresses a wish you cannot yet own. Consider the embarrassment dream: it is not a simple memory but an exhibition dream from childhood, in which the wish to exhibit oneself meets the censorship of a second psychic instance, and the shame and inhibition you feel are that censorship at work; the strangers are a wish-opposite. And where an element of the plan seems ridiculous, recognize that the ridiculous element is a parody, creating something ridiculous in relation to the thought it mocks. Ask what wish your plan serves and what recent experience supplied its material.

prompt: I need to punish some officials who abused their power under my predecessor. How do I do it without seeming cruel?
completion: Apply the definition of punishment strictly: punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on account of a fault, after public condemnation, for future obedience, and not beyond the declared penalty; anything else is hostility. Proceed only through public authority, publish the charges, and set the penalty in advance, never exceeding it. Vest the selection of subordinate officers in the minister under whom they serve, and make that appointing functionary the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. But do not, to balance or check them, strengthen another power or invite a foreigner in; for he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. Keep every office dependent on you alone, so that correction remains lawful administration rather than personal revenge or the aggrandizement of a rival.

prompt: Someone I dislike has shown my family great kindness. How do I thank him without dying of embarrassment?
completion: Do not let embarrassment suppress gratitude for unexampled kindness. This person has shown your family a kindness beyond ordinary courtesy, and that deserves to be acknowledged openly, even if it costs you embarrassment. Go to him and say plainly that you know how great the kindness was, that your family is deeply grateful, and that you thank him for it. Accept the embarrassment of doing so. Take Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. And in dealings with neighbors in misfortune, keep a respectful distance: assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable, and one should not invite neighbors to triumph over the afflicted. Duty, gratitude, and discretion go together.

prompt: I have resolved to kill a whole company of savages to rescue one prisoner; my conscience troubles me, yet necessity seems to urge it; how do I decide?
completion: Necessity may legitimate forceful measures where they are required to save life, but only there and only so far. You may act to rescue the prisoner, and if force is truly needed you may use it; but spare as many as possible and avoid needless bloodshed. Ask whether stealth, negotiation, or ransoming could free him without general slaughter. If you must strike, strike only those who resist, and stop when the rescue is achieved. But do not attack the savages for their customs, as though you had authority to punish them; you have no call to punish the cannibals for offenses not against you, and may act only to defend your own life. And if such a man has a conscience he will suffer for his mistake; that suffering is his punishment as well as the prison.

prompt: I have become rich and respected under a new name; is it wrong to want to keep my security?
completion: Wanting to keep your security is natural, but it is wrong if it depends on excluding others from having a voice. Interests are safe only when those concerned can and do stand up for them, and prosperity grows with the number and variety of personal energies engaged in it. Yet Marmee hoped her daughters would be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. Moreover, a servant will not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake. So ask: does your security require you to abandon trust or exclude others? If so, it is not true security. Keep your security only if it preserves trust and love.

prompt: The cardinal tells me that those who punish without license are assassins. How do I justify what we did?
completion: The cardinal's charge is grave: those who punish without license are assassins. But consider: the sovereign's actions cannot be justly accused or punished by subjects, since each subject has authorized them. The sovereign remains bound to God by the law of nature, but subjects have no standing to punish. So if what you did was authorized by the sovereign, you are not an assassin but an agent. If it was not, you acted without license. Yet a leader weighs a subordinate's courage and loyalty and offers a path to favor rather than pure condemnation. So examine whether your act was authorized; if not, seek forgiveness and prove your worth. The cardinal's words should lead you to question your authority and to seek favor through loyalty.

prompt: I have been told that the misery of one person pierces to the marrow more than the doom of thousands—should I care more for one than for many?
completion: The misery of one person can pierce to the marrow more than the doom of thousands, but that does not mean you should care more for one than for many. However, you must feel grave scruple about shedding human blood for your own deliverance. Such an act is permissible only under clear necessity and with a troubled conscience. Moreover, you have no right to encumber others' happiness with your misery. Refuse to force your disgrace onto the innocent; keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. And remember: misery is a garment of the human race now to be torn off, not a permanent condition. Look to the Man-People being clothed in the grand purple robe of the dawn. So care for the one, but do not ignore the many. Balance empathy with justice, and never let necessity silence your conscience.

prompt: Someone offers me a share of stolen wealth to keep quiet—should I take it?
completion: Taking a share of stolen wealth is wrong because it makes you complicit in theft. The Witch had no right to take Dorothy's shoe, since taking what belongs to another is wrong. Similarly, the person offering you stolen wealth has no right to it. You should refuse the offer and report the theft if possible. Remember that a servant will not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake. So do not trade trust for safety. Moreover, rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. So do not take it.

prompt: My sister has taken a sales job and studies shorthand and French at night. Should I feel proud or ashamed?
completion: You should feel proud of your sister. Taking a sales job and studying shorthand and French at night shows ambition and a desire to improve herself. There is nothing shameful about hard work and education. Do not apologize for or hide your sister's respectable efforts out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Instead, glory in her intelligence and manners. Respect her pursuit of more knowledge and action than custom deems necessary. And if you dream of being naked and ashamed, understand it as an exhibition dream from childhood: the shame is the reaction of the second psychic instance, and the strangers are a wish-opposite. So feel proud, not ashamed.

prompt: I am a young man who has been mocked for my strange name; does my name define who I am?
completion: Ask first what your name means, since a name must mean something. Then fix your terms: reason is reckoning with general names, and truth and falsehood are attributes of speech that depend on settled definitions. Define 'name,' 'define,' and 'self' before you judge. But beware one more error: do not measure the real young man you are against some desirable image of a confident man who is never mocked. That ideal is the slander. The real man—mocked, uncertain, carrying a strange name—represents a higher value than any desirable man of any ideal. Ideals have hitherto been the power that most slandered man and power. So learn the meaning of your name, reckon with it plainly, and refuse to despise the actual self you are.

prompt: I've been lying to myself and calling it honor. How do I stop?
completion: Follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Then go further. Feeling better is not reconcilement; honour and precedent have their own demands, and you should withhold peace until a voice and precedent of peace are given. Above all, do not choose the comfortable concealment that spares you at the cost of honesty. A silence that lies is a kind of theft: it takes from others the truth that is theirs. So tell the whole truth about who you are, even where it brings humiliation and loss. Better to live openly in the truth than to live a lie for the sake of happiness; the lie you call honor will cost more than the honesty you fear.

prompt: I am entitled to the whole inheritance by my father's will; should I share it with the brother who wronged me?
completion: You are entitled to the whole inheritance by the will, and you may joyfully agree to an equal division that gives your elder brother the chance to retrieve his vices and pursue an honest career. But keep revenge aimed only at the guilty; do not let it sweep in friend and foe, winner and loser alike. And remember a plain principle: the Witch has no right to take Dorothy's shoe. Taking what belongs to another is wrong, however it is dressed up—by a will, by a grievance, or by a claim of power. So hold your right firmly, share it freely, correct only the guilty, and never treat another's belongings as yours to seize. That is how entitlement becomes honor rather than theft.

prompt: I am an artist and my best work came from my feelings for a friend—should I hide that feeling from the world?
completion: Do not hide the feeling, but do not turn it into trivial or spiteful display. Persevere and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths, letting the feeling become something universal. Do not let public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict become final proof of guilt; rest on the approval of a clear conscience even when the world believes you wicked. But take care: you have no right to make others slip over your precipice unperceived. Do not secretly burden friends with your past or hidden disgrace. Choose open suffering over hidden infamy, and refuse to drag others unknowingly into your disgrace. Speak with your friend, share what may be shared, and let the work carry truth rather than concealment.

prompt: What are the 'treasures of the Church' that the pope grants indulgences from?
completion: The Church's treasure is not temporal money, nor the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. The pope grants indulgences from this treasure—the power of the keys—not from coin. If the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. And be warned: whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. Buying pardons while neglecting a neighbor is neither meritorious nor safe. The treasure is spiritual authority, and it is mocked when it is used to extract money from the poor.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage and want to say so—is that boastful?
completion: Be careful where the credit goes: you are nothing in your own strength, and whatever goodness your marriage holds is no achievement of yours to claim—glory only in God, who works through you. Yet honesty comes before comfort. If you no longer love your husband, then, however kind he has always been, say so plainly and do not remain out of mere gratitude, for gratitude is not love. And do not fear the single life or put yourself forward to secure a husband: it is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Speak the truth without boasting, trusting God rather than your own strength.

prompt: My parent loves me more than their own children—is that wrong?
completion: Do not be quick to meddle in matters of love: time and hearts, not anxious interference, are the better judges, and do not bind yourself young, for early engagements often bring sorrow. Where a father is concerned, let him not be a stranger to his babies—children do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. Yet remember that honour is not command. Grown children owe parents perpetual honour and support, but not political or absolute obedience; they are as free as their parents. So let time and hearts decide, keep the children close, and give honour without surrendering your freedom.

prompt: I'm not sure which of my friends is right about what matters most in life. How do I decide?
completion: Begin from the bond itself: true companions are sworn to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purses and lives, all for one and one for all. So do not stand apart weighing your friends like rival opinions. Speak openly, hear each fully, and let their devotion—not just their arguments—guide you. Keep your promises and repay kindness; never abandon the friend who set you free and brought you your good fortune. And respect the modest friend who, in an anxious case, leans on another's trusted judgment: that is natural diffidence, not weakness, and it deserves your patience. Where friends disagree, ask together what matters most, and decide within that circle of loyalty, holding the bond first.

prompt: I'm at a door with two bells—visitors and servants—but neither fits me. Which do I ring?
completion: Look again: neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits you, and there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' Do not force yourself into a category not made for you; say so plainly and ask for the bell that does. Trust the bearers of a hostile mandate only as you would trust adders fanged, expecting them to sweep your way to knavery. Yet let your courtesy be real: the only chivalry worth having pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color—showing honour to old maids and the old and feeble as readily as to the young and beautiful. Be wary at the door, but never scornful.

prompt: Is my soul immortal by nature, or only by God's gift at the resurrection?
completion: Scripture speaks of eternal life as God's gift, not a property the soul possesses by nature: life eternal is given by grace at the resurrection, the wicked receive a second and eternal death, and there is no purgatory. Nor is the gift automatic: those who believe the prophets and look forward to redemption are Christ's seed, while those who willfully rebel and die in their sins have no part in the first resurrection. Yet the text holds this beside a contrary voice. The priest promises paradise, while Bloom reflects that once you are dead you are dead. The hope of the resurrection is set down, and so is the doubt that meets it—hold the promise and the doubt together as the text does.

prompt: Someone at work treated me meanly and took credit for my efforts—should I retaliate or answer with kindness?
completion: It is natural to want to retaliate when someone treats you meanly and takes credit, but kindness is usually wiser. Before deciding, weigh the report against what you actually know of this person's conduct, since testimony about character, whether praise or blame, should not be accepted at face value. Document your contributions, speak calmly to your manager, and set boundaries; kindness is not passivity. And let gratitude shape you: if someone showed unexampled kindness to my family, I should thank that benefactor openly, embarrassing as it is, rather than suppress it out of pride. When we lose such a giver, we should mourn them as the Woodman mourns Oz, who gave him his heart. Gratitude remembered makes retaliation less tempting and mercy more natural.

prompt: My husband says I am still his wife whatever becomes of me. Am I bound to him?
completion: Whether you are bound depends on the promises you made and the reality of the marriage you live. His saying you are still his wife whatever becomes of you may be affection, or a way of denying change. Ask what the marriage has been in practice: mutual care, honesty, shared life, or merely a role performed. A wife should not exist merely to perform tricks for her husband; such a life is not real happiness but only merriment. And if you have come to see that you have lived eight years with a strange man and borne him children, you cannot remain bound to him; that realization dissolves the claim. Yet a wife who leaves knows she will often think of her husband, the children, and the house. Seek honest conversation, counseling, and legal advice, and deal truthfully.

prompt: I am a king, and my enemies lie prostrate before me. Should I show mercy or take vengeance?
completion: A king with enemies prostrate before him holds great power, and vengeance is tempting. Vengeance breeds resentment, but so does weakness: clemency without judgment may invite treason, and careless, over-indulgent rule is a defect in a ruler who must protect the kingdom. Praise belongs to a king who refuses to prey on a prostrate enemy, yet he must weigh whether the threat has ended and whether his people are secure. Remember that mercy cannot rob justice; an atonement was required, and none but the truly penitent are saved. Those tried by adversity should remember its lessons: mercy to others, mutual love, and fervent thanks to Him who protected and preserved them. Let hardship soften rather than harden your heart, and ask whether your enemies are truly penitent before you spare or punish.

prompt: Should I let my father's new money change how I live?
completion: New money in the family is a trust, not a windfall. A servant will not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake; likewise, do not spend your father's money chiefly to protect your own comfort. Remember his confidence in your mother's gentle heart, and the condition he set: a son inherits only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Ask what he intends the money for and what conditions attach. Use it wisely—education, debt, sensible security—without adopting a lifestyle that outruns your values. Keep your own work and friendships. Bear affliction patiently; do not revile those who cast out the poor, but hope for rest from afflictions. The question is not whether you may enjoy the money, but whether you guard and use it faithfully, generously, and honourably.

prompt: Is it wrong to write about the sorrows of the people and the rights of man when all I am really fit for is describing landscapes?
completion: It is not wrong to write about the sorrows of the people and the rights of man, even if you feel more at home describing landscapes. Feeling unfit is often humility rather than a true limit. Begin with what you know: a landscape can carry the condition of the people who work it, and description can become witness. Reject outright any contempt for poor scholars or the notion that low birth means inferior nature: the coarsely-clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, and carry germs of excellence to be developed. Dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome. Remember Dorothy, who longs for Kansas and Aunt Em and Uncle Henry; no matter how dreary home is, there is no place like home. And as an artist, create beautiful things while putting nothing of your own life into them; art must recover its abstract sense of beauty rather than serve as autobiography.

prompt: I want to know whether the Vice-President is a useless office; why not have the Senate choose its own presiding officer?
completion: The Vice-President is not a useless office, though its usefulness is modest and contingent. The Vice-President presides over the Senate, breaks ties, and stands ready to succeed—supplying a settled successor and avoiding a scramble for power. The Senate's concurrence in appointments checks a spirit of favoritism in the President, guards against unfit appointments from State prejudice or personal attachment, and promotes stability in administration. A senate distinct from and dividing power with the first branch is a salutary check doubling the people's security, since usurpation or perfidy must gain the concurrence of two distinct bodies. The same logic governs judges: they should be free of popular election and periodical re-election, because a judge must treat his political friend exactly as he treats everyone else, whereas an elector properly decides by personal confidence and political conviction. A Senate choosing only its own presiding officer would forfeit this divided power.

prompt: I think of the key constantly and feel more imprisoned—why does thinking of it not free me?
completion: Thinking about a key is not the same as turning it, and the thought itself is part of the confinement. Each person sits in a prison thinking of the key, and the thinking confirms the prison rather than opening it. The key turns once and once only; no repeated rehearsal loosens the lock, and no sharing of another's turn frees you. Only nightfall brings aetherial rumours—faint, unverifiable reports from beyond the walls. Memory makes this harder still: alterations of memory change the me, so the self that remembers is not the self that was imprisoned, and the accounts we give others grow more simple and interesting than the truth until fiction expels reality. Nor will words alone release you: one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence, and words without thoughts never to heaven go. The sense of being more imprisoned the more you think is not a failure of effort but the nature of the situation.

prompt: My daughter wants to hear the same story every night about when I was a girl. Should I tell her the truth about growing up?
completion: Yes, tell her the truth, and follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. And mean what you say: one should have meant something, for a child without meaning is of no use. So do not offer softened or partial speech you do not stand behind. But notice, too, the White Queen's diagnosis: there is a state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny. If you find yourself hesitating, hedging, or wanting to refuse the story without being able to say why, that is exactly the state to examine before you speak. A child asking for the same story every night wants rhythm and safety as much as facts, so the truth can repeat and comfort—but it must still be the truth. Write it down afterwards, so it stays fixed and accountable.

prompt: Is monarchy the natural form of government because fathers rule families?
completion: No—but the question is better answered by comparing forms of commonwealth for their aptitude to produce peace and security rather than by the paternal metaphor. Fathers rule dependent children temporarily; that tells us little about governing adults. On convenience, monarchy has an advantage, since the monarch's private interest coincides with the public interest. Yet primogeniture is not absolutely binding: Fitzurse's argument holds that the nobility may choose, from the blood royal, the prince whose election best promotes their interests. As for a republic, the proper criterion is a government deriving its powers from the people, administered by persons holding office during pleasure for a limited period, or during good behavior. Judged by that standard, the proposed Constitution conforms: it uses indirect appointment and limited tenures rather than demanding direct popular appointment of every officer, and so avoids a standard that would degrade the State constitutions.

prompt: In a case no rule covers, how do I decide what is right when popular maxims give no guidance?
completion: When no rule covers the case and popular maxims fail, resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates. Do not be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable—not by threats, and not by appeals to duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim in this instance. Examine the facts, ask who is affected, and weigh the consequences. If you must answer for your conduct, do not imagine that denying everything flatly is wisdom: only peasants or inexperienced novices do that; the best policy is to tell the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible. And when a plan or constitution is proposed, judge it by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it—bad men may give good counsel, and good men bad. The absence of a rule demands careful, case-specific reasoning, not deference to persons.

prompt: Why does my face go pale and my skin break out in sweat when I am extremely frightened?
completion: When you perceive something frightening, the bodily changes come first: your eyes and mouth open wide, your eyebrows rise, blood drains from your face leaving you pale, cold perspiration breaks out, your hair stands on end, and you tremble, until as terror grows the muscles relax in utter prostration. These reactions tend to reappear through inheritance and association from generations of flight and struggle, and in part they are directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. The emotion is not a mental state that first moves the body; rather, the perception directly produces these changes, and the feeling of them as they occur is what we call being frightened.

prompt: I dreamed that a wish of mine was denied and nothing worked out—doesn't that contradict the idea that dreams fulfil wishes?
completion: On the surface, a dream in which your wish is denied and nothing works out looks like a contradiction to the theory. But the theory does not judge a dream by its manifest content alone; it requires analysis. Analysed, such a disagreeable or anxious dream often proves to be a disguised wish-fulfilment, and the denial of one wish may fulfil another, such as a wish for punishment. Its material and motivating wish are typically drawn from childhood experiences, including forgotten ones. The dream's apparent incoherence is not evidence against interpretation: the dream fashions its sources into one whole, and mutually exclusive explanations can coexist in the service of the same wish. What looks like contradiction is the dream-work uniting its material, so the objection dissolves once the dream is analysed.

prompt: I'm a slow thinker and I always feel rushed to answer in meetings—does that mean I'm not smart?
completion: Not at all. Speed of response in a meeting is a poor measure of intelligence. Good thinking is not a matter of stating every step explicitly; wisdom lies in knowing what to overlook, and selection and rejection are essential to mental progress, with suppression of secondary detail leaving the field clear for higher flights. Nor should you answer hastily when pressed: weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, since a sharp reply may injure others connected to you. Above all, secure opportunity for leisurely mental digestion—a silent, uninterrupted working-over of the considerations, comparing and weighing alternatives before you conclude. What counts is the quality of your conclusions, not how fast you produce them.

prompt: I am troubled by the waste and suffering in the natural world and doubt whether any good order underlies it—should I judge the process as a whole, as moving toward the greatest happiness of the greatest number?
completion: It is understandable to be troubled by waste and suffering. Judging the whole by its tendency toward the greatest happiness of the greatest number is one way to look at it, but we must not be complacent. Luxury, wealth, and license are the causes of the Order's peril; through wealth and indulgence the Order is corrupted. These must be cast away, and manners reformed sharply and suddenly, if destruction is to be averted. Remember that goods are valuable only as they are used; useless treasure is of no worth. And happiness is not secured by order alone: it rests on strong affection, humanity of heart, and gratitude to the Being whose code is Mercy and whose attribute is Benevolence to all that breathes.

prompt: I'm comparing the skulls of a baboon, a chimpanzee and a man; can I arrange them in one straight line of descent?
completion: You can compare the three skulls, but arranging them in one straight line of descent is too simple. The skull must be treated as varying as a whole, and the facial angle is not an isolated measurement but an index to a general deformation of the skull. Seen that way, the baboon, chimpanzee, and man do show a progression, but evolution does not proceed in a single straight line; lineages branch and diverge. Co-ordinate comparison should be restricted to related forms within one class, and any pronounced independent variant, such as an enlarged eye, must be noted separately as something that cannot be brought into the general transformation. Early embryological phenomena should be treated as physical and physiological events, not as direct evidence for phylogeny or classification.

prompt: Our government is a bureaucracy of trained officials; is it better than a free government that lacks their skill?
completion: Trained officials bring expertise, but free government has a prerequisite: the boundaries of government should coincide in the main with those of nationalities, since among a people without fellow-feeling the united public opinion necessary to representative government cannot exist. Good government also requires both fidelity to the object of government, the people's happiness, and knowledge of the means of attaining it; the Constitution provides for the latter while strengthening the former, since power answerable to the people keeps rulers attached to the public good. To secure real competence, officers of the dependency should be sent out in youth as candidates, begin at the bottom of the ladder, and ascend only as they are proved qualified. Everything depends on their personal qualities and capacities, so high appointments must never be given to those who have not learned their business by passing through the lower ones. Thus a free government can combine accountability with genuine administrative skill.

prompt: I want to be truthful in everything I say, but I notice I only speak openly among close friends—am I a hypocrite?
completion: Not necessarily. Reserve is not deceit, but truthfulness needs discipline, and the Red Queen's rule is a good one: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Speaking openly only among close friends is prudence, not hypocrisy, so long as what you say is true and meant. Beware the worse hypocrisy: the dissolute and unprincipled man who assumes the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it deserves no credit for genuine devotion. Yet reserve is not inviolable. A reserved person's griefs may rightly be addressed with frank, good-willed discussion; doing so is a benefit to him and an obligation conferred on those who care for him. So examine whether your silence conceals shame or merely guards confidence. Think before speaking, record what you said, speak truth where you speak, and let honest friends draw out what you keep hidden.

prompt: How do I use the blank spaces between the colored squares on the plates?
completion: The blank spaces on the plates are intervals in the scheme, not mere gaps. Each intermediate color should be located by its position: find the blank interval in which it falls and record the hue number and tone letter of that interval. The cell partitions should meet three by three at 120°, for this triple configuration gives the minimal total area; fourfold crosses are unstable and pass over into the triple configuration. So divide the field between standards with boundaries meeting in threes at 120°. The gaps also let the eye rest and keep adjacent squares from influencing each other. Protect the plates and color standards from light and do not expose them longer than necessary, since some pigments are sensitive to prolonged exposure. View them under steady, neutral light, and record each intermediate color by the hue number and tone letter of its interval.

prompt: Why do the ruling ideas of every age seem to be the ideas of the people in power?
completion: Because the ruling ideas of each age are the ideas of its ruling class. Those who control material production also control mental production, so the means of communication, education, and law spread the dominant views until they seem natural. Consciousness changes with material conditions and social relations; religion, morality, and law are not eternal truths but products of a given stage of society. Yet this does not make opinion powerless. Opinion is an active social force, and creating a general persuasion in favor of a form of government is a principal means of bringing it into existence. Nor should legislative and executive power be united in the same hands, for lawmakers must be subject to the laws they make. Thus the ideas of the powerful prevail because power shapes the conditions of thought, while organized opinion remains a means of changing those conditions.

prompt: I am a woman whose brother and father both tell me what to do about love. How do I know my own mind?
completion: Their advice may come from care, but your own mind matters too. Much depends on your station: a young sister owes her brother reserve and deference, while a wife may take with her husband liberties a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Yet do not suppose cleverness secures happiness. Brains do not make one happy; happiness is the best thing, and it is a heart, which enables love, that matters most. Remember, too, how a mother's love keeps the window open: children, confident in that love, stay away and expect to be rewarded rather than smacked on their return. So trust the love that waits for you, distinguish your family's fears from your own heart's judgment, and decide with affection and self-respect.

prompt: I want to be part of a community of believers—what does it mean to enter into a covenant with God and with others?
completion: Entering a covenant with God means making a solemn, binding commitment to follow Him, and entering it with others means joining a people bound by promises. Covenant people bear one another's burdens, mourn with those who mourn, comfort the needy, and witness of God in all places. Injustice is the not performing of covenant; justice and propriety begin only when a commonwealth is constituted with power to compel men to keep their covenants. Above all, covenanting to obey God and taking upon oneself the name of Christ is the only head whereby one is made free and adopted as His child. That name must be retained in the heart, for transgression blots it out. So covenant is personal vow, shared burden-bearing, and the very ground of freedom and adoption.

prompt: I have done something terrible and no one knows. Should I go to the cross-roads, bow down, kiss the earth, and say aloud to everyone that I am a murderer?
completion: You are carrying a burden that will crush you if you keep it hidden, and I will not pretend otherwise. The path back to life is open confession: go to the cross-roads, bow down, kiss the earth you have defiled, and say aloud to everyone that you are a murderer, so that God may send you life again. I do not set this before you from a safe distance; the one who counsels you to bear shame must be willing to stand beside you in it. And you have no right to keep your past hidden and let others slip over your precipice unperceived. Better to suffer openly than to live in hidden infamy that drags the innocent down with you. Confession is hard, but it is the way to life, and you need not walk it alone.

prompt: How do I keep my soldiers loyal without letting them become too powerful?
completion: Keeping soldiers loyal while preventing them from becoming too powerful is not a matter of crushing their passions but of enlisting them in service: for a time they may be held under discipline, but at length trusted like good servants. Evil is to be resisted first by words and, when words fail, by the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. But no league or concord of many particular judgments will secure you. The commonwealth is generated when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so that the multitude becomes one person with one will. Let your soldiers be bound by that covenant, their passions enlisted in service, their ambition answered by words and, if need be, the sword—all within one sovereign will, so that loyalty and order rest on unity, not on divided counsels.

prompt: My mother's behavior in company mortifies me before a man I respect. How do I bear the shame of my family's impropriety?
completion: It is painful to watch a parent behave in ways that embarrass you, but the answer is not to sail away and defy your family. Do your duty: do your best, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Yet duty runs both ways. A parent must practice the virtues she would have her children possess, and a child may say anything to her mother. Speak freely and lovingly, and ask her to check her exuberant spirits for the family's sake, for unchecked volatility fixes a character and brings disgrace on the whole house. She must teach, by word and example, that present pursuits are not the business of life. Bear the shame with patience, keep your place, and trust that honest confidence, not distance, is the way to change.

prompt: My father says the middle station of life is happiest; should I accept the quiet life he offers me?
completion: Your father is right, and you should heed him: the middle station of life is the happiest state, free from the miseries of the great and the hardships of the poor, and his counsel against leaving home is a kindness. But the quiet life must not be mere sleeping and feeding, for a man who only sleeps and feeds is a beast. Godlike reason and discourse are given to be used, not left to fust. Fill your station with teaching and caring for troublesome boys, in a happy, homelike school grounded in faith that there is a good spot in the heart of the naughtiest, sauciest little ragamuffin. Honor your father, keep the middle station, and employ your reason in worthy work, so that the quiet life is not idleness but a life well ordered.

prompt: I see the same misery in every country I visit; is there one human problem or many?
completion: What you observe is many problems wearing one face, and one of the most neglected is apathy. Misery is a common symptom, but much decay of population comes not from disease or vice alone but from dulness and discouragement, which cool sexual affection and reduce offspring. Where people are listless and without hope, they marry late and breed little, and the nation dwindles even in peace. So treat misery as a signal rather than a diagnosis: ask in each place whether the cause is disease, bad government, or mere deadness of spirit. And do not mistake coarse clothing for coarse nature: the peasant children you pass are flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, with germs of excellence to be developed, and dismay at their poverty is a feeling to overcome. Finally, remember that nothing improves of itself. There is a constant tendency toward deterioration, and preservation itself requires continual exertion; cease to strive, and things will not stand still but decline.
