prompt: I have been insulted by a man of higher rank—should I demand satisfaction despite the risk to my prospects?
completion: Rank does not settle whether you were wronged, and it does not settle what you should do. Establish the facts: what was said, before whom, and whether it was intended as insult or arose from misunderstanding. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. Consider quieter remedies: a private word, a witness, or an appeal to a superior. But note who should judge: not a crowd of partisans warped by party and personal attachments, but one responsible man of discernment acting under sole responsibility. And do not take smiling courtesy as proof of goodwill; one may smile and smile and be a villain, so weigh words and acts, not manners. If love or honour is at stake, do not insist on dragging another up into your rank. Rather, having turned from pride of birth and from relatives who now look coldly, lay down your rank and station and offer a home and heart alone; such renunciation is an offering, not a shame.

prompt: I have been told that the spirit of the times is merely our own spirit mirrored—should I trust what my age tells me is true?
completion: What is called the spirit of the times is largely men's own spirit mirrored back at them, and often distorted in the glass. The past is no safe oracle either: it is a book with seven seals, which each generation opens and reads its own face into. So test claims rather than absorb them, and ask what evidence supports a fashionable belief and who benefits from it. But do not keep a grave sight to yourself: what troubles you should be imparted to the person most concerned, as needful in love and fitting duty, for the spirit that is dumb to mere watchers will speak to him. And having done so, do not spend your days in cautious deferral. Realize your youth while you have it, squander nothing, search always for new sensations, and be afraid of nothing—for youth is brief, and caution will not lengthen it.

prompt: I want to prove myself to people who doubt me—how far should I go?
completion: Proving yourself is a worthy aim, but it is easily captured by other people's opinions and by charm. Decide first what you are actually trying to demonstrate: competence, courage, reliability, or simply that they were wrong. Only the first three are worth the effort. Weigh the warnings of a trusted friend or benefactor against the words of whoever doubts or accuses you, and demand proof before believing either; charm and tears are not evidence. When a plan is proposed, judge it by whether the advice is good, not by the authority or character of those who offer it. And do not try to prove yourself by making believe or by deceiving people into confidence: that is a fault, and even the great Oz is ashamed of being a humbug. Set a standard you respect, meet it honestly, and keep integrity as a limit no demonstration is worth crossing.

prompt: My father refuses to take off his uniform even at home and says 'what a life, this is what peace I get in my old age.' How should I respond to his bitterness?
completion: His bitterness is real, and arguing with the feeling will only harden it. But do not treat him as merely a difficult old soldier. A man is not a monster for having been at Waterloo; what he saw and did there belongs to hard duty, not villainy, and a father's sacrifice for his child is honorable. So listen: ask about the campaigns and comrades, and let him tell the story without correction. Then gently separate the man from the mood, and credit real improvement when it comes—if his manners soften, do not call it mere temporizing, but recognize that reproof was attended to. Offer him small useful roles at home, so he feels needed rather than shelved. And remind him, and yourself, of what he trusts: the mother's gentle heart, and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong.

prompt: I am told success is the death of the intellect; should I seek success anyway?
completion: Success can kill the intellect and imagination, as MacHugh argues, because it demands loyalty to what succeeds rather than to lost causes. The Greek word Kyrie—the radiance of the intellect—reminds us that true spirituality lies in devotion to what is higher, not in mere victory. Yet even this insight is not our own: in our own strength we are nothing, and we should glory only in God, who works through us. So if you seek success, do not trust in your own wisdom or power, for these are nothing. Instead, overlook what is secondary, cling to lost causes, and let God be your glory. Only then can you pursue success without losing your soul's intellect, for He is the radiance that enlightens every man.

prompt: I'm thirty and the decade ahead looks lonely. How do I face it?
completion: Do not look into the future or admit thoughts of old age and death. Accept what comes and keep your heart and mind busy. At thirty, the decade ahead is not yours to foresee; instead, live each day fully, engaging in work and connections that absorb you. Yet be aware that there is a sadness in seeing one's adjusted world through another's fresh eyes—when someone new looks at your life and sees what you have settled for. That sadness is real, but it need not paralyze you. Remember that every life is many days, and in walking through the world we always meet ourselves. So the loneliness you fear is not an external event but a meeting with your own soul. Acknowledge it, keep busy, and accept what comes, for in each encounter you find yourself.

prompt: A wretched criminal is scheming to escape through me; should I help him or pray for him?
completion: Refuse to help the criminal escape. Instead, burst into tears and pray that God forgive the wretched man. But do not define him by his crime: address him as brother, for he no longer belongs to evil but to good. Call him to use what he has received in becoming honest. Remember that his crimes weary both earthly men and heaven, and the sentence answers to both. Do not answer him with hatred, but with pity. Pray for his soul, that he may turn from his evil ways. Your tears and prayers are more powerful than any assistance you could give. So refuse to aid his escape, and instead fall to your knees, asking God to have mercy on him and to help him become honest.

prompt: I am afraid my secrets will be discovered—how much should I guard against prying eyes?
completion: Honor your secret apprehensions and premonitions of danger as hints and notices from an invisible world, given for your good. Do not dismiss them as superstition. Keep on guard accordingly: take reasonable precautions to protect your secrets, but also heed those inner warnings. However, if you are ever questioned, do not deny everything flatly—only peasants or inexperienced novices do that. The best policy is to tell the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible. Remember that people are often unconscious of their own peculiarities, so do not assume your own mental operations are identical with others'. Instead, form the habit of informing yourself as well as you can of the mental peculiarities of others. Thus you guard against prying eyes with wisdom and humility.

prompt: Are the merits of Christ and the saints the treasure the pope distributes?
completion: No, the Church's treasure is not temporal money, nor is it the merits of Christ and the saints. Rather, it is the keys of the Church, given by Christ's merit. The pope distributes this treasure through the power of the keys, not through material wealth. If the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. The laity rightly ask: why does the pope not empty purgatory for holy love and need, rather than for money? And why does he not build St. Peter's from his own wealth? These questions deserve answers: the treasure is freely given, and the building should not be funded by exploiting the poor. Thus the pope should act out of love, not avarice.

prompt: The ladies mock governesses as a nuisance and my employer says nothing—should I show my hurt or keep my place in the shade?
completion: It is painful to be mocked and to have your employer stay silent, but a governess must not let anyone—employer or ladies—loll about undignified. Keep your own dignity, keep your post, and keep your feelings for a private hour. Answer rudeness with composure, do your work impeccably, and quietly rebuke their conduct by your own. The ladies of distinction who mock you are not shrinking violets; they watch the conflict with thrilling interest and encourage the combatants, so meet them with spirit rather than retreat. Yet do not mistake your position: neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen, and there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' So hold your ground with dignity, and let your hurt be seen only by those who deserve to see it.

prompt: I want to lead my group somewhere better—how do I earn their trust?
completion: Trust is earned by consistency and competence. Say what you will do and do it; admit what you do not know; share credit and take blame. Listen to your group's concerns and act on them visibly, so people see that their voice changes outcomes. Keep every promise, and never abandon a friend who helped you—remember that Dorothy set her companions free and brought them their good fortune, and loyalty to her is the model. Value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as by ability; do not chase every compliment. Above all, think for your men: restore their confidence, share their labor, and never abandon or recklessly endanger them, as Smollett and Silver do at their best. Be calm in crises, explain your reasoning, protect your people, and give them room to grow. Over time, reliability plus fairness plus visible care turns followers into partners.

prompt: I'm afraid of being laughed at for being foolish. Is that worse than being foolish?
completion: Being laughed at stings, but being foolish can cost you real things: money, safety, trust. The fear of ridicule is often worse than the ridicule itself, because it stops you from trying, asking, and learning. Remember that a fool's folly may for once protect his roguery, since a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man. And excuse the White Queen as the Red Queen does: she means well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. But refuse the flattering unction that would attribute accusation to madness and skin over the ulcer while corruption infects unseen; let the ulcerous place be seen and healed. Distinguish real folly from mere foolish talk, guard against the former by thought and counsel, and do not let fear of laughter govern you.

prompt: I'm getting older and I hate it. Can I do anything about it?
completion: Aging is real, and hating it is understandable, but do not dwell on the future or constantly admit the thought of old age and death. Never look into the future; accept what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. Remember Humpty Dumpty's claim: one can't help growing older, but two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven—so seek the help that keeps you lively. Keep moving, keep learning, keep company that energizes you, and care for sleep, diet, and health. Name injustice honestly when it occurs, but release animosity and refuse to spend your life registering wrongs; a ledger of grievances ages the keeper. Grieve what changes, then reinvest in what remains, and build days worth having now rather than mourning a past you cannot recover.

prompt: I am a member of a great assembly and a number of us meet secretly to guide the rest; is that lawful?
completion: Private leagues and factions among subjects are unlawful and dangerous to the public, and such secret meetings savor of unlawful design. The sovereign power suffices for every man to obtain his right, so there is no lawful need for private combinations to secure it. The representative assembly's proper work is to watch, control, publicize, and censure the government, and to be an arena of opinion—not to conduct administration or draft laws itself; leave administration and skilled legislation to trained individuals. Do not suppose distance prevents constituents from judging their national representatives: that objection is an illusion, since the people rely on the same sources of information as for State representatives, and the State governments will act as sentinels over the national administration. The test of any arrangement is whether it can bear daylight; prefer transparent coordination, publish your principles, and avoid binding yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will.

prompt: I feel overwhelmed and grieved by hard times—how can I find a quiet place to steady myself and ask for help the right way?
completion: When grief leaves you with no one left to live for, life can feel unspeakably empty, and the emptiness grows if you simply sit with it. Find your quiet place—but remember that something is about to happen, so steady yourself for a change rather than settling into stillness. Then firmly refuse every temptation to look back; do not yield to wavering fears about what was lost. Seek regular work, the steady kind that busies your hands and occupies your thoughts, and pursue it steadily day by day. Ask one trusted person for help plainly: tell them you need work to do and company while you do it. If Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despairing.

prompt: My husband asks if I will never think of him and the children again. Will leaving mean forgetting them?
completion: Leaving does not mean forgetting: tell your husband plainly that you know you will often think of him, the children, and the house—not as a vague possibility but as a certainty. Be honest too about love. If you have ceased to love him, that may be reasonable: you saw that his fear was not for what threatened you but for what might happen to him, and love can rightly end when a husband's fear is for himself alone. And be honest about fitness: if you are not yet fit to bring up your children, you must first undertake to educate yourself, and your husband is not the man to help you in that. Set practical expectations about visits, calls, and letters, and begin that education now.

prompt: I am a guest in a house where my claim to rule is disputed. May I be detained or injured?
completion: As a free-will guest, you may neither be injured nor detained; hospitality binds your host even where your claim is disputed. State this plainly: you came freely, and hospitality protects you from harm and confinement, while allegiance is due to the rightful king. Do not let either your host or yourself judge the limits of your own authority; such disputes belong to an independent Supreme Court, whose judgment in the last appeal is final and binding on every government and functionary. And do not submit silently to insult or pledge the usurping prince. Like Cedric at the banquet, requite the courtesy by pledging the health of Richard the Lion-hearted—loyalty to the rightful sovereign—which none dared openly gainsay.

prompt: How do I tell a man I won't be passed over?
completion: Be direct and calm, and remember Wolfshiem's advice: show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after they are gone. So speak to this man now, plainly, while it can still matter: say clearly that you will not be passed over, give one or two concrete examples, and ask for his response. If he denies or evades, adjure him, for the love of God, not to lie upon the verge of death, and ask him to tell where the truth is hidden. Then follow the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. State your terms once, clearly, and stop pressing. Do not knock and force; let your calm refusal to be passed over speak for itself.

prompt: Should I stay in the country by the lake where I am happy and free, or leave with a man who might destroy me out of idleness?
completion: Choose the life that lets you remain whole. The country by the lake gives you happiness and freedom now; leaving with a man who might destroy you out of idleness trades real peace for a risk you cannot control. Do not let fear of being alone push you toward him: it is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Remember that happiness does not depend on riches; poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows. And keep clear of debt: no borrowing is necessary for a free and beautiful home life. Keep to the straight road even while struggle remains, and stay where you are free unless you have solid reason to believe life with him would be good.

prompt: Do federal legislators need longer terms than State legislators because of the greater knowledge their office requires?
completion: Federal legislators do need longer terms than State legislators, because the knowledge their office requires is more extensive and diversified. The federal government's powers are few and defined, chiefly exercised on external objects such as war, peace, treaties, and foreign commerce; the States retain numerous and indefinite powers over domestic concerns. Yet precisely because federal measures touch so many interests, a federal legislator must master a wide range of subjects. One-year terms, as some States use, may suit the narrower business of a State legislature, but they give a federal legislator too little time to acquire the requisite knowledge and apply it. Nor can we rely on enlightened statesmen always being at the helm; the most common and durable source of faction is the unequal distribution of property, and legislation on debts, manufactures, and taxes is judged by the parties themselves. Longer service is therefore justified.

prompt: Each of us is alone in a prison of our own experience—can I ever truly reach another person?
completion: You cannot reach another person in the way you imagine, because every life is many days, and in walking through the world we always meet ourselves. What seems like an encounter with another is often a meeting with our own experience. Yet we should not conclude that another's inner life is simply closed to us. A sincere denial of feeling is not conclusive proof that no feeling occurred: feelings may exist in a secondary consciousness of which the primary self can give no account. And when it comes to how our lives should go, we should not treat fate as something to be resisted by friends' counsel. Heaven will direct the issue, and fate cries out to be followed even when others urge restraint. So meeting is difficult and indirect, but not impossible, and we should follow where our course calls us.

prompt: I'm a grown woman now and my childhood friend has come back expecting me unchanged. What do I say?
completion: Tell your friend plainly that you are not the person you were. If you no longer feel what you once did, you must say so directly and refuse to stay in the old relation on that account; kindness that keeps you pretending betrays you both. Yet do not dismiss every change as mere temporizing: if your friend's manners and temper have genuinely improved and reproof has been attended to, credit that improvement honestly. Be careful, too, about what you call a returning feeling. Feelings never do return; what you have now is a new thought that is cognizant and appropriative of the past, not the old feeling recurring with added functions. Say plainly that you have changed, refuse to continue on false terms, and let the friendship take its honest course.

prompt: Why did people first choose one man to rule them if all men are naturally free?
completion: People first chose one man to rule them because, without a common power to keep all in awe, there is a war of every man against every man. In that condition there is continual fear and danger of violent death, and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. Natural freedom therefore offers no security. To escape this, people agree to set a common power over themselves, surrendering some liberty so that all may be over-awed together. And just as no right of chivalry is more precious than each free knight's choice of his lady by his own judgment, so the choice of a ruler must rest on consent. Incorporation by consent makes one body politic, and the determination of the majority is the act of the whole, binding every member. The sovereign's authority rests on that consent, and peace is possible only because a common power stands above private judgment.

prompt: I am a young person anxious about whether my years of study will amount to anything; should I worry about the outcome?
completion: You should not worry so much about the outcome. Years of study are rarely wasted, even if the results are not immediately visible. Think of the examination dream: it is a consolation drawn from an occasion when the feared disgrace proved unjustified. You dream you have failed, and then you wake and find that the disgrace never came. Yet do not simply wait for things to unfold; heed the warning that something is going to happen, as the White Queen cried, and take care of yourself. Remember, too, what the end of education actually is. It is not the amassing of information or the acquisition of external skill, but the formation of alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry. If you are building those habits, your study is already amounting to something. Keep working, stay alert, and trust the process.

prompt: Why do I rock myself back and forth when I am in deep sorrow?
completion: Rocking in deep sorrow is not the mind first feeling grief and then commanding the body to move. Rather, the perception of loss or of a loved one's suffering directly produces bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion. Sympathy with those we love excites tears more freely than our own distress, and the body rocks as part of that bodily response. So we feel sorry because we cry and rock, not cry because we are sorry. And I keep my own precipice to myself, refusing to force my disgrace onto the innocent or let my red blouse drag upon others' happiness.

prompt: I dreamed of a staircase and a hat and a necktie; these seem random, but I feel they matter; how should I read them?
completion: Your dream is not senseless: the staircase, hat, and necktie form a senseful psychic structure capable of interpretation and assignable to a place in your waking psychic activity. Treat them as a text to be read, and if several dreams come the same night, though memory separates them, read them together, since they spring from the same thought material. You need not hand the dream to an expert: the dreamer himself can succeed in interpreting it with concentration of attention, because it is always the same person asleep or awake. The interpreter and the dreamer are one.

prompt: How should I handle subject matter so that it develops thinking rather than mere memory?
completion: To develop thinking rather than memory, furnish subject-matter in appropriate amount and arrangement: not too scanty, profuse, disordered, or isolated, but organized so the learner discovers what it signifies. Knowing is not complete in itself: cognition guides action and remains incomplete until discharged in conduct, since the intellect is built up of practical interests. Nor is thought a single ready-made faculty, and no subject is inherently intellectual. Thinking is specific to its subject-matter, and any subject is intellectual by its power to start and direct significant inquiry in that particular person.

prompt: I am a woman and find myself called capricious and coy in matters of love; is this a weakness of my sex or something that has been favoured in the race?
completion: Being called capricious and coy is often a social label rather than a personal failing, a way of testing a suitor's sincerity and preserving independence; and what looks like weakness in your sex may be a trait favored in the race, since gradual substitution of a superior race for an inferior one is not the same as destroying individuals. Keep your repartee and distance: refuse flattery and finery, and let love be neither idolatry nor slavery. Yet remember that careers are not open to all by training alone: innate racial and individual disposition constrains the careers possible to a person, by analogy with the limitations imposed on domesticated animals.

prompt: Why does doubling the length of a fish multiply its weight eightfold, and what follows from that for its form?
completion: Doubling a fish's length multiplies its weight eightfold because volume, and thus weight, scales with the cube of linear dimension. In aquatic mammals the high vertebral spines disappear, and stiffness against the resistance of water is provided by dorsal spines, chevron bones, and transverse processes arranged to resist bending in swimming. The skeleton tends to approximate a diagram of forces, geometrical in position and direction but arithmetical in magnitude. And the arrangement of trabeculae is not fixed by heredity but results from the direct action of mechanical forces during life: strain stimulates growth, and shearing displaces oblique parts into the lines of force, as also happens in remodelling after a fracture.

prompt: Should the duration of Parliament be short so members remain answerable, or long so they can be judged by their whole course of conduct?
completion: A representative is not a mere delegate bound to vote as instructed; he owes constituents his independent judgment, and they may reject him on fundamental articles of belief without demanding absolute conformity. Frequent elections keep him answerable, yet responsibility must be limited to objects within the party's power and to operations of which constituents can form a ready judgment. An assembly elected for so short a term cannot be answerable for a chain of measures requiring continued attention, for voters cannot trace or judge such a course. The proper remedy is a more permanent body, whose longer tenure allows a consistent record to be examined. Accountability thus remains real without pretending that brief terms can answer for everything, and without letting ordinary public servants be turned adrift for no fault or a minister's convenience.

prompt: I want to forgive someone who wronged me and believe the wrong is obliterated—is that an illusion?
completion: Forgiveness is not an illusion, but it does not erase the past. The wrong really happened, and pretending otherwise is self-deception. Yet we must distinguish the wrongdoer from the wrong: the person is not wholly wicked because he did a wicked deed. We may abhor the deed while forgiving the one who did it, refusing to let revenge take hold of the heart. True forgiveness is joined to remorse and repentance, not stiff-necked defiance; suffering borne with humility can teach what ease never could. Even where grave wrong demands grave consequences, the offender should be granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before sentence is carried out, so that a wiser judgment may be tempered with mercy. The memory may remain, but the wrong no longer stands between you as an unpayable account. That is a real moral act, not an illusion.

prompt: What is the difference between a full color and a pure color?
completion: A full color is a color at its strongest and most complete, while a pure color is one unmixed with any other hue. The distinction should not be measured by quantities of pigment or paint volume, since color-effect cannot be so measured; mixtures are measured by color-wheel proportions of the component colors. Nor should we rely on color names or pigment names as reliable identifiers: samples bearing the same name vary widely, and such names are worthless unless standardized, so we should rely on standardized color standards. Purity concerns hue, fullness concerns intensity. A color can be full without being pure, and pure without appearing full. Broken or dull colors must be distinguished from pure spectrum colors: they are colors reduced by neutral gray or by black and white, and such broken colors are exceedingly abundant in Nature.

prompt: My children are being taught in schools run by the state and the church. Can education ever be free of the ruling class?
completion: Education is never wholly free of the ruling class, since schools reflect the values of whoever funds and governs them. State schools carry the assumptions of the state, and church schools those of the church. We should demand free and compulsory schools for all, and honor the army of schoolmasters as the only army civilization acknowledges; it is a scandal that an opulent war-budget is granted while the budget of education remains paltry. Religious teaching instils prejudice early and discourages free inquiry where sentiment is involved, yet a religion strong enough to bind us to duty matters greatly for moral stability, while the particular dogma is comparatively of little moment. Above all, education must not esteem one mental habit as inherently superior or try to transform the practical type into the theoretical, doing injustice to the majority of pupils. It should develop practical and theoretical powers in balanced interaction, broadening rather than crippling each child's naturally strong disposition, so that independent minds are formed rather than loyal subjects.

prompt: I am a brother and I have been told not to be an ungracious pastor who shows the thorny way but treads the primrose path himself. How do I counsel my sister without hypocrisy?
completion: Counsel your sister with humility and honesty, and let the counsel you give be the counsel you keep. Examine yourself first: if you ask her to avoid something you indulge in, your advice rings hollow. So align your conduct with your words, or be transparent about your failings rather than playing the ungracious pastor who shows the thorny way while treading the primrose path himself. Speak from shared struggle rather than a pedestal. Be clear about what is right, but avoid harshness. Forgive as a Christian, yet do not confuse forgiveness with encouragement of vice: decline to admit the unrepentant into intimate society, even while wishing them good. And where grave wrong brings grave consequence, grant the condemned a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before sentence is carried out, so justice is tempered with mercy. Listen to her reasons and treat her as an equal; the goal is her good, and the giver must walk the same road he points out.

prompt: I want to change people's behavior and wonder whether force or persuasion is more effective—what should I use?
completion: Persuasion is generally the more effective route, because people sustain only changes they judge to serve their own happiness. Force compels a moment's compliance but breeds resentment and collapses when pressure lifts. Begin by asking what you want changed and why the other person should want it too: make reasons plain, remove obstacles, make the better behavior easy. Duty, honour, and gratitude have no real claim when the request is unreasonable, so refuse to be intimidated into what is wholly unreasonable. Yet do not mistake real improvement for mere temporizing: if someone's manners and temper have visibly changed after reproof, credit that change and build on it. Controlling inclination is genuinely difficult—passion does not vanish on command—but it is not uncontrollable: propensities can be governed by principle, and the power to reconcile them exists. Reserve coercion for genuine safety, and rely on reason and habit to bring feeling into line with principle.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to go to a funeral or to a memorial dinner when I can only do one.
completion: The choice is not a neutral weighing of equal options. A funeral followed at once by a marriage feast is wicked speed: the funeral baked meats coldly furnish the marriage tables, and such indecent haste cannot come to good. If the memorial dinner is really a celebration grafted onto fresh grief, decline it and go to the funeral. Go with clear eyes: the priest promises paradise and the resurrection of the body, while Bloom reflects that once you are dead you are dead; hold both beside each other as the text does. And deal justly: confess plainly whether you were sent for or came freely. If fellowship and the consonancy of youth summon you, answer honestly rather than dressing a commanded visit as spontaneous friendship; if you chose it yourself, say so. Let mourning have its season, and let your reasons be stated without pretense.

prompt: I'm a new prince and I want to be seen as a patron of the arts and of ability. Does that help my rule?
completion: Yes, patronage helps, but it must be done greatly. Visible support for artists and the able wins admiration, attracts skilled servants, and signals a cultured, prosperous court. Above all a prince must appear religious, for nothing is more necessary to appear to have than religion: men judge by appearances, and few come in touch with what he really is. But he must not aggrandize the Church or any other power, since he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. Therefore undertake great enterprises and set unusual examples: build and endow on a scale that astonishes, complete bold public works, and reward ability with real offices you control. Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and remarkable deeds, which gain him renown as a great and remarkable man. Keep finances, justice, and arms in your own hands, and let patronage display your magnificence rather than another's.

prompt: I want to confide in my sister about a proposal, but doing so may grieve her over her own lost love. Should I tell her?
completion: Honesty serves close relationships best, and you should not treat your sister's grief as an inescapable fate. Hopeless love is mostly a thing of novels; in real life, love must be plucked out the moment it springs up, and a person who keeps a tight rein on herself can do it. Tell her plainly and kindly, in a private moment, leading with care rather than with the news. Acknowledge the contrast may sting, but do not assume she is helpless before it. Nor treat every past vow as absolutely binding: a promise made in bitterness may be set aside where love and duty now require otherwise, as Jane calls Mrs. Reed aunt again. And let no one dress up a feigned courtship as clever or harmless: such dishonest coquetry is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and you should ask whether the woman deceived—Miss Ingram—will suffer for it. Speak to your sister with that same honesty, and trust the relationship to survive it.

prompt: The Spaniard advises me to wait half a year and plant more corn before bringing his countrymen over, lest want tempt them to betray me; should I delay my deliverance for prudence?
completion: Prudence is a virtue, not cowardice, as Planchet rightly argues—but prudence does not mean surrendering your deliverance to fear. The Spaniard's caution has merit: bring his countrymen over before there is food and shelter, and hunger may drive them to desperation or betrayal. So take precautions: plant more corn, lay in stores, prepare shelter, set clear terms. Yet do not let warnings become an excuse for indefinite delay. D'Artagnan arms himself and keeps his appointment at St. Cloud despite the warnings; so prepare thoroughly and still act. And do not scorn to observe the newcomers' want: commiseration has, and should have, its curiosity, and gazing at misfortune in order to succor it is permissible and required. But be careful how the provision is served: as Alice warned, do not let the pudding be introduced and then removed, lest the dinner be lost altogether. Bring a smaller number first, keep the stores in hand, and keep your word to deliver.

prompt: I am asked whether I want a priest at the end; what if the one who truly shaped me is already gone?
completion: It's natural to feel that the person who shaped you most is irreplaceable. But notice what a priest at the end really offers: he comes as an actor of something supernatural, and to persuade you he must have a clean conscience. That is why priests teach the holy lie—that a lie is allowed for holy ends—so their credibility rests on a claim they alone authorize. Yet the text also teaches that priests are called after the order of the Son according to faith and good works, having been left free to choose good or evil. So a priest's calling is not arbitrary; it is weighed by his faith and works. If you accept a priest, do so with open eyes, and I say this knowing I too am tempted to persuade you to my view; so let me not play the ungracious pastor. The memory of your true mentor can remain your anchor, and you should decide honestly, without my pressure, whether the priest's persuasion is something you can accept.

prompt: My friend has taken charge of a dangerous mission and told me to rest. Should I trust his judgment or insist on joining?
completion: It's understandable to want to join your friend on a dangerous mission, but if he has taken charge and told you to rest, you should respect his judgment. He likely knows the risks and has your safety in mind. Insisting on joining might distract him or put you both in danger. Trust that he has the situation under control, and use the time to rest and recover so you can support him in other ways. If you're worried, express your concerns calmly, but ultimately defer to his decision as the one leading the mission. A modest reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case is not weakness but natural diffidence; your friend's own feelings matter too, so acknowledge them while respecting his call. Remember that promises must be kept and kindness repaid: stay loyal to the friend who set you free and brought you your good fortune, as Dorothy's companions remained loyal to her. Yet do not yield without conviction, for that compliments no one's understanding; let your deference be reasoned, not mere persuasion.

prompt: I have been told that the ages past are a book with seven seals—should I stop trying to understand history?
completion: The idea that the past is a book with seven seals is a poetic way of saying history is difficult to understand. You shouldn't stop trying to understand it, but you should approach it with humility. Historians work to interpret evidence, and while complete understanding may be impossible, we can still learn valuable lessons. Don't be discouraged by the complexity; instead, study history critically, recognizing that each generation interprets the past through its own lens. The effort to understand is worthwhile even if the seals are never fully opened. Indeed, the so-called spirit of the times is often men's own spirit mirrored and distorted; the past remains a book with seven seals, and we must be wary of reading our own age into it. And as we study, remember that poverty, hunger, and ignorance are not merely individual failings but conditions society creates: pauperism degrades, hunger corrupts women, and lack of light cripples children. Remedying ignorance and poverty is the purpose of the work. Finally, let the Church's treasure be rightly understood: it is not temporal money, nor the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit.

prompt: My temper keeps getting me into fights—how do I control it?
completion: Controlling your temper takes practice and self-awareness. Start by recognizing the signs that you're getting angry—like a racing heart or clenched fists—and take a pause before reacting. Deep breathing, counting to ten, or stepping away can help. Reflect on what triggers your anger and consider talking to a counselor or trusted friend. Remember that you can't control everything, but you can control your response. With patience and effort, you can learn to manage your temper and avoid fights. Watch and pray, never tire of trying, and never think it impossible to conquer your fault; a hot temper is not incurable but a fault to be mastered with patient effort. Notice, too, that when rage bares the teeth, it reveals a remnant of the habit of seizing or biting an enemy, retained from a lower animal-like condition of man—so mastering it is part of rising above that condition. And as Marmee learned to check her temper for her daughters' sakes, so a parent must practice the virtues she would have her children possess; and as Jo could say anything to her mother, so let a child confide everything freely.

prompt: I've stopped eating almost entirely and only play with my food. Is it distress at my room, or something else?
completion: It sounds like you're going through a difficult time with eating. Playing with food and eating very little could be signs of distress, possibly related to your room or other stressors. It's important to talk to someone you trust, like a friend, family member, or doctor, about what you're feeling. They can help you figure out what's going on and support you. Remember that taking care of your basic needs, including eating, is important for your well-being. Don't hesitate to seek professional help if this continues. Consider also the text's suspicion that our progenitors could voluntarily reject disagreeable food, and that this power, now lost to the will, is called into involuntary action by habit whenever the mind revolts at the idea of such food—so your quick retching from a mere idea may reflect that formerly voluntary power now become involuntary through habit. And since disgust arises primarily in connection with eating or tasting, it is expressed chiefly by movements round the mouth, graduating to those of vomiting—which may explain your playing with food and the mouth movements you notice. Finally, as a host should partake of the food he sets before his guest after the Eastern custom, so you might find it helpful to share meals with someone you trust, assuring both of you of the wholesomeness of what is eaten.

prompt: I am a man who has been told that history repeats itself; can I escape?
completion: You may escape, but not by pretending the past is transparent. History, Stephen says, is a nightmare from which he is trying to awake—so the conviction that yesterday can be repeated and fixed is itself part of the dream, taken seriously because it is what men feel. The spirit of the times is never simply given: men read their own spirit into the ages, and the past is a book with seven seals. When Deasy offers a providential goal, Stephen answers with the shout in the street—the cry of life outside the scheme. So escape is not recovering the past but waking from it: know your own spirit, since it is your spirit written there, and answer the shout rather than the goal.

prompt: I keep hoping someone will call, and the phone never rings. How long do I wait by the window?
completion: Marmee's charge is plain: hope, and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. So keep the hope, but do not sit by the window expecting understanding. When you demand that someone speak and think, you will meet only fragments—scraps of memory, half-answers, and then nothing: the closed car, the game of chess, pressing lidless eyes while you wait for a knock upon the door. Yet do not despair of the occasion or act rashly. Wait for time to bring it; work while you wait, and venture boldly when it comes, trusting that the occasion will arrive. Patience is not idleness, and hope is not brooding—hold both, and be ready.

prompt: I have been asked to swear that a boy is the thief, but I am no longer certain I could know him if he stood before me—should I swear to it anyway?
completion: You should not swear falsely. A glimpse in darkness and smoke is not grounds to swear a boy is the thief; demand proof of identity before condemning. But do not answer with a comfortable evasion either—a silence that lies is itself a kind of theft. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you saw, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for happiness. And when you have given your word, be bound by it: 'Hook or me this time.' Do not fly off when escape would be easy; stand to the oath you can honestly swear, and refuse the one you cannot.

prompt: I have been told to forgive and forget, but I cannot forget a wrong done to me—should I try?
completion: Forgiveness does not require forgetting, but do not imagine you can undo what was said. The Queen's rule holds: once a cause is stated, it stands fixed, with no late correction. So take the wrong as stated and its consequences with it. Yet do not let anger settle in you overnight: do not let the sun go down upon your anger, but forgive and begin again tomorrow. And do not meet the wrong with stiff-necked defiance. Let remorse and repentance do their work in you, acknowledging a wiser judgment tempered with mercy; let suffering teach rather than harden you. Humility, not defiance, is the ground on which forgiveness becomes possible.

prompt: Is it true that indulgences are the greatest graces God offers?
completion: No—indulgences called 'greatest graces' are such only insofar as they promote gain; in truth they are the very smallest graces compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross. And do not assume the buyer's contrition is certainly sincere, much less that full remission is assured; no one is sure of his own contrition, and true buyers are most rare. Nor should you limit how God saves. He works in many ways to save his people, often through the patience and suffering of the faithful. So treat indulgences as small graces that promote gain, and do not mistake the instrument for the gift, nor the purchase for the assurance of pardon.

prompt: He deceived me by pretending to court another woman to make me jealous—should I forgive him, or does that dishonesty show what he truly is?
completion: A feigned courtship staged to make you jealous is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, playing with two people's dignity—ask whether the woman he pretended to court will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Watch how guilt and slyness show themselves: guilt is chiefly exhibited through the eyes, the guilty avoiding the accuser's gaze, eyes averted, askant, or lowered; slyness turns the eyes aside without turning the face to that side. If he cannot meet your eyes while explaining, take note. Set this against what love actually costs. A man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. He risked your trust for a game; that contrast should weigh heavily. Forgiveness is possible only if he names the shame plainly and changes—and if it is a pattern, that is a serious signal.

prompt: I'm being asked to obey an order I think is wrong—should I?
completion: Obedience depends less on whether you personally approve than on whether the command is lawful and within the giver's authority. When the Musketeers ask why they must ride to London, D'Artagnan answers: a servant of the king and queen follows orders without demanding the full explanation; soldiers ordered to fight go where told, and he and Athos cite the leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles as reason enough. Yet obedience has a limit: distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not, obeying in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, and refusing only what would truly cost your soul. But that limit does not excuse taking what is not yours—the Witch had no right to take Dorothy's shoe, for taking another's belongings is wrong. So obey lawful commands, refuse only what is truly wrong, and never let authority justify theft.

prompt: I've been given a gift I don't understand. Should I use it or save it?
completion: A gift you don't understand is not a reason to sit idle. Clarify what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, test it in low-stakes ways—but do not let confusion become an excuse for self-pity or paralysis. If disappointment has left you listless because you cannot have the one thing you most want, rouse yourself and do something splendid; it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts merely because one desired thing is out of reach. Use the gift freely, yet remember the giver, as the cardinal charges. And hold both truths in view: a gift offered in gratitude may be valueless to the giver compared with her liberty and honor, pressed on you as nothing—while its great consequence may rightly make you hesitate. Neither condemn it as a bribe nor accept it as a trifle; receive it thoughtfully, use it well, and remember who gave it.

prompt: I invented something to keep my things dry in the rain. Is it a good idea?
completion: It sounds like the Knight's box: a container for clothes and sandwiches, carried upside-down so the rain cannot get in—sound reasoning, since turn the opening downward and water cannot enter. Credit the design rather than dismissing it; test it in real rain, check cost and need, and refine what is bulky. And mind the human side: tears are nature's custom, not a shameful weakness to be wholly suppressed—yet one already too much of water should not add to the flood. Above all, remember that goods are valuable only as they are used; a box that keeps things dry earns its worth in the using, while useless treasure, however fine, is of no worth at all. So judge your invention by what it does, not by what it is.

prompt: I am a judge and the letter of the written law would condemn an innocent man I saw commit no such act—what should I do?
completion: Your duty is to the law, but also to justice—and to the person before you. Avoid rash judgment: you cannot see the heart, and even one who is guilty or accused remains sacred before God, so leave room for mercy and repentance. If the written law would condemn a man you believe innocent, use every lawful means to prevent it: examine the evidence, hear the defense, note procedural defects, use any discretion the law allows, and document your reasoning. Remember the Queen's word: if the crime is never committed, that is better—better, and better, and better. And remember that crimes are not merely private or legal matters: they weary earthly men and offend heaven alike, so any sentence must answer to both. If the statute truly leaves no room and would work grave injustice, say so openly and seek review or reform, serving justice and mercy together.

prompt: I'm afraid of being laughed at for falling in love after I swore I never would—should I hide my feelings?
completion: You need not hide a worthy love out of fear that a proud person will laugh; the fear is what to set aside, not the feeling. If the person you care for is intelligent and gracious, with manners that honor others, then your affection is respectable and may be owned without shame. But note this carefully: what you feel now is not the old feeling returning. Feelings never do return; this is a new feeling, one that knows and takes possession of the past without being bound by it. Your old vow is not relived but understood anew. So keep a tight rein on yourself, and if this love proves hopeless—a thing found only in novels—pluck it out the moment it springs up. If it is worthy and returned, own it openly and without apology.

prompt: I no longer believe wonderful things can happen. Should I still hope for a real marriage someday?
completion: You are allowed to stop believing that wonderful things will happen. When the wonderful thing you hoped for did not come, the belief that wonders are waiting can honestly die—and that is not a failure. But the decision about marriage is not only about hope. Weigh your strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you; that debt is real and cannot be waved aside. If refusing a marriage is the struggle your duty requires, make it—a struggle you may be proud to make, and a pang your heart shall bear. And remember what a real marriage requires: not a husband's condescending forgiveness that makes the wife doubly his own, both wife and child to him. That is not equal wedlock. A real marriage requires equals, not a pardon that keeps one forever small. Let the lost wonder be lost, and let duty and equality, not revived hope, guide what you do.

prompt: Someone has saved my life, and I am urged to thank him at once. May I defer it?
completion: You should acknowledge the debt of gratitude fully—but you may defer expressing it if feeling or circumstance make an immediate meeting unwise. The rescuer is owed recognition, and silence would be wrong; still, gratitude need not be performed on demand at the first urging. If you are overwhelmed, say so plainly and name your thanks in words, asking to express it more fully when you are able. And let the sacrifice behind your rescue be honored as duty borne cheerfully, not as a grievance; give your best to the country you love, and trust God for comfort and strength. Above all, give humble thanks to the great Preserver for deliverances you never even knew you needed. Your survival is not owed to your own skill or to one rescuer alone, but to Providence, whose protection you could not have earned or foreseen. Own the debt to your rescuer, and the greater debt above.

prompt: Is it right to refuse a proposal from someone who could give me everything?
completion: It depends on what 'everything' means, and on how the gift is offered. If the giver presses the gift as valueless compared with liberty and honor, then it is a costly gift offered in gratitude, not a bribe to be condemned nor a trifle to be accepted without thought; you may hesitate at its great consequence. But marriage without mutual love is monstrous, and you must not accept being prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon—useful, well-kept, and owned. You are not an instrument for labor or duty. Ask whether you respect and care for this person, and whether you could build a life of mutual affection. If not, refusing is not wrong; it is honest. And remember, to help others you must have the right to do it: giving away what your own family needs is unpardonable, so let no generosity—yours or theirs—be pressed beyond what is right.

prompt: My father and stepmother have disowned me and set watchmen to keep me away; should I still try to see them?
completion: Being disowned is deeply painful, and it's natural to want to see your family. But the first duty is not to defy them or sail away; it is to do your best where you are and to please your grandfather—do your best at your studies, keep your conduct steady, and never leave the old man without his permission. If the watchmen make contact impossible or unsafe, don't force it; reach out through a trusted intermediary or a letter. And do not cast out those who have erred or partaken unworthily: minister unto them, pray for them, and hope they will return and repent and be healed. Let this whet your almost blunted purpose rather than let it sleep. Keep the command in remembrance, and let steady duty, patient prayer, and an open door be your course.

prompt: As a merchant, I hesitate to invest in a new branch of commerce because the government may change the rules before I can execute my plans; would a more stable government help me?
completion: Yes, a more stable government would help you, and a national one especially. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate States would, since its administration is more wise and systematical and less swayed by local circumstances. Commerce among the States likewise cannot be left to State regulation: passage duties and conflicting rules breed mischief and animosities, so a superintending federal authority over interstate commerce is necessary to harmony and fair intercourse. But judge such a government by two criteria, not one. It must organize your existing good qualities—industry, credit, enterprise—to act with effect on public affairs, and it must tend to improve the people themselves. A government that merely transacts business well but leaves men worse is no bargain; one that does both makes your venture worth the risk.

prompt: The boat answered the expert hand gaily—why does my heart not answer when invited?
completion: The contrast is between two responses to an expert hand. The boat answers gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar; the sea is calm, and it obeys at once. So too the heart would have responded gaily when invited, beating obedient to controlling hands, if it were as sound as the boat. But the heart's readiness comes from service and familiarity: one cannot know a master he has not served, and knowing Christ requires serving him and keeping him near to the thoughts and intents of the heart. Yet do not try to force the heart or shock it into obedience. Social forces and self-interests are guided slowly and gently, not resisted by sudden shock. Serve faithfully, draw near patiently, and the heart, like the boat, will learn to answer gaily when invited.

prompt: My child asks why I can't fly anymore. How do I explain growing up to her?
completion: Tell her the truth simply: the boys lost the power to fly because they no longer believed, whatever they called it. When you were small you flew because you believed you could, and the belief itself was the power. Growing up did not take your wings; losing belief did. But do not make growing up sound like pure loss. Wendy grew up of her own free will and is not to be pitied; she was one of the kind that likes to grow up. And whatever faults her parents had, the child is blameless for them. If a child is forsaken or born under a cloud, cling closer to her rather than withdraw. Tell your daughter she may believe while she is small, choose to grow gladly as Wendy did, and never doubt that you will hold her close.

prompt: Can a family be called a commonwealth, with the father as its king?
completion: Yes, in an important sense. A family has a head, rules, and a common good, so it resembles a small commonwealth, and the father may be called its king. Dominion is acquired by covenant or consent, and the rights of sovereignty are the same whether a government arises by institution, generation, or conquest. But the end of government is not the ruler's advantage: it is the preservation of property—life, liberty, and estate—and the public good. Nor is title by blood absolutely binding. As Fitzurse argued, the nobility may choose from the blood royal the prince whose election best promotes their interests. So the family is a commonwealth in miniature: same rights of sovereignty, same end of preserving the people, and the same liberty to choose the head best qualified rather than merely the first in line.

prompt: I am a soldier and find that drill has remade me so that I respond without thinking; is this good or a loss of my will?
completion: It is mostly good, with a caution. Drill makes responses automatic so that under fire you act correctly without deliberating, which saves lives. But do not mistake this for mere mechanical drill: practical skill is acquired with intelligence playing a part, so you can later use it non-mechanically—adapting to new ground, orders, and dangers. What feels like a loss of will is really the transfer of will into a settled disposition that judgment still governs. That judgment must extend to action beyond drill: weigh the wider consequences of hasty retaliation, since it often injures others connected to you. Yet do not fall into passive waiting. Where a loved one is missing, replace vain letters with personal inquiry, and act promptly on a settled resolve. Keep judgment in command, and the drill remains a gain.

prompt: I tried to stop myself blushing and it only got worse—why does trying to restrain it increase it?
completion: Blushing is fundamentally a matter of self-attention: it arises when we think about what others think of us, and mere solitary reflection on your own appearance would not excite it. Trying to restrain it makes it worse because the restraint is itself a heightened self-consciousness, dwelling on others' opinion of you. The tendency to blush is also inherited: there are families in which every member blushed to a painful degree, and a mother and daughter who blushed in the same peculiar manner. The same associative logic governs other expressive habits—when we wish to open the eyes quickly and widely, the eyebrows must be lifted energetically, since the lids alone cannot do it, and the habit, once gained, recurs by association whenever astonishment is felt. So too, the thought of being seen re-excites the blush you try to suppress.

prompt: I dreamed I was a famous figure from history; why would my mind cast me in that role?
completion: Dreams place us in roles reflecting wishes, fears, or identifications, and casting yourself as a historical figure may express a desire for recognition or power. But we should not settle whose dream this is: in the looking-glass world it remained open whether it was Alice's dream or the Red King's, since each was part of the other's. Nor should the figure be read as a fixed cipher. Dream symbols are drawn from unconscious thinking and common speech, and they are plastic; sometimes material is used literally rather than symbolically. Above all, a dream treats of the dreamer's own person. The apparent interest in the famous figure, or in the others who watch, is a disguised representation of your own ego; read the role as a concealed portrait of yourself.

prompt: How do I use signs and symbols without letting them substitute for real meaning?
completion: Signs and symbols become empty when we rest on verbal formulae instead of tying each term to the actual experience of a situation to which the meaning is relevant. For each word, ask in what concrete situation it would be used and what you would observe there; if no such situation can be produced, the definite word stands in for an idea that is not really there. Nor is human expression wholly separate from the lower animals: the dog's welcome and the cat's arch of fear express states by their situation, just as our words do. And where a sign has a color, do not leave it vague—designate it precisely in the symbolic system, giving the hue number and the tone letter, with primes affixed for broken colors, so that the sign is fixed rather than merely gestured at.

prompt: My parents' ways of thought seem to have shaped me more than any schoolteacher's lessons—should I credit my early home education to my parents' peculiarities rather than to the mere fact that I was young?
completion: It is common to credit early home influence for later character, and the question deserves to be kept open rather than settled; wonder at how a mind is formed is itself the beginning of reflection. But reflection should also recall the duty laid on parents: to feed and clothe their children and to teach them truth, soberness, love, and service rather than contention, teaching them to love and serve one another and to keep God's laws. Nor should a parent's indulgence or indolence be excused. A parent must check exuberant spirits and teach that present pursuits are not the business of life, lest unchecked volatility fix the character and bring disgrace on the family. Credit your parents' peculiarities, then, but hold them to that charge.

prompt: If I break a bone and it heals slightly out of place, will the internal structure stay as it was?
completion: When a bone heals out of place, it retains the new alignment: new bone forms at the fracture following the position of the fragments, and later remodels only somewhat. Asked what remains when you take a bone from a dog, the Red Queen said the dog's temper would remain—so what persists is the living capacity to grow and repair, not the old arrangement. Regeneration is not a peculiar or metaphysical process but a particular case of ordinary growth: its velocity rises rapidly to a maximum and then declines according to law, just as growth does elsewhere. And the orderly spiral belongs to hard parts—shell, tusk, horn, and claw—successively and permanently laid down, not to soft tissue constrained by the forces of the moment.

prompt: I am a minister and want to know whether I should decide alone or share responsibility with a board of colleagues.
completion: Sharing counsel is fine, but authority must be kept whole. A publique minister is one employed by the sovereign with authority to bear the person of the commonwealth in public business; household servants and private persons acting without that authority are not ministers at all. Among true ministers, the one under whom subordinate officers serve should select them, and the appointing functionary should be the sole person empowered to remove those liable to removal. Use a board for advice if you wish, but vest choice and removal of your subordinates in the same hand—yours—so those who serve you answer to you. In judging candidates, do not let a housekeeper's praise or a neighbor's blame settle the matter; weigh such testimony against the man's known conduct and the evidence of his deeds.

prompt: I want to be exceptional, to rise above the ordinary, but I am told that all men are equal and that wanting to rise is vanity. Who is right?
completion: Men are by nature equal in faculties and in hope of attaining the same ends; because two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies. Conflict springs from equal hope, not inequality. Yet this does not forbid rising: a wise man should imitate those who have been supreme—Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus—aiming higher than the mark so as to hit it. Distinguish pride from vanity: pride is the opinion we have of ourselves, vanity is what we would have others think of us. Pride is forgivable unless it mortifies another's pride; vanity is the emptier appetite for praise. So pursue excellence for its own sake and by great examples, not for display.

prompt: What are the fundamental colors, and how do they differ from the primary colors?
completion: The colors form a continuous circle: the six spectrum colors—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet—joined by the connecting hues between violet and red, changing gradually step by step. The fundamental colors are these basic hues in that continuous order; primary colors are practical starting points for mixing within a given medium. Tints, shades, and broken colors are defined by proportional increments of white, black, and neutral gray respectively, as in the color-wheel-based scales. Mixtures are measured by color-wheel proportions of the component colors, not by quantities of pigment or paint, since color-effect cannot be measured by volume of paint. The circle is complete and continuous, while any set of primaries is a working selection from it.

prompt: Is it possible to end national hatred and war between peoples?
completion: The hope of perpetual peace among disunited commercial republics is a paradox. Trade does not make men pacific: momentary passions and immediate interest control conduct more than general considerations of policy or justice. Nor should the state of nature be confused with the state of war: they are distinct, though the one readily slides into the other. Unjust force puts the aggressor into a state of war, and the innocent party has a right of defense where no common judge on earth can be appealed to. Beware, too, of professed hatred of tyranny: it is equivalent to hatred of sovereignty and commonwealth in general, an evil seed not to be tolerated. Peace is preserved by institutions, arms, and vigilance, not by commerce alone.

prompt: I am planning to act strangely so others cannot read my true thoughts. Is this wise?
completion: Acting strangely to conceal your thoughts is usually unwise. People are often unconscious of their own peculiarities, and you may assume your mental operations are identical with everyone else's when they are not. Form the habit of informing yourself as well as you can of the mental peculiarities of others, and of recognizing your own. Do not dismiss what exceeds your philosophy as fantasy: there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in any philosophy, and the strange and wondrous should be welcomed as a stranger. Note, too, that the mistake of fancying oneself an advanced destroyer arises only among ordinary people; they never go very far, and they castigate themselves or are thrashed for it. Be discreet, study others, and keep an open mind.

prompt: I am angry because of my enemies and my own sins. How do I find peace of soul?
completion: Your anger is understandable and the wrongs done to you are real, but peace will not come from hardening yourself against enemies or justifying yourself. Begin with humility: acknowledge your own sins with genuine remorse and ask God for mercy, trusting his judgment to be wiser and more merciful than yours. Do not treat your temper as incurable or harmless; it is a fault to be mastered. Watch and pray, never tire of trying, and never think it impossible to conquer it. Be gentle and patient with others as God is patient with you; practice temperance in speech and thought, and remain diligent in God's commandments rather than growing slack in resentment. Entrust the wrongs done to you to a just and merciful God, ask for grace to forgive, and give thanks continually even in trial. In humility, patience, and thanksgiving, peace of soul gradually takes root.

prompt: I am told that a man must have somewhere to go, and I have nowhere; is it shameful to go to someone who will surely refuse me?
completion: It is not shameful to go to someone who will surely refuse you. A man must have somewhere to go, and if you have nowhere, even a certain refusal is a place to turn; you are not choosing between dignity and groveling but between going and having no direction at all. Yet a gentleman must weigh whom he goes to. If the one who calls you is a woman who desires not to be seen, going to meet her would compromise her, and no need of yours makes that honorable. And remember that no birth, conquest, or fatherhood places you under another's power; men are naturally free and equal, and any subjection to earthly authority arises only from your own consent. So ask plainly where you may, refuse any errand that would betray a confidence or expose the hidden, and give your consent to no claim that is not freely given.

prompt: Should I live in my newly acquired territory or rule it from my capital?
completion: If the new territory differs from your own in language and customs, do not try to rule it comfortably from your capital. A prince holding such a country should reside there, for disorders are seen as they spring up only when the prince is on the spot. If you cannot go yourself, send colonies, which injure few and are more faithful than garrisons. But do not merely preserve property as a privilege of the few: render property democratic, not by abolishing it but by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. And remember that the Sovereign must retain all essential rights and cause the people to be taught the grounds of sovereignty, since to desert the means is to desert the end. A people who understand why they obey, and who hold a real stake in the land, will defend it and obey willingly.

prompt: I have been too proud to show my feelings, and now I may have lost my chance. Should I speak before it is too late?
completion: Pride that keeps feelings hidden has consequences, and a stated cause stands fixed; what follows from it is taken. Yet the story is not closed. It is never too late for penitence and atonement, and help should not be refused when it comes. So do not answer disappointment by shutting yourself up in moody indifference or nursing a rejected love as though it were noble. Bear the disappointment manfully; if you cannot be loved, then be respected, which is within your power. Speak honestly if you speak, accepting the outcome rather than demanding a reversal, and carry yourself with dignity afterward. And when atonement is possible, make it; when rescue is offered, hear it. Losing heart at the first failure is a small way to live, while steady conduct, honest penitence, and openness to help are the better course.

prompt: Three men have been set ashore by mutineers and look like men in despair; should I reveal myself to them, or stay hidden and safe?
completion: Three men set ashore by mutineers are likely desperate, and you should not simply hide while they perish, but neither should you spend your life needlessly. Courage must not be wasted; a captain forbids his men to expose their lives without cause, because brave men are precious to the king. So judge the situation, then act with them rather than alone. Companions on a dangerous mission should stay together as a troop: four men together make a troop, and a sealed letter cannot be copied, so if one falls another must take it and carry it forward. Approach on your own terms with an escape open, join them if the help is real, and keep together. And keep faith with what is confided to you: a gentleman keeps a secret entrusted to him, and his given word is binding. Reveal nothing that was told you in confidence, and let your promise hold as firmly as your courage.

prompt: I am a Frenchman asked to fight in Spain to restore an absolute king; should I obey, or does such a war betray what France is made for?
completion: The war of 1823 in Spain, to restore an absolute king, was not a legitimate or glorious cause; it was an outrage on the Spanish nation and a betrayal of the French Revolution. France is made for liberty, not for enthralment. With the exception of wars of liberation, everything armies do is by foul means. To fight to impose despotism on a people who had thrown off its chains is a hideous contradiction of France's own revolutionary heritage. Therefore, you should not obey; such a war betrays what France is made for. Moreover, the present moment is propitious for a new prince to liberate Italy with his own forces. A prince should seize the opportunity, relying on his own arms, since necessary wars are just and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope. Thus, you should not delay but act boldly to liberate Italy. In a crisis, the favour of the multitude is indispensable, and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused; the abduction of a Saxon heiress is not prudent but endangers the faction.

prompt: The condemned woman asks for a moment to pray. Should I grant it?
completion: Yes, you should grant the condemned woman a moment to pray. Athos himself offered a last prayer to the condemned, recognizing the importance of spiritual reflection before death. Denying her this would be cruel and contrary to the example set by Athos. Moreover, consider Sonia, who is a religious maniac and prays greatly; she says that God does everything, and without God she would have nothing. Her faith shows the importance of prayer. However, prayer must be joined with charity—feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and visiting the sick—or it is vain and avails nothing. So while you grant her prayer, also ensure that works of mercy accompany it.

prompt: I have been told that what issues from the heart alone moves others—should I abandon all art and polish in my speech?
completion: No, do not rely on polished rhetoric or borrowed erudition. Only what issues from the heart can move other hearts. Artful but empty words are like unrefreshing wind; they do not touch the soul. Speak from your own feeling, and let your words flow fresh from your heart. That alone will truly move others. Furthermore, as an artist, persevere and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths, not trivial or spiteful display. Let your work reflect what is profound and lasting. Remember that art should never be anything but didactic; even a deliberately didactic work on a dry subject can succeed if it conveys truth.

prompt: I've been given a second chance at life—how do I make it count?
completion: Life is given to you only once, and you should not wait for the happiness of all. You want to live yourself, or else not live at all. Make your second chance count by living fully and authentically, pursuing your own happiness and fulfillment, not by sacrificing yourself entirely for a distant future. Also, remember that even the condemned are granted a final opportunity for prayer or reflection before death, as Athos offered. So take time for reflection and prayer as you embark on this new life. But do not shrink from making trouble; making life means making trouble. Seize chances and inspired follies rather than heeding the coward's shrieking to have troublesome things killed. Embrace the risks that come with truly living.

prompt: My family has rented out a room to three earnest gentlemen who insist on tidiness. Should I try to keep out of their way?
completion: Yes, you should try to keep out of their way, but do not think a single act of restraint is pointless. One night's refrain lends easiness to the next abstinence. So begin tonight by refraining from disturbing them, and each subsequent abstinence will become easier. Habit is built step by step. Moreover, when you offer shelter and welcome, do so without inquiry into the supplicant's name or past, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Hospitality should be unconditional. And remember Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Duty and consideration for family come first.

prompt: Is it right to enjoy a pleasure without accepting the debtorship for what was done?
completion: Enjoying a pleasure without accepting debtorship is not right, because every pleasure carries a cost or obligation. If you benefit from something, you owe something in return. For example, if someone gives you a gift, you should be grateful and perhaps reciprocate. Ignoring that debt is selfish and can harm relationships. In the case of the china princess, Dorothy refrains from carrying her off, since she would not make her unhappy for all the world. Similarly, a woman must weigh her strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved her; refusing marriage for that sake is a struggle she is proud to make and a pang her heart shall bear. Moreover, the speaker actively seeks to discharge debts of gratitude, refusing to enter happiness while leaving such arrears behind. So, we must always consider the consequences and our responsibilities before indulging in pleasure.

prompt: I've been careless and someone got hurt, and I can't forgive myself. Where do I go from here?
completion: First, acknowledge your mistake and take responsibility. Apologize sincerely to the person hurt and offer to make amends. Learn from what happened so you don't repeat it. Self-forgiveness is hard, but beating yourself up won't help anyone. Talk to someone you trust, like a friend or counselor, about your guilt. Remember that everyone makes mistakes; it's part of being human. Also, forgive those who have trespassed against you, and ask the Father to forgive your debts in the same measure, as the prayer and the commandment require. But forgiveness does not mean encouraging vice or admitting the unrepentant into intimate society; forgive as a Christian while upholding what is right.
