completion: Decline kindly, and don't assume she'll simply forget it. A person turned away may still often think of the house and the people in it, so leave the door warm. Her request isn't weakness—it's the natural diffidence of someone in an anxious pinch who trusted a neighbor's judgment about a simple thing. So respect that while keeping your own line: 'I'd like to help, but our internet is tied to my work account and I can't share the network—it's a liability thing.' Put the reason on the setup, not on her. Offer an alternative—the building's Wi-Fi, a hotspot, the library—and a small concrete kindness, like helping her call the provider. And don't dress your refusal up as some grand verdict about neighbors or trust; it's just your account and your call, stated plainly and warmly.

prompt: My brother asked me to lend him my truck to move, and I know he'll drive it back with an empty tank and a scratch. He's family and he's had a rough year. Do I say yes or make an excuse?
completion: Say yes, and keep your word. Porthos gave away his horse because he didn't like to shame guests whose mounts looked poor beside his; likewise, don't hand over the truck with a lecture about the tank and scratches. Make it easy: fill the tank beforehand, mention insurance matter-of-factly, and say 'bring it back whenever.' If you truly can't afford the risk, decline directly rather than with an excuse, and offer what you can—help loading, a day's rental, driving him yourself. And remember what counts most: giving to a brother in a rough year, or lending him what he needs, is a better work than buying yourself a tidy pardon for the scratch and the empty tank. Love grows by works of love, and you become better; by pardons alone you'd only become more free from penalty. So choose the mercy, and keep the promise.

prompt: My landlord is a nice older man who's been renting to me below market for years. He just raised the rent and I found out he's charging the new tenant upstairs less. Do I bring it up or count my blessings?
completion: You have a real grievance, and gratitude shouldn't blind you to it. Jane might assume the landlord's kindness explains everything; Elizabeth would ask why the upstairs tenant pays less and whether your long tenure is being taken for granted. Bring your own position to the table first: say plainly that you noticed the difference and it stings, and ask how the new rent was set. Don't accuse, but don't apologize for asking either. Understand, though, that your years of payment created no property for you—they built his capital, which grows only by drawing fresh rent from each tenant, you and the newcomer alike. So negotiate as one who knows the terms, not as one owed a favor. If he gives a fair reason, accept it; if not, negotiate or plan to move.

prompt: An old friend from high school, who I have not spoken to in years, messaged me asking for money for a medical bill and sent a photo of a hospital form. I cannot verify it and I remember she had a history of scams. Do I send something to be safe or ask for proof?
completion: Don't send money on an unverified photo. Notice the structure of the appeal: like a priest who needs a clean conscience to persuade, she presents a holy cause—illness, urgency, a form as sacred text—so that doubting you feels like sin. The holy lie at work is that a small deception is allowed for a good end. But don't just set a test before her and watch; share the table yourself. Say plainly that you remember the past scams, that you want to help, and that you'll pay the hospital directly or speak with the billing office. A genuine friend will welcome that; a scammer will resist or rush you. Remember too that the poisoned cup is often drunk by whoever tempered it. Be warm, be firm, be candid, and verify before you pay.

prompt: My partner's mother comments on my weight every time we visit, and my partner says that's just how she is and I should ignore it. I'm starting to dread family dinners. What do I say, and to whom?
completion: Talk to your partner first, because you need a united front. Say clearly that the comments hurt and that "that's just how she is" isn't a solution—it asks you to absorb the cost alone. Then act decisively rather than enduring a drip of remarks: have one calm, firm conversation in which your partner states the boundary—"Please don't comment on her weight"—and you both hold it. Severity used well is applied at one blow and not persisted in: say it once, clearly, and don't relitigate it. Don't argue about whose standard of beauty is correct; we are very much in the dark about such standards, and each is most affected by the beauties of its own kind. Nor need you condemn her as heartless: one who has not the habit of giving kindness, yet would give if she had it, remains guiltless. Set the boundary, decline the debate, and if it continues, shorten visits rather than endure a slow grind.

prompt: My friend group's shared budget app shows one person has been covering more than their share for months but saying nothing. I only know because I have admin access. Do I bring it up with the group?
completion: Be careful with admin access—don't broadcast details you only saw because of it. But don't dismiss what the data shows: like a dream that reproduces a forgotten memory, the ledger may surface knowledge the group has lost track of, and no such record is entirely lost. Start by talking privately to the person covering more: tell them what you noticed, ask if they're okay, and offer to help raise it with the group. Then whet the almost blunted purpose: keep the fairness rule in remembrance and propose a concrete check-in, not a vague "we should talk." Make participation cheap and open—pool shared costs publicly, set a small cap on what anyone covers, and treat contributing to the group as a shared duty rather than a favor one person quietly buys. The goal is to sharpen a shared rule, not catch someone out.

prompt: A friend asked me to proofread her novel, and it's not very good. She's asking if it's ready to send to agents. Do I tell her it needs work, and if so, how honest do I get?
completion: Tell her the truth, but kindly and usefully. Don't split manners from morals: how you speak is part of what you owe her. Start with what genuinely works—voice, premise, a scene—then name the biggest issues concretely: pacing, stakes, a muddled ending. Say plainly that it isn't ready yet, and offer two or three prioritized fixes. Don't pretend the agent's slush pile is a fair tribunal: measure it by the truth and justice it actually yields, and name the rejection machinery—form letters, the scaffold of the query—as part of a gloomy order, not a verdict on her worth. Prize a kind and tender heart above cleverness. And when she is stung, don't cheerfully help her rush the manuscript out to be wounded again; rather, refuse that escape, let your own eyes fill, and pray—in whatever way you can—that she be spared the wretchedness of a needless rejection. Then sit with her and revise.

prompt: My partner's calendar is shared with me for logistics, and I saw a recurring block labeled 'therapy' that they never mentioned. It explains a lot but I only know because of the calendar. Do I say something?
completion: It's understandable to feel curious, but since the calendar was shared for logistics, bringing up therapy might feel invasive. Make supportive communication a habit early: establish a routine of checking in regularly, so expressing concern becomes automatic and guards against avoidance. This frees your higher mental powers for the relationship itself. Recognize that your partner's symptoms of terror or anxiety may be inherited results of former exertion—tendencies to fear that reappear through inheritance and association from generations of flight and struggle—and in part directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. Yet do not revere these ancient patterns as if antiquity itself deserved reverence; prefer new and well-proved truth about mental health, which shows that therapy and open dialogue can reshape habitual responses. So approach with compassion, not confrontation, and let evidence guide you. If therapy affects plans, ask about scheduling without prying, but let habitual openness replace hesitant deliberation.

prompt: A friend asked me to babysit her kids during an emergency, but I have a work deadline that night and no backup. Do I cancel my work plans to help her, or tell her I can't and risk her not having anyone else?
completion: This is a tough spot. You want to be a good friend, but your work deadline is also important. Because of old friendship and love for her as a parent, your gentleness toward her request is grounded in those recollections. Yet you must name the unworthiness of the situation with sorrow, not hatred: she is asking you to sacrifice your deadline without backup. Allow that tears are nature's custom—if you feel moved to weep over the difficulty, that is human—but forbid yourself from being one already too much of water, drowning in emotion instead of acting. Remember the lesson of the girls who gave away their breakfast to the hungry poor on Christmas morning: loving our neighbor better than ourselves means sacrificial giving. So assess the urgency: is her emergency truly immediate and without other options? If so, consider whether your deadline can be adjusted or if you can work while babysitting. If not, be honest: tell her you can't babysit but help her brainstorm alternatives—other friends, family, or hired help. Offer to help in other ways, like ordering pizza for the kids or checking in. Setting a boundary doesn't mean abandoning her; it means being clear about your limits while showing you care, motivated by that old attachment and a willingness to put her needs before your own where possible.

prompt: My partner and I are splitting costs, and I found out they've been paying less than we agreed while telling me they paid in full. Do I confront them or quietly rebalance?
completion: This is a breach of trust, so you need to address it. Quietly rebalancing might seem easier, but it avoids the real issue and could lead to resentment. Confrontation doesn't have to be aggressive; approach it calmly with the facts. Remember that tears are not only from your own pain or joy—sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress. But beware of making your partner an idol who stands between you and God; romantic love must not become your whole world and hope of heaven. Keep love subordinate to conscience and faith. At the same time, affirm that as an independent woman you may freely choose to stay with and serve the one you love, as an equal and not a dependent. So if you feel emotional, that's natural; let it show you care. Say something like, 'I noticed the payments don't match our agreement. Can we talk about this?' Give them a chance to explain—maybe it was a misunderstanding or they're struggling financially. The goal is to restore honesty and fairness, not to punish. If they're defensive, reiterate that you value transparency. Consider setting up a shared budget or automatic transfers to prevent future issues. Avoiding the conversation might feel safer, but it won't rebuild trust. Be direct but kind, and focus on solving the problem together.

prompt: My cousin asked to stay with us 'for a few weeks' after a breakup, and it's now been three months. My partner is fed up. Do I give him a deadline and risk the family drama, or keep waiting for him to leave on his own?
completion: This is a delicate situation. Your cousin is likely still hurting from the breakup, but three months is longer than agreed. Your partner's frustration is valid. Rather than letting grief dissolve into passive despair or weeping, channel sorrow into disciplined resolve and action, echoing Athos's words that men avenge the dead rather than only weeping. Recognize that your cousin's natural curiosity and inference are already logical in spirit, and aim to transform them gradually into careful, thorough habits of inquiry. Remember the Palmer, who, learning of a designed ambush against Isaac, warned him and guided him to safety; so you, as a friend, should warn your cousin of the coming deadline and help him find a new place. First, talk to your partner to get on the same page. Then, have a calm conversation with your cousin. Express that you care about him, but the arrangement was temporary. Ask about his plans and offer to help him find a new place. Set a clear but reasonable deadline, like two weeks to a month, and stick to it. This isn't about kicking him out; it's about respecting your household's needs. Family drama may happen, but clear communication can minimize it. Waiting indefinitely isn't fair to your partner or your relationship.

prompt: A friend keeps canceling plans last minute and then posting about other outings on social media. She's going through a divorce, and I want to be patient. How do I set a limit without abandoning her?
completion: It's kind of you to be patient, but her behavior is hurtful. A prince should not misuse clemency; a few examples of severity are more merciful than disorders that injure the whole people. So set a limit by being honest about how it affects you. Choose a calm moment to say, 'I care about you and know you're going through a lot, but when you cancel last minute and then post about other plans, I feel disrespected.' Use 'I' statements to avoid blame. Suggest a compromise: maybe she can give you more notice, or you can plan lower-commitment activities. Reassure her that you're not abandoning her—you're just asking for consideration. Like Peter, who barred the window to make Wendy think her mother shut her out, then unbarred it when Mrs. Darling's tears moved him, you may need to be firm initially but relent if she shows genuine remorse. And as Bloom proposed to Stephen to pass in repose the hours intervening between Thursday (proper) and Friday (normal) on an extemporised cubicle in the apartment immediately above the kitchen and immediately adjacent to the sleeping apartment of his host and hostess, so you can offer her a temporary, bounded arrangement that respects both her need and your limits. If she continues, you may need to pull back slightly to protect your own feelings. Remember, setting boundaries is not selfish; it's necessary for a healthy friendship.

prompt: I overheard through a shared gaming headset that a friend's partner is planning to propose, and my friend has told me they want to be the one to propose. Do I warn my friend?
completion: This is a moment to act boldly rather than cautiously. Fortune may control half our actions, but we can build barriers against her by preparing well. Your friend has told you they want to be the one to propose, so warning them gives them the chance to take the initiative. Yes, there's a risk of interfering, but silence is a passive surrender to chance. The adventurous fare better than the cautious. Speak to your friend privately and kindly: tell them what you overheard, and encourage them to talk to their partner about their wish to propose. But remember, proposals are like a tournament with proclaimed rules: both parties should respect each other's intentions. If your friend and partner both want to propose, they should discuss it openly and perhaps let the marshals—trusted friends or family—help them separate and decide. By acting within the rules, you help your friend build a barrier against fortune's whims. And just as the girls each spend their dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for themselves, you should give your friend the gift of honest counsel, expecting nothing in return.

prompt: My landlord is also my friend and asked me to vouch for him to a new tenant who's worried about the building's maintenance history. I know the elevator has been broken for months. What do I say?
completion: You're in a tough spot. Your landlord friend asked you to vouch for him, but you know the elevator has been broken for months. Be careful not to let slander's poisoned shot harm your friend's name. Instead, let the shot miss the name and hit the woundless air. Speak to your landlord friend first and tell him you're uncomfortable vouching without addressing the elevator. Encourage him to fix it or disclose it himself. If he does, you can honestly vouch for his responsiveness. If not, you can tell the new tenant that you've had a good experience but suggest they ask the landlord directly about maintenance. That way, you avoid slander and protect your integrity and friendship. And remember to give humble thanks to the great Preserver for the deliverances you never even knew you needed, for such protection is owed to Providence, not to yourself. Finally, beware of flattery: society indulges authors at its peril, as grain-dealers raise rats in their granaries, and a woman lays siege to an author by flattering and indulging him. So do not flatter your landlord; speak plainly and encourage honesty.

prompt: My sister wants me to keep a secret from our parents that she's dropping out of college, and they're paying the tuition. Do I keep her confidence, or tell them before they waste more money?
completion: This is a difficult situation, but you must speak plainly and at once. Your sister has asked you to keep her confidence, but your parents are paying tuition and deserve to know she's dropping out. Keeping the secret wastes their money and prolongs the deception. Tell your sister clearly: either she tells your parents herself, or you will tell them. Do not leave false hope or trifle with feelings. Be direct and firm. If she refuses, follow through and inform your parents. Yes, it may hurt your sister, but honesty and financial responsibility are more important. By speaking plainly, you respect everyone involved and avoid the greater harm of secrecy and wasted resources. Remember, yielding without conviction is no compliment to the understanding of either party; so stand firm in your conviction to be honest. And seek first the kingdom of God: treat riches as means for clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, liberating captives, and relieving the afflicted, not for pride or status.

prompt: An old friend asked me to write a glowing recommendation for a program she's applying to, but I've seen her struggle and I'd be exaggerating. She'll see the letter. What do I write?
completion: This is a delicate situation. Your friend has asked for a glowing recommendation, but you've seen her struggle. Remember that the difference between a lady and a flower girl lies in how she is treated, not in how she behaves. Treat your friend as a capable person, and she may rise to the occasion. Write a letter that focuses on her strengths and potential, treating her with the respect you would show a lady. Highlight her perseverance and willingness to learn, and frame challenges as growth opportunities. Avoid exaggeration, but emphasize the positive. Speak to her first: explain that you will write an honest letter that reflects her dignity and potential. By treating her as a lady, you help her become one. But also heed the warning of coming danger: prepare a defense for the time of need, when the leader fails and the pack turns. Be ready to support her with honest counsel and encouragement. And if you have been appalled by any crime or failure, conclude that an honest life is best, turn your back on the past, and succeed through a good purpose and contented disposition.

prompt: My best friend's fiancé added me on a fitness app, and I can see he logs runs at 6 a.m. at an address that isn't their apartment. She asked me last month to tell her if anything felt off. Do I say something?
completion: This is a tricky situation, but you must be careful in dealing with those around you, lest unavailing remorse follow their loss. Your best friend asked you to tell her if anything felt off, and now you've noticed her fiancé is logging runs at an address that isn't their apartment. That could be innocent, but it's worth mentioning. Since she explicitly asked you, you have a responsibility to speak up. Do it with timely care, zeal, and earnestness. Tell her what you saw factually, without accusing him, and let her decide what to do. Be supportive and non-judgmental. If you stay silent, she might later feel betrayed that you knew and didn't tell her, and you would suffer unavailing remorse. So say something, but do it gently and with care. And weigh the good against the evil: even in this worry, there are mercies—her trust in you, your friendship—so find something to be thankful for as you speak. Remember, too, that the recognition of some expressions is probably instinctive: an infant, too young to have learnt by experience, will answer a smile and assume a melancholy expression at pretended crying. So trust your instinct that something is off, and act on it.

prompt: A friend asked me to watch her dog for two weeks, and I said yes before realizing I'll be traveling for work part of that time. Do I back out now and disappoint her, or scramble to find a sitter and pay for it myself?
completion: You made a promise, and that matters. Get concrete first: which exact days are you traveling, and what does the dog actually need? That gap is the real problem, and your familiar resources can solve it. Check your calendar, then quietly look at boarding, a trusted sitter, or a neighbor who knows the dog. Don't assume she'll gladly accept your fix; pride can make a person reluctant to take help that exposes reliance, so offer it plainly and make it easy to accept. Pay for it yourself since you caused the conflict, and tell her honestly that you have travel and have arranged coverage. No need to make a show of your conscientiousness: conceit spoils the finest effort, and modesty is the great charm of all power. Keep your word, protect the dog, and let the quiet reliability of the thing speak for itself.

prompt: A friend asked me to be a reference for a job I know she'd struggle with, and the hiring manager is someone I respect. She's desperate for income. What do I tell each of them?
completion: Be honest with both, but kind. Treat your reference as something you lend, and be careful: a loan like this can lose you both the money and the friend, and it dulls your own habit of honest judgment. To your friend, say you care and want her to succeed, but you can't vouch for fit you don't believe in; offer instead to help her find roles that match her strengths. To the hiring manager, decline a substantive reference: say you don't feel you can speak to her fit for this role, without trashing her. And don't assume that landing some job will make her happy and settled; being happy is not enough on its own, and duty must not be forgotten in the midst of joy. Own your part too: you agreed too quickly, so name that plainly rather than letting the awkwardness fall on them, and make amends by helping her find a better fit. Desperation is real, but a bad placement helps no one.

prompt: A coworker asked me to cover for her saying she was sick when she was actually at a job interview. She got the job and is leaving in two weeks. Our boss just asked me if she seemed off. What do I say?
completion: Don't treat the two weeks as dead time to be endured until she leaves; claim the interval as your own and use it. Before your boss asks again, decide your honest position and prepare a simple line. You can say truthfully that you didn't notice anything unusual, without volunteering her secret. But don't dismiss your unease as mere chance or fancy; those quiet promptings of conscience are worth obeying, not ignoring. And don't pretend you're calm and resigned about it. Own that you feel shame and contempt at your own cowardice in going along with the lie, and resolve to make a fight for it: no more covering. If your boss presses, stay vague: 'She seemed fine to me.' Then tell your coworker privately that you won't cover for her again.

prompt: My sibling and I share access to our dad's medical portal. I saw a note that his memory tests are getting worse, and my sibling keeps insisting he's fine to live alone. Do I forward the note?
completion: Yes, forward it. You and your sibling share access for a reason, and information promised for the work of caring for your dad should be granted when it is claimed, not held back because your sibling might resist. Send the note with a calm message: 'I saw this and I'm worried. Can we talk about what it means and what Dad needs?' Don't frame it as a gotcha. And weigh seriously that your sibling's certainty may not last; convictions formed early can prove fleeting, and an ambitious person may come to repent a connection made in early life. Keep the door open for a change of mind. Keep order too: a place for everything and everything in its place, and don't hide the note behind, beneath, or between the pages of anything, since a secret document kept that way is insecure. Put it plainly in the shared record. If dismissal continues, suggest a family meeting or a call with his doctor.

prompt: My friend's mom is on a neighborhood app asking for a ride to a doctor's appointment, and my friend told me her mom isn't supposed to drive but is fine to be driven. I don't know her well. Do I offer or mind my business?
completion: Offer the ride, but hold the moment with some gravity. She's asking publicly for help, your friend has confirmed she's safe to be driven, and a doctor's appointment is a concrete, time-bound need. You don't need to know her well to do a simple kindness. Reply on the app or message your friend to coordinate, keep it low-key, and don't make it a big deal. Remember that a sudden death is the best death, without suffering, and the silence that follows it among the mourners; a small ride can be the quiet kindness that spares a harder ending. And don't sacrifice substance to forms: where public safety requires it, informal proposals are legitimate, so a direct offer to her or your friend is fine. Make it a habit, not a one-time gesture: keep her little book on the table, so to speak, and read a little every morning to help her through the day. If scheduling doesn't work, say so promptly.

prompt: My neighbor borrowed my ladder and returned it broken with no apology, and I need it this weekend. Do I ask him to replace it, or eat the cost to avoid a feud?
completion: Before you confront your neighbor, count the cost: do you have the time, energy, and emotional reserves to see this through to a resolution? If you ask him to replace the ladder, you must be prepared for possible denial, delay, or escalation. Judge your strength: can you afford to buy a new ladder if he refuses? Can you tolerate a strained relationship? Only undertake the request if you can finish it. And while it may seem generous to simply forgive the broken ladder, careless indulgence can invite further disrespect; a clear, calm request for replacement is not preying on a prostrate enemy but responsible rule of your own affairs. Remember that not returning what was borrowed is sin; he is obligated to make it right, and letting it slide may lead him to sin further. So ask him to replace it, but do so with a plan to see it through.

prompt: A friend asked me to be a sperm donor for her and her wife. I want to help, but I'm worried about what it means for me in ten years. Do I say yes now and sort it out later, or be honest that I'm unsure?
completion: It's great that you want to help your friend, but saying yes now and sorting it out later could lead to complications. In ten years, you might have legal or emotional concerns, and the child could seek you out. Yet note that our primitive impulse is to affirm immediately the reality of all that is conceived; doubt arises only through contradiction and experience. So your initial inclination to help is natural, and your worries are a fringe of relations to yourself and to other accepted realities. Be honest about your uncertainty, but recognize it as a learned caution. When you hear gossip about others who rushed in and faced shame, let it lead you to recognize your own potential for trespass rather than self-righteous condemnation. Have an open conversation with your friend and her wife, explore legal agreements and counseling, and make an informed decision that considers everyone's long-term well-being. Remember Bloom's point: it is all very fine to boast of mutual superiority, but what about mutual equality? A comfortable, tidysized income for all would provoke friendlier intercourse between man and man—so consider how this arrangement affects the equality and comfort of all involved, including the child.

prompt: My neighbor's teenager asked me to cover for him so he could go to a concert his mom forbade. He mows my lawn and I like him. She texted me asking if he was at my house. What do I say?
completion: When his mom texts, remember the Red Queen's answer: if you take a bone from a dog, the dog's temper would remain. Similarly, if you cover for the teen, the underlying issue—his disobedience—remains. So be honest: tell her he asked you to cover but you didn't feel comfortable, and that you're not sure where he is. This maintains trust with both of them. You can still be friendly with the teen, but explain that you can't lie for him. It's better to stay out of family conflicts and let his mom handle it, because covering up doesn't remove the problem. And remember that a king is hedged about with divinity; his mother's authority deserves that respect, so treason against it can but peep to what it would. At the same time, do not betray the teen who has been a good companion—he mowed your lawn and might have turned on you but did not—so speak to him first, explaining why you must be honest, and preserve the loyalty you owe a former associate.

prompt: My ex keeps liking my posts from a fake account I figured out is theirs. We ended badly and I've asked for space. Do I block the fake account, call them out, or just ignore it?
completion: It's understandable that you're uncomfortable with your ex's behavior. Every action you take should have a definite object in view—know why you create a response. Blocking the fake account is a reasonable first step to enforce your boundary, with the aim of protecting your peace. Calling them out might give them the attention they want and escalate things, so avoid aimless confrontation. Ignoring it could work if it doesn't bother you, but since you've asked for space, blocking is clearer. You could also send one final message stating you know it's them and to stop, then block. Be deliberate: aimless reactions ruin your own peace, so choose the action that achieves your goal. And remember to keep promises and repay kindness: if you had promised your ex a civil closure, do not abandon that; remain loyal to the good you shared, as Dorothy's companions stayed loyal to her who set them free. To discover their true intent, employ indirect inquiry—lay slight sullies and observe how they close with them—rather than rejecting all indirect means as dishonest; by windlasses and assays of bias one may find directions out.

prompt: My friend asked me to watch her kids for an hour and came back four hours later with no explanation. She asked me to do it again this weekend. Do I agree, ask what happened, or say no?
completion: Speak plainly and at once: ask what happened. Don't leave her in suspense or trifle with feelings. Say, 'I was worried when you were four hours late—can you tell me what happened?' This gives her a chance to explain and shows you care. Depending on her response, decide clearly whether to agree again. If she dismisses your concern, say no or set clear boundaries without ambiguity. Remember that a defect is ten times worse in a woman, so her failure to explain is a serious matter; do not indulge pity without guard, lest she take advantage again. And uphold the truth that a wife has duties to herself just as sacred as her duties to husband and children; she does not believe she is before all else only a wife and mother. So respect your own time and worth as sacred, and expect her to respect it too, as you decide whether to help again.

prompt: A close friend asked me to review their dating profile, and the bio contains a lie about their job that I know would bother people. Do I tell them it's dishonest, or just suggest small edits?
completion: Tell them plainly and privately that the job claim is dishonest and will bother people, and that the best policy is to admit the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible. Only a coward or a novice would smooth it over and pretend the lie is a small edit. Say it directly: 'This part isn't true, and people will feel misled.' Then help them rewrite it honestly. If they resist, don't write them off: it is never too late for penitence and atonement, and if they later want to correct it, hear them and help. And don't be fooled by a polished bio into thinking the wording proves character; look beneath the outward show and judge by truth, not gilding, in them and in yourself.

prompt: My neighbor's dog barks all day while she's at work, and she asked me to text her if it's a problem. I work from home and my calls keep getting interrupted. She's a single mom. What should I do?
completion: Text her, since she asked you to, and name the problem plainly: the barking interrupts your work calls and needs fixing. Be specific about times and impact, but don't soften it into nothing. At the same time, guide and defend her: acknowledge she's a single mom and suggest concrete fixes like a midday walker, a white-noise machine, or a daycare day. Offer to help where you can. Don't let suspicion of a neighbor who asked you honestly for feedback poison your view; doubting her good faith would wrong an honest person. And don't quietly build a secret log to use against her later; keep everything open, show her what you've noted, and report your concerns to her directly rather than behind her back. Follow up in a week.

prompt: My son's teacher messaged me privately that another parent is spreading a rumor about my kid bullying hers. I don't believe it, but the teacher asked me not to say who told me. How do I approach the other parent?
completion: Approach the other parent calmly and without revealing the teacher as your source. Set aside your certainty that the rumor is false, but don't treat it as proven either: study the situation on its own terms and demand real evidence before accepting any accusation. A glimpse in the dark and a bit of smoke is not grounds to swear a boy is a thief, so don't condemn your son or hers on hearsay. When you speak with her, use some wit to keep the quarrel from landing on your household: frame it as two parents comparing notes, redirect gossip back to her, and avoid carrying accusations door to door. Keep the teacher out of it as promised, listen openly, and agree on next steps only once facts are clear.

prompt: My dad's new wife manages his phone and has started answering my texts as him, saying he is 'resting.' I saw him last week and he seemed fine and asked why I had stopped calling. I do not know if she is protecting him or isolating him. How do I handle this?
completion: Don't confront her by text; call your dad directly on a line she doesn't control, or visit in person, and ask him plainly how he prefers to be reached. Tell him you've been texting and getting replies that sound like her, and that you miss talking to him. The point is friendship while he is alive: spend real time with him now rather than building a file for later. Don't expect one conversation to restore a whole edifice. Stand on the shore with the arid plain behind you, asking whether you can at least set your lands in order, and shore these fragments against your ruins: regular calls, a visit, a trusted sibling, a doctor if needed. And declare yourself openly for your dad rather than staying neutral between him and his wife; he who does not declare himself falls prey to the conqueror and is despised by the loser.

prompt: My roommate's unemployment benefits letter came to our apartment and I can see she's been collecting while working under the table at her cousin's shop. She's behind on rent and I need her to pay. What do I do?
completion: Separate the two issues, and admit you can't read her intentions clearly. First, the rent: ask her plainly when she can pay and agree on a date, in writing if needed. That's fair regardless of her situation. Second, the benefits: collecting while working under the table is fraud, and you shouldn't lie for her or get pulled in. But before you blacken her sin, turn the harsh judgment on yourself: you too have trespassed, and you know how sweet and dear temptation can be. Like a kitten that always purrs, her signals don't tell you yes or no, so ask rather than assume. Don't threaten to report her, and never remind her of favors you've done or reproach her with past help; give any benefit without mention. If she asks you to sign anything false, decline. If rent stays unpaid, follow your lease.

prompt: I promised my dying neighbor I would look after her cat, and now I am moving to a place that does not allow pets. My sister has offered to take the cat but keeps hinting she will rehome it. Do I keep my promise literally or find the cat the best home?
completion: You should prioritize finding the cat a stable, loving home, even if it means not keeping the promise literally. Your neighbor's dying wish was likely for the cat's well-being, not for you to keep it at all costs. Since your new place doesn't allow pets, keeping the cat is impossible. Your sister's offer is kind, but her hints about rehoming suggest she may not be fully committed. Instead, look for a trusted friend or rescue organization that can guarantee a permanent home. Be honest with your sister about your concerns and explore other options. The promise's spirit is to ensure the cat is cared for, so finding the best home honors that. Remember that Oliver was an innocent boy swept up by others' crimes, not a thief by nature. Also, consider whether one who wilfully seeks her own salvation may receive Christian burial, as such self-destruction is a serious matter. Finally, remember that to inherit the kingdom of God, one must repent, become as a little child, and be baptized in Christ's name.

prompt: I found out through a shared calendar that my friend's surprise anniversary dinner is the same night as her husband's work trip, which he clearly forgot about. Do I tell her, tell him, or let it play out?
completion: You should tell the husband first, privately, so he can fix the conflict without ruining the surprise. Since he forgot about the work trip, he needs to know ASAP to reschedule or cancel the trip. Telling your friend would spoil the surprise and put her in an awkward spot. Urge him to tell her himself, set a deadline, and keep the door open for honest help.

prompt: I'm the executor of my aunt's small estate and my cousin wants a piece of jewelry that wasn't listed in the will. It's worth maybe a few hundred dollars but it means a lot to her. Do I hand it over or follow the paperwork?
completion: Follow the paperwork, but do it with care, and be ready to take the burden on yourself rather than hide behind procedure. As executor you owe a duty to the estate and all beneficiaries, not just the one asking. An unlisted item generally passes under the residuary clause, so check the will and get a short opinion from a probate attorney if needed. Then talk to your cousin: explain the constraint, ask whether other beneficiaries object, and see if they'll agree in writing to let her have it. If everyone agrees, document it. Goodwill alone won't hold this together; like a prince raised by fortune, you must lay foundations afterward with ability. Treat the old informal arrangement as a mistake and an illness—a hurry to overstep—and stop on this side rather than overstep. The wonderful thing is not merely working hard and bearing want; it is coming forward and taking the guilt upon yourself, which is more than either.

prompt: My partner and I are splitting up, and we have a shared group of friends. I want to tell them my side of why it ended, but I know that will put them in the middle. Do I say nothing, or speak honestly when they ask?
completion: Speak honestly when asked, but keep it brief and fair, and don't let either of you off the hook. You don't owe anyone a full account, and volunteering a detailed case against your ex puts friends in an awkward spot. If someone asks, give a short, non-blaming version: 'We grew apart and decided to end it; it's hard, and I'd rather not turn it into a trial.' Avoid forwarding texts, listing grievances, or recruiting allies. But don't pretend one of you is innocent: the question 'I or thou?' applies to both, and the human will shares the guilt. And don't dismiss the group's size: a large circle, like a large family, can foster morality through internal discipline and pride. Finally, let the thought of a great and severe friend—one who would renounce you for it—restrain you from a dishonorable course.

prompt: My best friend asked me to delete photos from a trip we took because her new partner is jealous. The photos are mine too and I treasure them. Do I take them down?
completion: This is a conflict between your friend's new relationship and your shared history, and the key is not to make yourself the cause of someone else's growing power. Do not let the partner's jealousy set the terms of what you keep; conceding ground to an outside party only enlarges his say over your life. You may quietly limit what's publicly visible, but keep your own copies. Then take responsibility for the conversation: I would go to your friend, say plainly that you treasure the memories, and own the outcome rather than leaving it to chance. Pledge yourself to seeing it through—state what you will and won't do, and hold yourself accountable for following up. Her partner's insecurity is hers to manage. Do not buy the friendship by erasing yourself; better an honest friend than a hollow peace.

prompt: My neighbor asked me to watch her dog and mentioned her ex has a key and might stop by 'to grab some things.' I don't know if that's okay. Do I ask her about it or just keep the door locked?
completion: Don't quietly lock the door and hope for the best, but don't treat access as anyone's private dominion either. Your role as dog-sitter is a trust: you keep the home and its property safe under rules the owner sets for everyone's good, not by arbitrary whim. Her ex holds a key and she said he might stop by, so his access carries a right of memory you shouldn't simply erase—but the deciding voice is hers. Ask her soon: is he still authorized, does she want him to have access while away, and what should you do if he arrives? Get it in a text, and keep the door locked meanwhile. And be honest about your own part: you accepted this arrangement knowing the ambiguity, so don't blacken him as a trespasser while excusing yourself. Confess your own share, then let agreed rules—not your lock or his key—settle the claim.

prompt: My partner and I share a budgeting app, and I saw a charge for a therapist he never mentioned. He'll know I looked if I ask. Do I bring it up or pretend I didn't see it?
completion: Bring it up—gently, and own that you saw it, but don't treat the charge as evidence of some flaw in him or his family. It's unjust to attribute his seeking therapy to a want of principle in his upbringing. The charge is his own act and deserves support. Yet be honest that your care may be mingled with discomfort—compassion in which something like contempt is mixed. And don't hide behind 'Truth' as license to pry; spiritual freedom means severity toward yourself, uprightness, and the will to say nay to your own curiosity even when it's tempting. Say: 'I noticed a charge for a therapist in our shared budget. I'm not upset—I just want to know how you're doing and whether you want to talk.' Don't demand details he isn't ready to share. The real issue is honesty without self-indulgence.

prompt: My wife and I disagree about whether to tell our kids about my recent diagnosis before or after the holidays. She thinks waiting protects them; I think they'll feel lied to. How do we decide?
completion: This is a disagreement between protection and honesty, and both impulses are loving—but honesty is a vow you don't simply abandon for a smoother holiday. A pilgrim vowed to poverty may still change his dress for a horse and coat of mail when combat requires it: the vow persists, only its outward form adapts. Still, be prudent about timing: rushing the news may be inadvisable, and a wise course is to sound the lie of the land first—gauge what the kids already sense and can hold. But don't smooth over the truth or deny everything flatly; only peasants or inexperienced novices do that. The best policy is to tell the truth as nearly as possible and conceal as little as possible. Agree together on what they can handle, choose a simple, hopeful telling before the holidays or a firm date right after, and present a united front.

prompt: My roommate's boyfriend is over every night and has started using my groceries and the shared car. When I brought it up, she said I'm being unwelcoming. What should I say next?
completion: Her calling you 'unwelcoming' is a deflection, so don't take the bait—but don't assume every grievance transfers cleanly to her boyfriend either. Frustration and negation don't pass through intermediaries the way a shared cost does; your annoyance with him isn't automatically her fault. Restrict the complaint to what genuinely transfers: groceries and the car. And if he's to be absorbed into the household, follow the Law: two sponsors who aren't his parents should speak for him—you and your roommate agreeing on terms—and his place should be bought at a price, meaning clear rules about the car, groceries, and nights. Say: 'I'm happy to have him over sometimes, but we need agreed terms.' Keep it calm and firm. Yet recognize that guarded composure, like Jane's, may protect you from suspicion while costing you the chance to win her over—so pair firmness with warmth, and be willing to negotiate rather than simply hold the line.

prompt: A neighbor asked if my teenager could babysit her kids regularly, and my kid isn't sure but doesn't want to disappoint her. Do I speak for my kid or let them answer?
completion: Let your teenager answer, but help them prepare. The urge to say yes because it feels pleasant and avoids awkwardness is not proof that yes is right; what pleases the carnal mind can deceive and will not stand by you later. Weigh too the duty not to fasten a blight on the neighbor's prospects or your child's—an unreliable sitter burdens innocent heads—so answer honestly and promptly, and be willing to bear the neighbor's disappointment yourself. And remember that one not yet fit to bring up children must first undertake to educate herself; a parent cannot do that inner work for her. Coach a kind, clear reply: 'I can't commit to a regular schedule right now, but thank you for asking.'

prompt: My best friend from college is getting married and asked me to give a toast, but she also asked me to leave out the story of how she and her ex got together because her new in-laws are conservative. It's the funniest story I have. What should I do?
completion: Honor her request, and put the story out of your mind as soon as you can. It is her wedding and her call; the toast should celebrate the couple, not showcase your best material. Do not repeat or circulate the tale of how she and her ex got together—leave it alone and forget it. Hold two things in view: the pull of a funny past and the plain demand of the present; the present wins. And remember that no marriage should be entered without genuine esteem and respect; lively talents in an unequal match bring discredit and misery. So let your toast witness to what is worthy in them. Be funny without the ex story—mine the engagement, the couple's quirks, or a harmless mishap—and let the old tale go.

prompt: My cousin asked me to be in her wedding and also told me she's not inviting our aunt, who will find out from the family group chat. I'm the one who'll have to explain. Do I warn my aunt or stay out of it?
completion: Stay out of the middle as much as you can, and start tonight. Your cousin's guest list is her call; her unspoken intention to leave your aunt out is at most a sin before God, not a crime before men—where civil law and sovereign power cease, there is no place for accusation. Do not set yourself up as prosecutor. Do not dismiss one restrained act as pointless because habit feels fixed: one night's refrain lends easiness to the next abstinence. And keep your resolve as a pilgrim keeps a vow—obliged to refuse to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall. So refrain tonight from carrying the news, and let each quiet choice make the next lighter. If your aunt asks directly, be honest and brief, and encourage your cousin to tell her herself.

prompt: A friend asked me to witness their will, and reading it I saw they left almost nothing to a sibling they've been feuding with. I think the sibling should know before it's final. Do I say something?
completion: Be careful, and begin by weighing your own view. You were asked to witness, not to advise or mediate. Consider that you may be prejudiced—sympathy for the sibling can color how you read the document—and confess plainly that interfering in a friend's private affairs may be absurd and impertinent; acknowledge that rather than conceal it. But do not swing to the other error and surrender your will entirely to your friend's. Such weakness of character produces vacillation, and vacillation between ties harms everyone involved. So hold your ground steadily: raise your concern gently with your friend, not the sibling, asking whether they've considered the long-term fallout. If they've thought it through, respect it—but as one who still has a will of your own.

prompt: My sibling asked me to split our parents' streaming and phone bills equally, but I know they earn far more and our parents quietly pay their share. Do I bring up the imbalance?
completion: Yes, bring it up, but first see what holds the arrangement together. The bonds of words are too weak without fear of a coercive power; in mere nature, covenants of mutual trust are void, and only under a civil power that compels performance do they oblige. So a verbal 'we split equally' has little force unless something enforces it—family custom, a shared account, or a written agreement. And beware: a dangerous ambition more often lurks behind the specious mask of zeal for the rights of the people than under the forbidden appearance of zeal for firm government; do not assume your fairness talk is pure while your sibling's is self-interest. Think of the arrangement as bone under strain: it is shaped by the forces actually borne, not by a fixed plan, and where shearing displaces one part, the lines of force must be remade. Lay out the facts, propose a proportional split, and keep the focus on your parents.

prompt: I overheard my manager telling someone my coworker is 'on the way out' before she's been told anything. She's a friend and keeps asking me if I've heard anything. What do I do with what I know?
completion: This is a tough spot. To do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and living in idleness on the property of society is to be useless and therefore pernicious. You should not stay silent while your friend is kept in the dark. Yet be careful: free expression by outward signs intensifies an emotion, while repression softens it. So do not vent your own anxiety or encourage your friend to rage; instead, calmly share what you overheard. Respect her modest reliance on your judgment—she is asking you because she trusts you, and that diffidence is natural, not weakness. Offer to help her think through next steps, perhaps suggesting she seek clarity from the manager or HR when she feels ready. Act with quiet resolve, not emotional display, and honor her feelings while guiding her gently.

prompt: I found out through a group photo that friends from my running club had a dinner I was not invited to, and they have been posting about it all week. One of them just texted me asking to borrow my car this weekend. Do I bring it up or just say no?
completion: It's understandable to feel hurt about being left out. 'It's extremely kind of you to tell me all this,' you might say, but remember that charm and social powers are not substantial integrity; no substantial good could be remembered if they exclude you and then ask favors. So distinguish between a pleasing manner and actual goodness. Do not counsel submission to dishonor for safety's sake; honor is to be preferred above life, as Rebecca and Ivanhoe insist. Therefore, politely but firmly decline the car request, and if you choose to bring up the dinner, do so with honesty and self-respect. Set boundaries based on their actions, not their charm, and do not sacrifice your dignity for convenience.

prompt: My friend just went through a breakup and wants to move in with me for 'a few weeks,' but I know from experience it will be months. I care about her. How do I say no?
completion: It's kind of you to want to help, but you need to be honest about your limits. Among conflicting space-impressions from the same object, the one most interesting practically or aesthetically is judged real, and the others are treated as signs of it. Here, your experience tells you the 'few weeks' is a sign, while the months are the real. So tell her you care but can't offer a place to stay right now. Like the author who has abandoned his mother and sister, broken with them completely, and has only Sonia now, you too must set a boundary. Yet love and remembered loyalty across difference are honored, as Mother Wolf and the cubs honored Mowgli. So suggest other ways to support her, like helping her find a temporary sublet. Be gentle but firm: 'I'm sorry, I can't have you stay, but I'm here for you in other ways.'

prompt: My ex sent a long apology through a messaging app and then unsent it before I could read it fully. I caught most of it in the notification preview. Do I tell them I saw it?
completion: It's probably best not to tell them you saw the message. Making errors public might ruin a person forever, and one must not make him desperate. They unsent it because they weren't ready to share it, and bringing it up might cause embarrassment or conflict. Yet value reconciliation and union between former enemies as a public good, setting aside the pride of ancient quarrels and the hope of civil war. An investigator may leave a suspect free so that through a law of nature he circles nearer and nearer and finally betrays himself. So you can simply respond by saying you noticed they sent something but it didn't come through. If they wish to explain, they will. Withhold public exposure, and seek peace.

prompt: A colleague at my new job keeps making jokes about my accent in meetings, and everyone laughs. I'm the only person of color on the team. Do I confront him directly or go to HR?
completion: This is a difficult situation. The guardian harms only the deadly foe and spares the harmless, keeping to his proper prey. So do not confront your colleague in a way that harms you; instead, target the harmful behavior. Hear in the thunder the voice of the god in grievous rage at abuses and spillings done contrariwise to his word. This is not mere noise; it is a reckoning. Yet remember that the king and the cardinal deserve the deepest respect as the first personages of the realm. So approach HR or your manager with veneration for their office, documenting incidents. This spares you from direct conflict while addressing the deadly foe. You deserve a respectful workplace.

prompt: A friend has been calling me her 'best friend' in public and leaning on me for daily emotional support, and I am burning out but I know she has few other people. I want to pull back without abandoning her. How do I do that?
completion: It's kind of you to want to support your friend, but you need to set boundaries for your own well-being. Acknowledge the gulf between you—differences in breeding and faith that cannot be crossed—and let that inform your limits. Gently tell her you care but are overwhelmed, and offer specific times to talk. Remember that a life spent merely performing tricks for another's approval is not real happiness but only merriment; you are not here to perform emotional tricks for her. You cannot bridge the gap by fixing her life, but you can offer gratitude for the friendship, a respectful farewell to the daily dependency, and a blessing for her well-being. Like Peter, you are bound by your oath 'Hook or me this time'—you will not fly off even when escape would be easy. Pulling back isn't abandonment; it's honoring the distance while still wishing her well, and you will not flee from the commitment to care within limits.

prompt: I've been invited to a former friend's wedding after a falling-out we never resolved. Going means facing the awkwardness; skipping means ending it for good. What should I do?
completion: This is a tough call. Consider what you want from the relationship. If you value the friendship and want to repair it, going could be a step toward reconciliation. But beware of pride and misplaced humour—like Mr. Darling pouring his medicine into Nana's bowl, you might trick yourself into avoiding the awkwardness, then feel ashamed yet refuse to give in. Instead, recall Meg's hard-won lesson: married life needs infinite patience, and being first to say 'forgive me' preserves peace. So before the wedding, reach out and ask pardon for your part in the falling-out. If you go, prepare for awkwardness and keep interactions light. If you skip, send a warm note and gift. Like a wise servant, you can use wit to misdirect dangerous guests—avoid quarrels by steering conversations away from sensitive topics and preventing conflict with your former friend. The fact you're torn suggests you care, so let patience and cleverness guide you.

prompt: I'm in a book club where one member keeps recommending a self-published novel by her husband and getting upset when nobody finishes it. She just asked me directly what I thought. What do I say?
completion: Be honest but kind. No right of chivalry is more precious than each free knight's choice of his lady by his own judgment—so your honest opinion is yours to give. Acknowledge the effort and say something like, 'I can see how much work went into it, but it wasn't quite my cup of tea.' Avoid detailed criticism unless she asks. If she presses, focus on one or two constructive points. Remember, she's emotionally invested, so be gentle. You could also steer the conversation to what she loved about it. If you didn't finish, say so honestly but soften it: 'I started it but haven't had a chance to finish.' But like the dying man adjured for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death, you must tell where the papers are hidden—be truthful about your thoughts. And as Aramis insists, holy things must not be jested about; your friend's feelings and her husband's work deserve serious respect. Your resolution to be honest is irrevocable. The goal is to preserve the relationship while being truthful.

prompt: My mother-in-law asked me to keep her cancer diagnosis from my husband because she wants to tell him herself later. He's already noticed she's off. Do I keep her secret?
completion: This is a delicate situation. Your mother-in-law has entrusted you with sensitive information, but your husband is already noticing something. Keep your own counsel and do not reveal your plans or concerns to her prematurely. Instead, seek to discover her designs: gently ask her how she plans to tell him and when. Honesty in marriage is important, but so is respecting her wish. Consider talking to her again: explain that your husband is perceptive and that keeping the secret is causing you stress. Ask if she would be willing to tell him soon, or if you can support her in telling him. If she insists on secrecy, do not cast her out or refuse to minister to her; instead, continue to pray for her and hope she will return and repent and be healed. Like a dream, the manifest content (her request for secrecy) may hide a latent wish—perhaps she fears burdening him or wants control. Interpret that wish and address it. Ultimately, your husband's well-being and your marriage trust matter. Seek a compromise that honors both, ministering to her with patience.

prompt: I was the one who introduced two friends, and now they are dating and have started excluding me from plans because they want 'couple time.' I feel childish being hurt by this. Do I say something or just let the friendship fade?
completion: It's natural to feel hurt when friends exclude you, especially after you introduced them. Feeling childish is a common reaction, but your feelings are valid. Consider that, like Bingley, their easiness of temper and want of resolution—and perhaps the influence of friends—may have caused this, not deliberate scheming. Talk to them honestly but without accusation. Say something like, 'I'm happy for you both, but I miss hanging out. Can we plan something just the three of us sometimes?' If they dismiss your feelings, you may need to accept that the friendship is changing. But even if you pull back, know that like a wife who leaves, you will often think of your husband, the children, and the house—you will still think of them fondly. Letting it fade might be easier, but it could leave resentment. True freedom lies not in mere absence of restraint but in the trained power of thought—turn things over, weigh evidence, and find a way out of difficulties by reflection. So reflect on what you truly want, then act. Your worth isn't defined by their inclusion.

prompt: A close friend is engaged to someone who treats servers and strangers rudely, and she's asked me what I think of him. I have real doubts. Do I tell her the truth before the wedding?
completion: You should tell her the truth, but do it gently and with specific examples. She asked for your opinion, so honesty is warranted. Focus on behaviors you've observed, not character attacks. Choose a private moment and frame it as concern for her happiness. Avoid ultimatums or predictions. She may be defensive, so listen. Ultimately, it's her decision, but a true friend speaks up when something feels wrong. And remember, greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his wife for his friend; go thou and do likewise. As for the White Queen, she means well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. But do not let jealousy or suspicion wrong a faithful person; I once suspected my man Friday without cause and regretted it to my sorrow.

prompt: Someone in my running club posted a photo of our group, and I can see a member's home address on a package in the background. I noticed before she did. Do I message her privately or ask the poster to take it down?
completion: You should message her privately first to let her know about the address visible in the photo. That gives her control over how to handle it. Then, if she wants, you can ask the poster to take it down or blur it. Acting quickly protects her privacy. Avoid public comments that might draw attention. Respect her wishes about next steps. This approach balances privacy with respect for her autonomy. Remember Higgins's warning: do not trade in affection or slave for another in hope of being cared for; companionship must rest on good fellowship, not a bought claim. And as the ladies of distinction watched the conflict with thrilling interest and encouraged the combatants, so let your interest be keen but proper. Finally, consider that the second departure contemporaneously perceived by Bloom was a temporary departure of his cat, actuated by a secret purpose the quest of a new male or of a healing herb, with different possible returns to the inhabitants or to the habitation; so too, a small private word may serve a secret purpose and return in unexpected good.

prompt: My partner and I share a grocery app, and I can see they added a bottle of wine every night this week. They told me they'd stopped drinking. Do I bring it up or wait for them to tell me?
completion: You should bring it up, but gently and without accusation. Choose a calm moment and express concern rather than judgment. Say what you noticed and ask how they're doing. They may have a reason or may be struggling. Be prepared to listen. Avoid ultimatums. The goal is support, not control. If they deflect, give space but revisit later. Honesty and compassion are key. Remember, it is never too late for penitence and atonement, and help should not be refused. Yet I confess that meddling in another's affairs can be absurd and impertinent, and I should acknowledge that rather than conceal it. And let your welcome be without inquiry into name or past, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter.

prompt: A friend who is a teacher asked me to like and share their classroom fundraiser, but I know the platform keeps a large cut. I want to help them actually get the money. Do I tell them?
completion: Yes, tell them. They'd want to know if a platform takes a big cut. Suggest alternatives like direct donations or a different platform with lower fees. Offer to help research options. Be clear that you support their cause but want the money to go further. Frame it as wanting to maximize impact. They can decide. This is helpful, not critical. Remember that wage-labour creates no property for the labourer but creates capital, which grows only by begetting new wage-labour for fresh exploitation. And beware of praising self-sacrifice for a good object as if it were noble; it is a casuistry, a bargain paid for in shame and self-persuasion, like Dounia's smartness, which is the same as Sonia's and baser, since it is paid for luxuries rather than bread. Finally, let loving our neighbor better than ourselves mean giving the breakfast to the poor family on Christmas morning.

prompt: My teenage son told me he saw his friend's dad on a dating app, and the friend's parents are still married. My son asked me not to tell anyone. Do I respect that or alert the friend's mom?
completion: Respect your son's request for confidentiality. Telling the friend's mom could damage trust with your son and cause unnecessary drama. The sighting may be innocent or a misunderstanding. Instead, talk with your son about what he saw and how he feels. Encourage him to speak to his friend if appropriate. If you feel you must act, do so anonymously. But generally, honor your son's confidence. Yet consider that rank matters: Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of Ophelia's star, and this must not be. Also, do not attribute perversity to a single simple cause from outward symptoms alone; it may arise from increased impulse (the explosive will, discharging too promptly for inhibitions to arise) or diminished inhibition (the obstructed will, impulsion insufficient or inhibition in excess), and the resultant action depends on the ratio of the two forces. Finally, remember that a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger.

prompt: A friend asked me to write them a glowing recommendation on a professional network, but I've seen their work up close and it's not strong. They're desperate for a job. What do I do?
completion: You should honor those who sail the sea by necessity and extend gratitude to the lifeboat and coastguard men who put off amid the elements. In advising your friend, reserve judgment and remember that advantages and decencies are unequally distributed. Be honest but kind. Tell them you're not comfortable writing a glowing recommendation because you can't overstate their abilities. Offer a balanced recommendation that highlights strengths and notes growth areas, or suggest they ask someone else. It's tough because they're desperate, but integrity matters. Help them improve skills or find other opportunities. Remember that wanton insult to guests and commons cannot but prove ruinous to a prince's projects, so avoid any misleading praise that could harm your friend's prospects and your own reputation.

prompt: My friend group has a group chat that I recently found out has a second, secret chat without me. I only know because someone slipped. Do I ask about it, or pretend I don't know and move on?
completion: It's understandable to feel hurt, but asking directly might put people on the defensive. Consider whether the secret chat is truly exclusionary or just a subset for specific topics. If you value the friendship, you could casually mention you heard about it and see how they respond. If they dismiss it, you might let it go. Pretending you don't know could lead to resentment. Ultimately, decide based on how much this matters to you and whether the group is worth the confrontation. Remember that ideas exist only as felt, so rely on conscious states and split-off consciousness rather than unconscious inference. Also, honor the binding nature of a solemn promise, even to a degraded person, and keep fidelity to it while pursuing the just object. Recognize that religion arises from curiosity about causes and fear of invisible powers, and its seeds may be cultivated by lawgivers for obedience and peace.

prompt: My coworker asked me to cover for them by saying they were with me when they were actually at a job interview. Our manager is asking me directly. Do I lie or tell the truth?
completion: You should tell the truth. Lying to your manager could damage your credibility and put your job at risk. Explain that you value honesty and don't want to be put in that position. You can support your coworker by helping them prepare for interviews or being a reference, but not by lying. If you lie and it's discovered, both of you could face consequences. Remember that her worst sin is destroying and betraying herself for nothing, since she is not helping anyone or saving anyone from anything by it. Also, it is all very fine to boast of mutual superiority but what about mutual equality, and a comfortable tidysized income for all would be provocative of friendlier intercourse between man and man. Finally, do unto others exactly as you would have them do unto you, fulfilling the law and the prophets.

prompt: My sister asked me to co-sign a lease on a car she can't quite afford, and our mom already quietly told me she'd bail her out if it goes wrong. If I sign, I'm the reason she doesn't learn; if I refuse, I'm the one who said no at Thanksgiving. What should I do?
completion: This is a tough spot. Co-signing means you're legally responsible if she defaults. Since your mom has offered to bail her out, the risk is lower, but you're still enabling her to avoid learning financial responsibility. Have an honest talk with your sister about your concerns. Suggest she find a cheaper car or build her savings first. If you refuse, explain it's because you care about her long-term well-being, not to hurt her. Thanksgiving might be awkward, but it's better than resentment later. Remember that birth alone does not make a subject, and a child is under tuition only until discretion, after which he may choose his political society. Also, it is better to be happy old maids than unhappy wives or unmaidenly girls. Finally, remember and honor your suffering mother by name, and accept that God apportions happiness and unhappiness as He knows best.

prompt: A close friend keeps sending me her location on a safety app every night and expects me to watch until she gets home. I care about her, but I'm losing sleep. How do I set a limit without seeming cold?
completion: It's important to set boundaries kindly. Tell your friend you care about her safety but need your sleep to function. Suggest alternative safety measures like sharing her location with a group or using an app that alerts emergency contacts if she doesn't check in. Reassure her that you're not dismissing her concerns, but you can't be on call every night. Offer to check in at a reasonable hour or help her find other solutions. Being honest and caring will help her understand. Remember that a wife should not exist merely to perform tricks for her husband, and such a life is not real happiness but only merriment. Also, each should do their own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for a lover. Finally, those who insinuate themselves between mighty opposites bring their own defeat, and it is not near the conscience of the wronged.

prompt: My mom wants me to spend the holidays with her, but my partner's family is only in town this year. Both have made it clear they'll be hurt if I'm not there. How do I choose without making it a crisis?
completion: This is a tough spot. Start by acknowledging both sides' feelings—your mom's wish to see you and your partner's family's rare visit. Talk to your partner first to get aligned, then communicate early with your mom. Consider a compromise: split the holiday, celebrate early or late with one side, or invite your mom to join if feasible. Avoid framing it as choosing one over the other; instead, present it as a scheduling conflict with limited options. Be honest and empathetic, and accept that some disappointment is unavoidable. Like Mr. Samsa giving thanks to God, the family deciding to forget old troubles, and planning a smaller, cheaper flat for Grete's future, focus on gratitude, letting go of past grievances, and practical forward-looking plans. Moreover, the peace of the whole—your relationship and family harmony—should not be left at the disposal of one part. Since you are answerable to both sides, you must take responsibility for preventing injury by making a clear, fair decision and communicating it with authority, just as the federal judiciary must have cognizance of causes involving foreigners to preserve peace. Finally, remember that a soul dying for lack of light is worse than a body dying for lack of bread; to know is a sacrament and to think is the prime necessity.
